title: What Is Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)? A Plain Guide
content:
Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is the work of making your website easy for AI search tools to find, understand and quote. These tools include ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, and Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode. Instead of a list of ten links, they write one answer. GEO aims to get your brand named in that answer, ideally with a link.

This guide explains GEO in plain words. You will learn how AI tools pick sources, how GEO differs from SEO, what the research says, which tactics are worth your time and which are noise. It includes two worked examples, a first-week checklist and a 90-day plan. Our view is simple: GEO is built on good SEO, with a few extra habits on top.

What is generative engine optimization?

Generative engine optimization is the practice of improving your content and site so that AI systems use it when they write answers. A "generative engine" is any search tool that writes an answer instead of only listing links. The goal is not a rank. The goal is a mention, a quote or a citation inside the answer.

The term comes from a 2023 research paper by Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues from Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Princeton University, Georgia Tech and the Allen Institute for AI. It was later published at the KDD 2024 conference. The authors tested which changes to a page made an AI tool more likely to use it. They reported that the best methods raised visibility by up to 40% in their tests.

That number needs care. The tests used a research benchmark and a test setup, not your market. Treat it as a sign that content choices matter, not as a promise for your site.

You will see other names for the same work: AI search optimization, answer engine optimization (AEO), LLM optimization and "AI SEO". The names overlap. In practice they all ask the same question: when someone asks an AI tool about your topic, does it know you, trust you and quote you?

What is GEO marketing?

GEO marketing is marketing work aimed at being mentioned and cited in AI-written answers. It covers the content, the facts on your site and the mentions elsewhere that AI tools draw on. Do not confuse it with geo-targeting, which means showing ads or content by location. That is a different subject.

Why does GEO matter now?

People now ask questions in AI tools that they used to type into a search box. They ask longer, more detailed questions. They also get an answer without clicking. That changes what visibility means for a business.

Three changes make this a real business issue:

  • Answers replace lists. If an AI answer names three suppliers, the buyer may never see the ten blue links.
  • Brand mentions carry weight. A named recommendation from a tool a buyer trusts can start a shortlist.
  • Measurement is harder. Rankings tell only part of the story, so you need new checks (more on that below).

Here is what published studies show, with their limits:

  • Clicks fall when an AI summary appears. The Pew Research Center tracked the browsing of 900 US adults in March 2025. Users clicked a regular result link in 8% of visits to Google pages with an AI summary and 15% of visits to pages without one. They clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits.
  • AI summaries are common for long questions. In the same study, 18% of all Google searches produced an AI summary. That share was 8% for searches of one or two words and 53% for searches of ten words or more.
  • Ranking is no longer the whole story. Ahrefs found that about 38% of the pages cited in Google AI Overviews ranked in the top 10 for the same query in March 2026, down from about 76% in July 2025.
  • Answers vary. SparkToro and Gumshoe found less than a 1 in 100 chance that ChatGPT or Google's AI would give the same list of brands twice for the same prompt.

These studies cover Google in particular months and a set of test prompts. They do not tell you how much traffic AI tools send to your site. We found no solid public figure for that, so we do not quote one. You can test where your own brand appears today.

How do AI search tools choose their sources?

Most AI search tools follow a similar loop. Google describes two parts of it for AI Overviews and AI Mode: retrieval-augmented generation and query fan-out.

  1. Understand the question. The tool reads the prompt. It often splits one question into several smaller searches. Google calls this query fan-out. A question like "how do I fix a lawn full of weeds" can become searches for weed killers, natural methods and prevention.
  2. Retrieve pages. The tool looks up pages and passages in a search index. It can only retrieve pages it has crawled and indexed.
  3. Read and select. The model reads the passages. It keeps those that answer the question clearly and agree with other trusted sources.
  4. Write and cite. The model writes its answer from those passages and links some of them.

Two lessons follow from this loop. First, if a tool cannot reach your page, nothing else matters. Second, because of fan-out, a page that answers one small sub-question well can be picked even when it does not rank first for the main question.

There is also a second source of knowledge: what the model learned in training. You cannot change that quickly. Over time, clear facts about your brand that appear in many trusted places help here.

What is the difference between GEO and SEO?

SEO aims to rank pages in a list of results. GEO aims to be named and cited inside a written answer. The foundation is shared: a page that cannot be crawled, loads slowly or says nothing useful will fail at both.

TopicSEOGEO
GoalA high position in resultsA mention or citation in an AI answer
Main unitThe page and the keywordThe passage, the fact and the brand
What helpsRelevance, links, technical health, page experienceThe same, plus quotable answers, clear facts and mentions elsewhere
How you measureRankings, clicks, Search ConsolePrompt tests, mentions, citations, referral visits
Speed of changeWeeks to monthsLive answers can change quickly, training knowledge slowly

Google is direct about this. Its own guidance says that, from its point of view, optimizing for generative AI search is still SEO. It also says a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to appear as a supporting link, and that there are no extra technical requirements.

So do you need a separate GEO program? Usually no. You need strong SEO first, then a few habits that make your answers easy to lift and your brand easy to recognize. If your site has crawl or indexing problems, fix those before anything else. Check robots.txt first, because it is the first gate.

What does Google itself say about GEO?

Google published guidance on how its AI features work and how to appear in them. The main points are worth knowing, because they cut through a lot of hype.

  • Use normal SEO. Crawlable pages, internal links, a good page experience and helpful content are the base.
  • Make non-commodity content. Google asks for content with a point of view and first-hand experience, not a summary of what everyone already says.
  • Keep structured data honest. It should match the visible text. It is not required for AI features, and no special markup is needed.
  • Ignore some "hacks". Google says you do not need llms.txt files, special chunking, rewriting only for AI, or fake mentions to appear in its AI features.
  • Measure in Search Console. Google reports AI feature traffic in Search Console and warns about tools that claim to use internal Google metrics.

One caution. This is Google's view of Google Search. Other tools, such as ChatGPT and Perplexity, have their own crawlers and rules. Some site owners choose to publish an llms.txt file for those tools. Google says it ignores the file, so it will neither help nor hurt there. Treat it as optional, and never as a substitute for good pages.

What helps a page get quoted?

Across the research and the guides we read, the same habits appear again and again. They also fit what the Aggarwal paper tested, such as adding citations, quotations and statistics to a page.

Answer first

Put a short, direct answer under each question heading. Make the first one or two sentences make sense on their own. That is the piece a tool can lift without the rest of the page.

Be specific and name your sources

Numbers, dates and named sources give a tool something it can check. A claim such as "most buyers prefer short pages" is easy to skip. A claim with a source and a year is easier to trust. Link to the original source, not to another blog that repeats it.

Use real questions as headings

People ask AI tools full questions. Headings that match those questions make your page easier to match. Pull questions from sales calls, support emails and the "People also ask" box.

Be clear about who you are

Use one brand name everywhere. Keep an accurate About page, real author bios and consistent facts: what you do, where you work, who runs the company. Add Organization, Article, FAQ and Person markup if it matches the page. It will not force a citation, but it removes doubt.

Cover a topic in depth

A cluster of pages that answer related questions gives fan-out searches more places to land. Google warns that making many near-duplicate pages just to catch every variation is spam. Write each page because a reader needs it.

Keep pages fresh

Update facts and examples on your best pages on a schedule. Show an honest "last updated" date. Old numbers are an easy reason for a tool to prefer a competitor.

Earn mentions that are real

Third-party articles, reviews, comparisons and directories that mention you give the tool a second source to match. Look at which pages AI tools cite for your topic, then ask whether you have a real story for those publishers. Buying mentions or faking them is not worth it, and Google says it does not help.

How do you do GEO step by step?

Work in this order. Each step builds on the one before it.

  1. Check access. Make sure Googlebot and the AI crawlers you want can reach your pages. Check robots.txt, your firewall, your CDN and any bot protection. A firewall that blocks every unknown bot can block the ones you want.
  2. Check indexing. In Search Console, confirm your key pages are indexed. A page that is not indexed in Google cannot be a supporting link in its AI features.
  3. Make the text readable. Important content should be in the page text, not hidden in images or loaded only by scripts that crawlers may not run.
  4. List the questions that matter. Write 15 to 25 questions your buyers ask. Group them by stage: learning, comparing, buying.
  5. Test them. Ask each question in ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Mode. Record whether your brand is named, whether you are linked, who else is named, and which pages are cited. This is your baseline.
  6. Fix the pages that should win. Add a clear answer at the top, a named source or two, a short FAQ and an honest update date. Do this for your five most important pages first.
  7. Fill the gaps. Where the tools cite competitors or third-party pages and you have nothing, plan one useful page or one real outreach story.
  8. Clean up your brand facts. Make sure your name, services, location and leadership facts match across your site, your profiles and your listings.
  9. Measure and repeat. Run the same tests monthly, record the results, and update the pages that slip.

Worked example 1: a B2B software company

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company that sells invoice software to small accounting firms. It ranks on page two for "invoice software for accountants" and gets few leads from search.

The team lists 20 questions buyers ask, such as "what invoice software works with UK VAT" and "how do accountants bill clients on retainer". They test all 20 in four AI tools. The brand is named in 2 of 80 answers. Two competitors and a review site appear in most of them.

They find three problems. The pricing page text is inside a script and is thin. The VAT page is five years old and has no sources. Several third-party review sites list an old product name.

They fix these in order. They put pricing in plain page text. They rewrite the VAT page with an answer at the top, the tax authority's own guidance as a source and a clear update date. They ask the review sites to correct the product name. Then they publish two new pages for the retainer billing questions, written by the head of customer success, with real screenshots.

At the next monthly test they compare against the baseline. They do not expect a jump. They check whether the brand appears in more answers, whether the cited pages are theirs, and whether visits from AI tools show up in analytics. If nothing moves after three months, they look again at access, content depth and mentions, in that order.

Worked example 2: a local professional firm

Again, this is an illustration. Imagine a small law firm that handles tenant disputes in one city. Buyers ask AI tools questions such as "can my landlord keep my deposit" and "who can help with a tenant dispute in this city".

The firm tests 15 questions. For the general question, the tools quote the government's own pages and a national charity. The firm cannot beat those for that question, so it does not try. For the local question, the tools name two competitors and a directory that lists them.

The plan is narrow. The firm makes its Google Business Profile and directory listings match its site. It writes one clear page on deposit disputes in that city, with the real steps, the local court details and a note on when to call a lawyer. A partner signs it as author with a short bio. It asks the directory to add the firm.

The lesson is to pick fights you can win. A small firm will not out-rank a government site on a general question. It can be the clear local answer to a local question.

How do you measure GEO?

There is no single report for all AI tools. Use a mix of simple checks and keep them consistent.

  • Prompt tests. Run the same 15 to 25 questions every month in the same tools. Record whether you are mentioned, linked or missing, and who else appears. AI answers vary from one run to the next, so look at the trend, not one result.
  • Search Console. Google reports performance for its AI features there. Use it for the basics: indexing, queries and clicks.
  • Analytics. Look at referral visits from AI tool domains such as chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai, and at what those visitors do next.
  • Brand checks. Search for your brand and your leaders by name and read what the tools say. Note anything that is wrong and trace it to a source you can fix.
  • Business results. Track leads and the question "how did you hear about us". Ask new customers whether they used an AI tool. A short form field is enough.

Be careful with paid tracking tools. Some are useful for running prompts at scale. None can see inside Google's ranking systems, and Google warns against tools that claim to. Check any tool's advice against official guidance before you act on it.

What are the risks and limits of GEO?

GEO is a young field, and honest advice includes the limits.

  • Results are not guaranteed. No one controls what an AI tool writes. You can improve your odds, not buy a result.
  • Answers change. The same question can give different sources on different days. One good test proves little.
  • Tools differ. What helps in Google AI Mode may not help in another tool. Test in the tools your buyers use.
  • Shortcuts can backfire. Fake mentions, hidden text and mass-produced pages go against Google's spam policies and can hurt you.
  • Some answers send no clicks. A mention can still help a buyer remember you, but it is harder to track. Plan for that.
  • Research has limits. The 2023 study used a benchmark and test engines. Real results depend on your market and your competitors.

Common GEO mistakes

  • Starting with tools, not access. A tracking tool does not matter if crawlers are blocked.
  • Chasing llms.txt first. It is optional at best. Fix pages and facts first.
  • Burying the answer. A long introduction before the point makes a page harder to quote.
  • Claims without sources. Unsupported claims are easy for a tool to skip.
  • Writing for tools, not people. Google says to write for your audience. Pages that read like a keyword list help neither.
  • Inconsistent facts. Two different descriptions of your company across the web confuse people and tools.
  • One test, one conclusion. Run the same test over several months before you decide something works.
  • Ignoring SEO. If you are not indexed or you rank nowhere, GEO has little to work with.

Your first-week GEO checklist

  1. Confirm robots.txt, your firewall and your CDN allow the crawlers you want.
  2. Check that your top ten pages are indexed in Search Console.
  3. Write 15 to 25 buyer questions.
  4. Test them in four AI tools and save the answers, the cited pages and the date.
  5. Pick your five most important pages.
  6. Add a direct answer, one named source and an honest update date to each.
  7. Check that your company name, services and location read the same everywhere.
  8. Check that each article has a real author and bio.
  9. Look at your analytics for visits from AI tool domains.
  10. Set a monthly date to run the same tests again.

A 90-day GEO plan

Days 1 to 30: access and baseline

Fix crawling and indexing problems. Build the question list and run the first tests. Record the baseline. Fix facts that are wrong or out of date.

Days 31 to 60: improve and fill gaps

Rewrite your five most important pages. Add answers, sources and update dates. Write one or two new pages for questions where you are missing. Fix directory and profile details.

Days 61 to 90: earn and measure

Pitch one or two real stories to publishers that AI tools already cite for your topic. Rerun the tests. Compare against the baseline, note what moved and decide what to repeat.

A small team can do this alongside normal work. The point is a steady rhythm, not a big launch. We suggest a few pages per month rather than a burst, because quality and steady updates matter more than volume.

How Reinforce Lab approaches GEO

Reinforce Lab sells GEO and AI search services, so you should weigh this section with that in mind. Our approach follows the plan above. We start with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility, then build a 90-day plan that covers access, content, entity facts and measurement. You can read more on our generative engine optimization service page, or see how an SEO and AI search audit works.

We also build GEO into the wider system. Search, content and automation work best when they are planned together, which is what we mean by an AI Growth System.

Final thoughts

GEO is a new name for a familiar job: be clear, be useful, be easy to find and be easy to trust. Google says that optimizing for its AI features is still SEO. The extra work is in making answers quotable, keeping facts consistent and checking how you appear in AI tools. Start with access, test a set of real buyer questions and improve a few pages at a time. If you want a hand with the baseline, get your free diagnostic.

The 2023 GEO study reported up to 40% higher visibility in its tests, but real results depend on your market.

Is GEO the same as SEO? | They overlap a lot. SEO aims to rank pages in a results list. GEO aims to be named or cited inside a written answer. Google says optimizing for its AI features is still SEO, so strong SEO is the base for GEO.
Does GEO work? | It can help, but no one can guarantee a result. A 2023 study reported up to 40% higher visibility from some methods in its tests. Results in your market depend on your competitors, your content and the tool.
How do AI tools choose which sources to cite? | They turn a question into searches, retrieve pages from a search index, read the passages and keep those that answer clearly and agree with other trusted sources. Pages that cannot be crawled or indexed cannot be retrieved.
Do I need an llms.txt file? | Google says it does not use llms.txt files and that they neither help nor hurt in Google Search. Some other services may read them. Treat the file as optional and fix your pages and facts first.
Does structured data help GEO? | Google says structured data is not required for its AI features and no special markup is needed. It still helps with rich results and removes doubt about who you are, so keep it accurate and matched to the visible text.
How do I measure GEO? | Run the same 15 to 25 buyer questions each month in several AI tools and record mentions, links and cited pages. Add Search Console data, referral visits from AI tool domains and a lead source question on your forms.

What is GEO marketing? | Marketing work that helps AI tools mention and cite your brand. It is about generative engine optimization, not about targeting people by location.

title: GEO vs SEO: What Changes and What Stays the Same
content:
GEO and SEO are two ways to be found, and they overlap more than most articles admit. SEO aims to rank your pages in a list of search results. GEO, or generative engine optimization, aims to get your brand named or cited inside an answer that an AI tool writes. Most of the work that makes a page rank also makes it easier for an AI tool to quote. What changes is where you appear, what you measure and how much of your visibility depends on other websites.

This guide compares the two in plain terms. It shows what changes, what stays the same, what the data says about ranking and AI citations, and how to split your time. It includes two worked examples, a decision table, a measurement plan and a 90-day plan. If you need the basics first, read our guide to what generative engine optimization is.

What is the difference between GEO and SEO?

SEO is the practice of improving your site so it ranks in search engines such as Google and Bing and earns clicks. GEO is the practice of improving your content and brand so AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Mode mention or cite you in their written answers. SEO competes for a position in a list. GEO competes for a place in the paragraph.

TopicSEOGEO
GoalRank and earn clicksBe named or cited in an AI answer
Where you appearLinks on a results pageInside an AI written answer
Unit of competitionThe page and the keywordThe passage, the fact and the brand
Where mentions come fromMostly your own pagesOften other sites that talk about you
Main measuresRankings, clicks, conversionsMentions, citations, share of voice, AI referral visits
FeedbackClicks show in analyticsA mention may send no click at all
FoundationCrawlable, fast, useful pagesThe same, plus clear facts and corroboration

That table is a simplification. It matches the comparisons published by Ahrefs and Semrush, and it matches what Google says about its own AI features. The last row is the important one. The foundation is shared.

What stays the same?

A lot stays the same. Google states that the technical requirements for appearing in its AI Overviews and AI Mode are the same as for Google Search. A page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. There are no extra technical requirements. Google also says that the SEO basics still apply: allow crawling, link pages together, give people a good page experience, keep important content in text and keep structured data matched to the visible page.

These parts do not change:

  • Access. If your page is blocked or not indexed, neither a ranking nor an AI citation is likely.
  • Useful content. A page that answers a real question well helps in both.
  • Search intent. People still want a clear answer to a clear need, whether they type it into a search box or ask it in a chat.
  • Trust. Real authors, honest facts and a reputation outside your own site help in both.
  • A working site. Slow pages, broken pages and content hidden behind scripts make both jobs harder.

This is why we do not sell GEO as a replacement for SEO. If your site has crawl, indexing or content problems, fix those first. Our search engine optimization service starts there for the same reason.

What changes?

Five things change in practice.

1. The result is a mention, not a position

In SEO you can see "position 3". In an AI answer there is no position 3. You are named, cited or missing. A link may appear as a small icon, a side panel or a card at the bottom of the answer.

2. The journey may end without a click

The Pew Research Center studied the browsing of 900 US adults in March 2025. When a Google search page showed an AI summary, people clicked a regular result link in 8% of visits. When there was no summary, they clicked in 15% of visits. They clicked a link inside the AI summary in only 1% of visits. They also ended their browsing session more often on pages with a summary: 26% of the time, against 16%.

These figures describe Google AI Overviews in one month for one group of US adults. They do not describe ChatGPT or other tools, and they do not describe your site. They do show why a mention can matter even when it sends no click.

3. The scoreboard is different

For SEO you track rankings, clicks and conversions. For GEO you track how often your brand is named and cited, which pages are cited and who else appears. Because answers vary from run to run, you read the trend, not a single result.

4. Other sites matter more

AI tools often draw on third-party pages: reviews, "best of" lists, news and forums. Ahrefs reported that branded web mentions showed the strongest link with brand visibility in AI Overviews, with a correlation of 0.664 in its data. A correlation is not proof that mentions cause visibility, but it points to why PR and reviews matter more in GEO than in classic SEO.

5. Questions are longer

Pew found that only 8% of one or two word searches produced an AI summary, while 53% of searches with ten words or more did. Searches that began with a question word such as who, what, when or why produced one 60% of the time. People use AI tools for longer, more detailed questions, so pages that answer specific questions have an edge.

Do you still need to rank in Google to be cited by AI?

Ranking helps, but it is no longer enough on its own, and the numbers have moved quickly. Here is what we could verify from the sources themselves.

  • July 2025: Ahrefs found that about 76% of pages cited in Google AI Overviews also ranked in the top 10 for the same query. That study looked at 1.9 million citations.
  • March 2026: Ahrefs repeated the study with 863,000 keyword results and 4 million AI Overview URLs. About 38% of cited URLs ranked in the top 10 when it counted every block on the page. When it counted blue links only, 37.1% were in the top 10, 26.2% ranked 11 to 100 and 36.7% did not rank in the top 100.
  • AI assistants: In an earlier Ahrefs study, an average of about 12% of citations from AI assistants also ranked in Google's top 10 for the original prompt. Perplexity was the outlier, with nearly one in three.

Ahrefs suggests that fan-out explains part of the drop. The tool splits a question into related searches and cites pages that show up for those sub-questions, even when they do not rank for the original query. Google confirms that AI Overviews and AI Mode may use query fan-out. Treat Ahrefs' explanation as an informed guess, because Google does not publish the fan-out queries.

You may see other numbers online, such as claims that overlap fell below 20%. We only quote studies we read at the source. Numbers differ by method, tool and date, so avoid building a plan on one percentage.

The practical reading is simple. Ranking for your main keyword gives you a better chance, but a page that ranks nowhere can still be cited, and a page that ranks first can be skipped. This is why topic coverage matters. A set of pages that answer the related questions gives fan-out more places to find you.

Is GEO the same as AEO and LLM optimization?

The names overlap, and people use them in different ways. Answer engine optimization (AEO) usually means writing short, direct answers that can be shown as a featured snippet, a voice answer or an AI summary. LLM optimization and "AI SEO" usually mean the same goal as GEO: being used by large language models when they write answers. Ahrefs describes GEO as also known as AEO or LLMO.

Google makes a point about these labels. Its guidance says that "AEO" and "GEO" are terms used for work aimed at AI search, and that from its view, optimizing for generative AI search is still SEO. It also advises caution with third-party "AEO" or "GEO" advice and services. That is fair advice. Ask any provider what exactly they will change, how they will measure it and which of their claims you can check yourself.

For your own planning, you do not need to settle the naming. Pick the work that fits your buyers: clear answers, reliable facts, strong pages, real mentions elsewhere and honest measurement.

How should the content differ for SEO and GEO?

Good content for one is mostly good content for the other. A few habits matter more when you want an AI tool to quote you.

  • Lead with the answer. Put a direct answer in the first one or two sentences under each question heading. A tool can lift that piece without the rest of the page.
  • Use specific facts. Add numbers, dates and named sources. A claim with a source and a year is easier to trust than a general statement.
  • Cover related questions. A cluster of pages that answer the follow-up questions gives fan-out more places to find you. Write each page because a reader needs it, not to catch every wording.
  • Show who wrote it. Use a real author, a short bio and a clear update date.
  • Add what only you know. Google asks for content with a unique point of view and first-hand experience. Your own data, your own process and your own results are the parts nobody else can copy.

None of these habits hurt your rankings. That is the main reason to run both together.

What does GEO SEO mean?

People who search "GEO SEO" usually want to know how the two fit together. In practice you do both: SEO keeps your pages findable and trusted, and GEO work makes sure AI tools can quote and name you. The base is the same, so most teams treat GEO as an extra layer on their SEO and not a separate project. "GEO" here means generative engine optimization, not location targeting.

Should you focus on SEO or GEO?

For most businesses the answer is SEO first, then GEO on top. SEO is the established channel and the base that AI tools draw on. GEO adds habits for AI answers and a new way to measure. The balance depends on how your buyers search.

Your situationLean towardWhy
Buyers search "near me", "buy" or "pricing"SEO and local SEOThese searches still send people to pages and maps
Buyers compare options or ask "best X for Y"GEO and PR as well as SEOAI answers often list and compare options
Your pages are not indexed or load badlySEO fixes firstNeither channel works without access
Competitors are named in AI answers and you are notGEO nowThe gap is visible and you can measure it
You sell in a regulated fieldBoth, with reviewAccuracy and approvals matter in AI answers too

Should you hire separate teams? In most cases no. The work shares one technical and editorial base, so splitting it can create two sets of pages that compete. You do need a GEO measurement method on top of your normal SEO tools.

Worked example 1: a page that ranks but is not cited

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company that sells payroll software for small shops. Its page "payroll software for small business" ranks fourth on Google. The team tests 20 buyer questions in four AI tools. The brand is named in 3 of 80 answers, and the ranking page is cited in none.

They compare their page with the pages that are cited. The cited pages have a short answer in the first lines, a clear price range with a date and a named source for tax rules. They also see that two review sites and a news article are cited often, and that none of them mention the company.

The fixes are plain. The team adds a short answer at the top of the page, adds the price range with an update date, and links the tax authority's guidance as a source. They write two new pages for the related questions that came up: "how to run payroll for part-time staff" and "what payroll records to keep". They also ask the two review sites to review the product.

Their SEO work stays in place. They do not rewrite the page for AI tools. They watch the trend in monthly tests, and they check Search Console for the ranking page. If the ranking falls after the changes, they roll the edit back, because a lost ranking costs more than a missed citation.

Worked example 2: a local service where SEO leads

Again, this is an illustration. Imagine a plumbing company that serves one city. Most of its leads come from searches such as "emergency plumber near me" and from the map pack. The owner asks whether to spend the budget on GEO.

The team tests 15 questions in AI tools. For emergency searches, the tools often show a map list or name a few firms from directories. For general advice questions such as "why is my water heater leaking", the tools quote guides from larger sites, and the company cannot win those.

The plan puts most of the work into local SEO. It checks the Google Business Profile, fixes name, address and phone details across directories, and gathers real reviews. A small share goes to GEO. The owner writes one clear page on what to do when a water heater leaks, with real steps and a note on when to call a plumber, and signs it with a short bio.

The lesson is to match the effort to the channel where buyers act. For a local emergency service, rankings and maps drive most of the calls, so SEO leads and GEO plays a smaller part.

How do you measure both?

Run one report with two sections.

SEO section

  • Rankings for your target terms
  • Organic clicks and conversions from Search Console and analytics
  • Indexed pages and technical health

GEO section

  • Prompt tests. Write 15 to 25 real buyer questions. Run them each month in the same AI tools. Record whether you are named, whether you are linked, which pages are cited and which competitors appear.
  • Mention share. The share of answers that name your brand.
  • Citation share. The share of answers that cite your domain.
  • AI referral visits. In analytics, filter visits from AI tool domains such as chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai. Check your own data to see which domains actually appear.
  • Brand accuracy. Note when an answer gets a fact about you wrong and trace the source.

Be careful with early results. Ahrefs reported that AI search visitors on its own site were a tiny share of traffic yet a large share of signups. That is one company. Another study it cites found that not every site sees that lift. Measure your own site before you assume AI visitors convert better.

There is also no public "prompt volume" for AI tools. Search Engine Land notes that ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity do not share what users ask, so you cannot size a topic the way you can with keyword tools. Use your sales calls and support emails to find the real questions.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Treating GEO as a replacement. SEO is the base. Dropping it can remove your chance of being retrieved at all.
  • Using one study as proof. Citation overlap numbers changed sharply within a year. Plan on principles, not one percentage.
  • Splitting the work in two. Separate teams can publish pages that compete with each other.
  • Chasing special files. Google says it does not use llms.txt files and that special markup is not needed. Fix pages and facts first.
  • Ignoring other sites. If AI tools cite review sites and lists, your own pages are only part of the picture.
  • Testing once. AI answers change. One test tells you little.
  • Writing for tools, not people. Google asks for content with a real point of view and first-hand experience. Pages built only to catch every variation of a question can break its spam policy.

A 90-day plan to run both

Days 1 to 30: base and baseline

Check crawling and indexing. Fix technical problems. Write your list of buyer questions. Run the first prompt tests and record rankings, clicks and AI mentions side by side.

Days 31 to 60: improve your best pages

Pick your five most important pages. Add a direct answer, named sources and an honest update date. Write one or two pages for questions where AI tools cite others and not you. Check that your company facts match across your site, profiles and listings.

Days 61 to 90: earn mentions and review

Find the review sites, lists and news pages that AI tools already cite for your topic. Pitch one or two where you have a real story or real data. Run the tests again, compare with the baseline and decide what to repeat. Keep the pace steady, with a few pages a month rather than a burst.

How Reinforce Lab approaches it

Reinforce Lab sells both SEO and GEO services, so weigh this section with that in mind. We treat them as one program. We start with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility, then build a 90-day plan. You can read about our generative engine optimization service and our SEO and AI search audit.

Final thoughts

GEO and SEO are not rivals. They share a foundation, and GEO adds a few habits and a new scoreboard. Start with access and useful pages, test real buyer questions in AI tools, and fix the pages that should be winning. Do not rely on one statistic, because the numbers in this field move fast. If you want help with the baseline, get your free diagnostic.

title: AEO vs SEO: What Answer Engine Optimization Is and What Changes
content:
Answer engine optimization, or AEO, is the work of getting your brand and your pages used as the answer when someone asks a question. SEO aims to rank your pages in a list of results. AEO aims to be the source that a search tool, a voice assistant or an AI chatbot quotes, names or links when it gives a direct answer. The two share one foundation. AEO adds a focus on short, clear answers, on facts that other sources agree with, and on being mentioned across the web.

This guide explains AEO against SEO in plain words. You will see what each one is, what stays the same, what AEO adds, how AEO differs from GEO, and what to do about schema, featured snippets and voice. It has two worked examples, a step-by-step plan, a measurement method and a 90-day timeline. Google's own view comes first, because it shapes everything else: for Google Search, optimizing for AI answers is still SEO.

What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?

Answer engine optimization is the practice of making your content visible and useful to systems that give direct answers. Those systems include Google's featured snippets and AI Overviews, voice assistants, and chat tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Claude. Ahrefs describes AEO as being mentioned and cited directly in answers, rather than only ranking pages. It also calls AEO a specialized subset of SEO, not a replacement.

An "answer engine" is any tool that responds to a question with an answer instead of a list of links. The idea is not new. Featured snippets, the "People also ask" box and voice assistants have given direct answers for years. What changed is the scale. AI tools now write full answers, and they often draw on several pages at once.

Two terms you will see next to AEO are GEO and LLM optimization. We use them like this:

  • AEO is the broad idea of being the answer, including snippets, voice and AI tools.
  • GEO (generative engine optimization) focuses on being cited in answers that AI tools write. Read our guide to what generative engine optimization is.
  • LLM optimization focuses on how large language models use and describe your brand.

In practice the work overlaps almost completely. Pick one name for your plan and move on to the work.

What is the difference between AEO and SEO?

SEO is about ranking pages and earning clicks. AEO is about being the answer, whether or not anyone clicks. SEO treats the page as the unit. AEO treats a passage, a fact or your brand as the unit.

TopicSEOAEO
GoalRank pages and earn clicksBe the quoted, named or cited answer
Where you appearLinks on a results pageSnippets, AI answers, voice answers
Content shapeComplete pages that cover a topicClear answers inside those pages
QueriesShort keywords, including local and buying searchesQuestions and longer, more specific prompts
SignalsLinks, relevance, technical health, page experienceThe same, plus clear facts, entity clarity and mentions elsewhere
MeasuresRankings, clicks, conversionsMentions, citations, share of voice, accuracy
Click behaviorPeople visit the pagePeople may get the answer without visiting

This matches the comparisons from Ahrefs and Semrush. It also matches Google's position that the foundation is the same. For the wider comparison with GEO, see our post on GEO vs SEO.

Answer engine optimization vs traditional SEO: the short version

Traditional SEO aims to rank a page in a list of results so people click it. Answer engine optimization aims to get your answer, and your name, inside the response that an AI tool or a search answer box writes. People also write it as "SEO vs AEO," "AEO versus SEO" or "answer engine optimization vs SEO." They mean the same comparison.

The two are not rivals. A page that is hard to find, slow or thin rarely gets used as an answer. So most teams do SEO first and add AEO habits on top: a direct answer near the top, questions as headings, named sources and clear facts.

SEO vs GEO vs AEO: how do the three terms differ?

People use three labels, and they overlap. There is no official standard for AEO or GEO, so read every definition with care. This is the plain version we use.

TermGoalWhere you appearMain signals
SEOEarn rankings and clicksRegular search resultsCrawlable pages, relevance, links, page experience
AEOBe the short, direct answerFeatured snippets, voice answers, AI answersClear answers, structure, trusted sources
GEOBe cited or named in generated answersChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI OverviewsConsistent facts, citations, clear entities

One good page can serve all three. It opens with a direct answer, explains the detail, shows proof and links to related pages. For the GEO side, read our guides to GEO vs SEO and generative engine optimization.

Which should you do first?

Start with SEO basics. If a page cannot be crawled, indexed and trusted, neither AEO nor GEO can help it. Then rewrite your top pages so the answer comes first, add proof, and keep your facts the same across your site and profiles. Measure what changes before you add more.

What stays the same?

Google says that to appear as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, a page must be indexed and eligible to show in Google Search with a snippet. It adds that there are no extra technical requirements. The same SEO basics apply: allow crawling, link pages together, give people a good page experience, keep important content in text and keep structured data matched to the visible page.

  • Access. A blocked or unindexed page cannot rank and cannot be retrieved for an answer.
  • Useful content. A page that answers a real need well helps in both.
  • Search intent. Whether someone types a keyword or asks a question, you still need to match what they want.
  • Trust. Real authors, honest facts and a reputation beyond your site help in both.
  • A working site. Slow or broken pages hurt both.

So the answer to "do I need AEO if I already do SEO?" is that good SEO gets you most of the way. AEO is the layer that checks whether your answers are clear and quotable, and whether other sources agree with you.

What does AEO add on top of SEO?

Five habits matter most.

1. Answer first

Put a direct answer in the first one or two sentences under each question heading. Write it so it makes sense out of context. A snippet, an AI tool or a voice assistant can then use it without the rest of the page. Ahrefs reports that 44.2% of the citations it studied came from the first 30% of a page. That figure comes from Ahrefs' own data, so treat it as a pointer, not a law. The advice is simple and costs nothing: do not bury your answer.

2. Questions as headings

Headings that match how people ask make a page easier to match. Take the questions from sales calls, support emails and the "People also ask" box. Use the wording your buyers use.

3. Specific, sourced facts

Numbers, dates and named sources give a tool something it can check. A claim with a source and a year is easier to trust than a general one.

4. Clear entities

An entity is a clearly identified thing, such as your company, a product or a person. Use one brand name, and keep your services, location and leadership facts the same on your site, your profiles and your listings. If the facts conflict, a tool may leave you out or describe you wrongly.

5. Mentions beyond your site

Answer tools do not only read your pages. They also weigh what the wider web says about you. Reviews, lists, news pages and directories that mention you give a tool a second source. Ahrefs says that most brand mentions in AI answers come from third-party sites. Earn these through real stories and real data. Google says seeking fake mentions is not helpful.

Do you still need to rank to be the answer?

Ranking helps, but it is no longer the only way in. Ahrefs found that about 76% of pages cited in Google AI Overviews also ranked in the top 10 in July 2025, and about 38% in March 2026. It also found that, on average, about 12% of citations from AI assistants ranked in Google's top 10 for the original prompt. These figures come from Ahrefs' own studies and cover different tools and dates, so use them as a direction and not as a target.

The cause is probably query fan-out. A tool splits one question into several related searches, and a page that answers one of those sub-questions can be cited even if it does not rank for the main question. Google confirms that AI Overviews and AI Mode may use query fan-out. We cover the numbers in more detail in our GEO vs SEO guide.

The lesson for AEO is to cover a topic in full. A set of pages that answer the related questions gives these searches more places to find you.

What about schema, FAQ markup and featured snippets?

FAQ markup

Many older AEO guides tell you to add FAQ schema to win snippets. Google changed this. Its documentation updates list the FAQ rich result as deprecated: it stopped appearing in Google Search from 7 May 2026. You can still write FAQ sections for your readers, and a clear question and answer pair is still easy for a tool to quote. But do not expect a special FAQ result from Google.

Structured data in general

Google says structured data is not required for its AI features and that no special markup is needed. It still recommends using it as part of SEO, because it helps with eligibility for rich results. Keep the markup honest and matched to the text on the page.

Featured snippets

A featured snippet is a box that shows the answer text first, above the usual results. Google decides which pages appear there, and clicking one takes the reader to the matching section of the page. You cannot buy the spot. You can write a clear, direct answer under a heading that matches the question, and then see whether Google uses it.

Voice answers

Voice assistants read out short answers. The same habits help: a short, plain answer near the top, a clear question heading and accurate business details. If you are a local business, keep your Google Business Profile and listings correct.

llms.txt and "chunking"

Google says it does not use llms.txt files and that there is no need to break content into tiny chunks for AI. Ahrefs likewise tells readers to skip llms.txt. If you want the file for other services, it is harmless, but it is not a priority.

Worked example 1: an industrial supplier

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company that sells stainless steel fasteners to manufacturers. Its product pages rank well. Buyers also ask detailed questions, such as "which stainless grade resists salt spray best" and "what is the difference between A2 and A4 bolts".

The team tests 18 of these questions in four AI tools and in Google. For most of them, the answers name competitors, a standards body and two trade sites. The supplier is named in 2 of 72 answers.

The gap is clear. The product pages list sizes and prices but do not answer the technical questions. The team plans one page for each question that buyers raise. Each page opens with a two-sentence answer, adds a short table of grades with the standard named as the source, and ends with a note on when to ask an engineer. The head of engineering signs each page as author.

They keep the product pages as they are. They also check that the company name, address and product range read the same on the website, the trade directory and the profile pages. At the monthly test they compare against the baseline. They watch for more named mentions, for cited pages that are theirs and for visits from AI tool domains in analytics.

Worked example 2: a software help center

This is another illustration. Imagine a small company that makes scheduling software. Its help center has hundreds of articles. Customers and prospects ask AI tools "how do I set up recurring shifts in this tool" and "does this tool work with payroll software".

In tests, the AI tools give a mix of answers, some of them out of date. One tool describes a feature that was removed a year ago. The team traces it to an old article that still ranks and to a third-party review that was never updated.

The fixes are specific. The team updates the old article and adds a clear date. It rewrites the setup article so the first lines state the steps in order. It adds a short "what changed" note where features were removed. It also asks the review site to correct its page and sends the reviewer the updated feature list.

The lesson is that AEO includes accuracy. If tools describe your product wrongly, the fix is often to update your own pages and the third-party pages they rely on.

How do you do AEO step by step?

  1. Check access. Make sure Googlebot and the AI crawlers you want can reach your pages. Check robots.txt, your firewall and your CDN, which can block bots by default.
  2. Check indexing. In Search Console, confirm your key pages are indexed and eligible to show with a snippet.
  3. List the questions. Write 15 to 25 questions your buyers ask. Include "best X for Y" questions, brand questions and technical questions.
  4. Test them. Ask each question in Google, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. Record whether you are named, whether you are linked, which pages are cited and who else appears.
  5. Fix wrong facts. Where an answer is wrong, trace the source. Update your own page, or the third-party page, or both.
  6. Rewrite the key pages. Add a direct answer at the top, question headings, a named source or two and an honest update date.
  7. Fill the gaps. Where answers cite others and you have no page, write one useful page. Where a competitor is named in a list and you are not, plan one real story to pitch.
  8. Clean up your entity facts. Make your name, services, location and leaders read the same everywhere.
  9. Measure and repeat. Run the same tests every month and record the trend.

How do you measure AEO?

Use one report with two parts, SEO and AEO.

  • Prompt tests. Run the same 15 to 25 questions monthly in the same tools. Record mentions, links, cited pages and competitors. AI answers change from run to run, so read the trend.
  • Mention share and citation share. The share of answers that name your brand, and the share that cite your domain.
  • Brand accuracy. The share of answers about you that get the facts right.
  • AI referral visits. In analytics, filter visits from AI tool domains such as chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai. Check your own data to see which domains appear.
  • Search Console. Google reports AI feature traffic there, together with the rest of your search data.
  • Business results. Add a "how did you hear about us" field to forms.

Be careful with paid tools. They can help you run prompts at scale, but none can see inside Google's systems, and Google warns about tools that claim to. There is also no public prompt volume for AI tools, so you cannot size a topic the way you can with keyword tools. Use your own sales and support questions.

What are the common AEO mistakes?

  • Trusting old advice. Some guides, including recent ones, still promise FAQ-based wins. Check the date and check Google's documentation.
  • Using unsourced statistics. Many AEO pages quote exact multipliers with no source. Quote only what you can trace to a study.
  • Rewriting everything for tools. Google says you do not need to write in a special way for AI. Write for your readers.
  • Making thin pages for every variation. Google warns that doing this mainly to influence AI answers can break its spam policy.
  • Ignoring SEO. If your pages are not indexed, AEO has nothing to work with.
  • Not checking accuracy. A wrong answer about your product can cost more than a missed mention.
  • Testing once. Answers vary. One test proves little.

A 90-day AEO plan

Days 1 to 30: access and baseline

Fix crawling and indexing problems. Write your question list. Run the first tests in four tools. Record the baseline and list every wrong fact you find.

Days 31 to 60: fix and rewrite

Correct wrong facts on your own pages and on key third-party pages. Rewrite your five most important pages with direct answers, question headings, sources and update dates. Write one or two pages for questions where you are missing.

Days 61 to 90: earn and review

Pitch one or two real stories to sites that AI tools already cite for your topic. Rerun the tests. Compare against the baseline. Decide which fixes to repeat. Keep a steady pace of a few pages a month, because quality and updates matter more than volume.

How Reinforce Lab approaches AEO

Reinforce Lab sells AI search services, so weigh this section with that in mind. We treat AEO as part of one program with SEO. We start with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility, then build a 90-day plan. You can read about our AI search optimization service and our SEO and AI search audit.

Final thoughts

AEO is SEO with a sharper focus on being the answer. Start with access and useful pages, write clear answers, keep your facts the same everywhere and check how tools describe you. Skip the old tricks, such as FAQ rich results, and do not trust statistics you cannot trace. If you want help with the baseline, get your free diagnostic.

rl_fields.rl_answer: Answer engine optimization (AEO) is getting your brand and pages used as the answer in snippets, voice answers and AI tools. It builds on SEO: Google says AI features have no extra technical requirements. AEO adds answer-first writing, question headings, sourced facts, consistent brand facts and mentions on other sites, and it is measured with monthly prompt tests, not rankings alone.

Google says AI features need no extra technical requirements, so access and indexing come first.
Google's FAQ rich result stopped appearing on 7 May 2026, so do not plan around FAQ schema wins.
Lead each section with a direct answer, use question headings and name your sources.

Test 15 to 25 buyer questions in several tools each month and track mentions, citations and accuracy.
rl_fields.rl_faqs:
What is answer engine optimization (AEO)? | AEO is the practice of making your content and brand visible and useful to systems that give direct answers, such as Google snippets and AI Overviews, voice assistants and AI chat tools, so you are quoted, named or cited.
What is the difference between AEO and SEO? | SEO ranks pages and earns clicks. AEO aims to be the quoted, named or cited answer, whether or not anyone clicks. They share a foundation of crawlable, useful, trusted pages.
Do I need AEO if I already do SEO? | Good SEO gets you most of the way, since Google says AI features have no extra technical requirements. AEO adds a check that your answers are clear and quotable, your facts are consistent and other sources mention you.
Is AEO the same as GEO? | The names overlap. AEO is the broad idea of being the answer, including snippets and voice. GEO focuses on being cited in answers that AI tools write. The work is almost the same.
Does ranking on Google get you cited by AI? | Ranking helps but is not required. Ahrefs found about 38% of pages cited in Google AI Overviews ranked in the top 10 in March 2026, down from about 76% in July 2025, and about 12% of AI assistant citations ranked in Google's top 10.
Should I add FAQ schema for AEO? | Google's FAQ rich result stopped appearing in Google Search on 7 May 2026, and structured data is not required for its AI features. FAQ sections are still useful for readers, and clear question and answer pairs are easy to quote.
Do I need llms.txt for AEO? | Google says it does not use llms.txt files and Ahrefs advises skipping them. Some other services may read them. Fix your pages, access and brand facts first.
How do I measure AEO? | Run the same 15 to 25 buyer questions each month in several tools and record mentions, links, cited pages, accuracy and competitors. Add Search Console data, referral visits from AI tool domains and a lead source question.
What content works best for AEO? | Pages with a direct answer at the top, question headings, specific sourced facts, a clear author and an honest update date. Original data and first-hand experience help, as Google asks for non-commodity content.
Does AEO reduce website traffic? | AI answers can reduce clicks. Pew found Google users clicked a result link in 8% of visits with an AI summary against 15% without one. A mention can still build awareness, so track visits and brand measures together.
What is the difference between AEO and GEO? | AEO aims to make your page the direct answer to a question. GEO aims to get your brand cited or named in answers that AI tools generate. The two overlap, and no official standard separates them.
Do I need both AEO and SEO? | Yes. SEO gets your pages found, crawled and trusted. AEO shapes those pages so an answer can be taken from them. AEO built on weak SEO rarely works.
Can you optimize one page for both SEO and AEO? | Yes. Open with a direct answer, then give detail, proof and links. That serves readers, search results and answer tools at the same time.
Does AEO replace SEO? | No. AEO builds on SEO. Answer engines still need pages they can find, read and trust.
What is the difference between SEO and AEO? | SEO helps a page rank in a list of results. AEO helps your answer and your brand appear inside the written answer an AI tool or answer box gives. Most of the work is shared: useful pages, clear structure and trust. AEO adds direct answers, question headings and named, sourced facts.
Is answer engine optimization different from traditional SEO? | Yes, in the goal. Traditional SEO aims at a ranking position and a click. Answer engine optimization aims at being quoted or named in an answer. The base work, such as crawlable pages and helpful content, is the same.
What is the difference between AEO, GEO and SEO? | SEO targets ranked results. AEO targets direct answers in answer boxes and AI replies. GEO targets mentions and citations in generative AI tools. In practice the three share most of their tasks, and the labels overlap.
Is FAQ schema still useful for SEO and AEO? | Not for a special Google result. Google lists the FAQ rich result as deprecated and says it stopped appearing in Search on 7 May 2026. You can still write clear question and answer sections for readers, because they are easy to quote.
Do you need structured data for AI search? | Google says structured data is not required for its AI features and that no special markup is needed. It still recommends using it for rich result eligibility. Keep it honest and matched to the page text.
Is AI SEO different from traditional SEO? | The goal differs. Traditional SEO aims at a ranking and a click. AI SEO aims at being named or cited in an AI answer. The base work, such as crawlable, helpful pages, is the same.
What is the difference between generative engine optimization and SEO? | Generative engine optimization aims at mentions and citations in AI-written answers. SEO aims at ranked results. Most of the tasks overlap.
