title: AI Brand Visibility: How to Check If AI Tools Mention Your Brand
content:
AI brand visibility is how often AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Mode name, describe or link to your brand when people ask questions about your market. You can get a first reading in about 30 minutes with a spreadsheet and three browser tabs. This guide gives you the test, the scoring, two worked examples and a plan to repeat it each month.

It also tells you what a 30-minute test cannot do. AI answers change from run to run, so one check is a sample, not a verdict. A large study by SparkToro found that AI tools almost never give the same list of brands twice. So we show you how to read a first test fairly and how to build a trend over time.

What is AI brand visibility?

AI brand visibility is a set of separate questions, not one number. A tool may name you but not link to you. It may link to you but describe you wrongly. It may name your competitors and leave you out. Measure each question on its own:

  • Mention rate: in what share of answers is your brand named?
  • Citation rate: in what share of answers does the tool link to a page of yours?
  • Share of voice: of all the brands named across your test, what share is yours?
  • Accuracy: when you are named, is the description right?
  • Sources: which pages does the tool cite, and are they yours or someone else's?

Ahrefs lists similar measures in its AI visibility audit guide: mentions, citations, share of voice, and a check of accuracy, tone and whether you are the lead recommendation. Some tools combine these into one "AI visibility score". Treat a combined score with care until you know what goes into it.

Why does one test not tell the full story?

AI tools write each answer fresh. The same question can give different brands on different runs, in different orders. SparkToro and Gumshoe tested this in a study published in January 2026. About 600 volunteers ran 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, for nearly 3,000 runs in all. The main findings were:

  • There was less than a 1 in 100 chance that ChatGPT or Google's AI would give the same list of brands in any two responses to the same prompt.
  • There was less than a 1 in 1,000 chance of seeing the same list in the same order.
  • Even so, some brands came up again and again across dozens of runs. Appearing in most runs of a prompt showed a brand the tool tended to link with that question.

The authors draw two lessons. First, a "position in AI answers" figure is not meaningful, since the order is close to random. Second, the share of runs in which you appear is a reasonable measure, if you run each prompt many times. Our 30-minute test gives you a baseline sample. To turn it into a real rate, you repeat it, which we cover below.

Google makes a related point for its own tools. It says no third-party tool has access to its internal ranking or AI systems, and it tells site owners to use the Generative AI performance report in Search Console to see how their content does in its AI features.

How do you run the 30-minute test?

You need a spreadsheet, a notepad and the ability to open ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. If you can only test two tools, test the two your buyers use most. Here is the time budget.

StepTimeWhat you do
1. Write the prompts5 minutesWrite 10 buyer questions in three groups
2. Run them15 minutesPaste each into three tools and copy the answers
3. Log the results5 minutesFill six columns for each answer
4. Score and read5 minutesWork out four numbers and note the gaps

Step 1: Write 10 prompts (5 minutes)

Use three groups. The mix matters, because a tool may know you well when asked by name and still leave you out of a category question.

  • Category prompts (4): questions where no brand is named. Example: "What is the best invoicing software for a small accounting firm?"
  • Comparison prompts (3): you against a named competitor, or two competitors. Example: "How does [your brand] compare with [competitor]?"
  • Branded prompts (3): questions about you. Example: "What does [your brand] do, and who is it for?"

Take the wording from real sources: sales calls, support emails, the "People also ask" box and the questions prospects send you. Write the way a buyer writes, not the way your product page reads. Keep the prompts fixed once you pick them, because changing them makes later comparisons useless.

Step 2: Run them in three tools (15 minutes)

Open each tool in a fresh session. Where you can, turn off memory and personalization, or use a private window and log out, so your own history does not shape the answer. Paste each prompt, wait for the full answer and copy it into your sheet. Use the web search mode if the tool offers one, since that is how many buyers use it.

For Google, run the same question in a logged-out window and check whether an AI Overview appears. Not every question triggers one. Pew Research found in March 2025 that about 18% of Google searches in its study produced an AI summary, and that longer and question-style searches produced them more often. If no overview appears, write "none" and move on.

Step 3: Log six columns (5 minutes)

For each answer, record:

  1. Named: yes or no.
  2. Linked: does the answer link to a page on your domain?
  3. Position: first, middle, last or not applicable. Treat this as a rough note only, given the random order.
  4. Competitors named: list them.
  5. Accuracy: right, partly wrong or wrong, checked against your own facts.
  6. Cited pages: copy every URL the tool shows, yours or not.

If you have time, add a seventh note: the tone. Mark each mention positive, neutral or negative. "The best option for beginners" and "the expensive option" are both mentions, but they do very different work for you. Ahrefs lists sentiment and framing, differentiation and whether you are the lead recommendation as things to check in an AI visibility audit.

Step 4: Score it (5 minutes)

Work out four numbers.

  • Mention rate = answers that name you, divided by all answers.
  • Citation rate = answers that link to your domain, divided by all answers.
  • Share of voice = your mentions, divided by all brand mentions across every answer.
  • Accuracy rate = answers about you that are right, divided by answers that name you.

Then list the cited pages that are not yours. That list shows where the tools get their facts about your market.

Worked example 1: an HR software company

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company that sells HR software to firms with 50 to 200 staff. It runs 10 prompts in three tools, so 30 answers in all.

  • It is named in 6 of the 30 answers. Mention rate: 6 divided by 30, which is 20%.
  • A page on its own domain is linked in 2 answers. Citation rate: about 7%.
  • Across all 30 answers, the tools name 84 brands in total, and 6 of those mentions are the company. Share of voice: 6 divided by 84, about 7%.
  • Of the 6 answers that name it, 4 describe it correctly. Accuracy rate: about 67%.

The breakdown by prompt type tells more than the totals. The company is named in all 3 branded answers in one tool but in only 1 of the 12 category answers. The wrong descriptions all repeat one error: they say the company serves "enterprises only", based on a review page from three years ago.

The fixes follow from the data. The team corrects the old review page by contacting the site. It updates its own "who we serve" page with a clear first sentence and a date. It writes one page that answers the category question "what HR software suits a firm with 100 staff", with real pricing ranges and a named source for the legal points. It then repeats the test a month later with the same 10 prompts.

Worked example 2: a cybersecurity consultancy

This is another illustration. Imagine a consultancy that sells security reviews to mid-sized companies. It runs the same test: 30 answers.

  • It is named in 14 of 30 answers. Mention rate: about 47%.
  • It is linked in 3 answers. Citation rate: 10%.
  • All 9 branded answers name it. Only 5 of the 21 other answers do.

At first the 47% looks healthy. The split shows the real position. The tools know the brand when asked by name, but they rarely recommend it for category and comparison questions. The cited pages for those questions are two review sites and a trade association list, and the consultancy is on none of them.

The plan is not to rewrite its own pages. It is to earn a place where the tools already look. The team checks which review sites list its competitors, applies to be listed, and offers the trade body a short, original guide with data from its own reviews. It also adds a direct answer to its main service page.

The lesson is to split your results. A good total can hide a gap in the questions that matter most for new buyers.

How do you read your results?

What you seeWhat it usually meansFirst fix
Not named anywhere, even for branded promptsThe tools have little or no information about youCheck access, indexing and basic brand facts across your site and profiles
Named for branded prompts onlyThe tools know you but do not link you to your categoryBuild category pages and earn mentions on sites the tools cite
Named but described wronglyAn old or wrong source is being usedUpdate your page and the third-party page the tool cites
Named but never linkedThe tool uses other sites for facts about youAdd direct answers and clear facts to your own pages
Competitors named often, you rarelyThey appear on more pages the tools trustStudy the cited pages and plan real outreach
Different results on each runNormal variationRepeat the test and use the rate, not one run

Check access early. Ahrefs notes that some content delivery networks block AI crawlers by default, so a site can be hidden from some tools without anyone deciding it. Make sure robots.txt, your firewall and your CDN allow the crawlers you want. For Google, a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in its AI features.

How do you turn the test into a trend?

Repeat it. A baseline plus four monthly rounds with the same prompts gives you a rate and a range, which is far more useful than one number.

  1. Keep the prompts fixed. Add new ones in a second list, so the trend stays clean.
  2. Use the same tools and conditions. Same fresh-session method, same country, same month day.
  3. Run important prompts more than once. If you can spare time, run each prompt three times per tool. If you appear in one of three, that is inconsistent visibility, which is different from appearing in all three.
  4. Record the average and the range. Report "named in 3 to 5 of 10 runs", not "named".
  5. Add competitors. Track three to five, since share of voice is a ratio.
  6. Note what changed. A new page, a press story or a model update can explain a shift.

When your list grows past 30 to 40 prompts or covers several markets, a paid tool saves time, because it can run many prompts often. Be careful with any tool that sells a "ranking position in AI answers". Given the order findings above, that figure has little meaning. Look for tools that report the share of runs in which you appear, show the full answers and name the sources.

What should you do after the test?

Work from the gaps, not from a generic list.

  1. Fix wrong facts first. A wrong answer about your price, service or location costs more than a missed mention. Update your page and the cited third-party page.
  2. Add direct answers. Put a clear answer in the first sentences of your key pages and name your sources.
  3. Make brand facts consistent. Match your name, services, location and leaders across your site, profiles and listings.
  4. Close content gaps. Where the tools answer a buyer question and cite others, write one useful page.
  5. Earn mentions where tools already look. Use the cited-page list to plan outreach with a real story or real data.
  6. Check traffic. In analytics, look for visits from AI tool domains such as chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai. Check your own data to see which domains appear.

Our guides on generative engine optimization, GEO vs SEO and AEO vs SEO cover the page-level work in more detail.

Why does my brand show up in one tool and not another?

Each tool builds its answers from its own sources and methods, so a brand can be visible in one and missing in another on the same day. Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode draw on Google's search index, and Google says a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to be a supporting link. Other tools use their own crawls and partner indexes.

Ahrefs has measured the difference. In its study, on average only about 12% of the citations from AI assistants also ranked in Google's top 10 for the original prompt, and Perplexity was the outlier at nearly one in three. Ahrefs also found that the most cited brands differ between Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Perplexity.

So do not blend the tools into one number too early. Score each tool on its own first, then compare. A pattern such as strong in one tool and weak in two others points to a source problem. You may be present on the pages that one tool trusts and absent from the pages the others use. The cited-page list from step 3 shows which pages those are.

What is a good AI share of voice?

There is no reliable public benchmark. Share of voice depends on how many brands the tools name for your prompts, and that number differs a lot between markets. In a market where the tools name three brands per answer, a share near 33% is average. In a market where they name 15, a share near 7% is average. So compare yourself with the competitors in your own test, and with your own baseline from last month.

A few rules keep the number honest:

  • Use the same prompts and tools each time.
  • Count a brand once per answer, however many times the answer repeats its name.
  • Track three to five named competitors, so you can see who gains when you lose.
  • Look at the number by prompt type. Your share on category questions matters most for new buyers.

Be wary of any article that gives a "good" percentage without saying how it was measured. Without the prompt set, the tools and the market, a benchmark means little.

Can analytics track AI mentions?

Only in part. Analytics tools such as Google Analytics can show visits that arrive from an AI tool, if the tool sends a referrer. They cannot show a mention that sent no click. Pew Research found that people clicked a link inside a Google AI summary in only 1% of visits in its March 2025 data, so many mentions will never appear in your reports.

That is why the prompt test matters. It measures the part analytics cannot see. Use both together:

  • Prompt tests show whether you are named, linked and described correctly.
  • Referral visits show how many people clicked through, and what they did next.
  • Branded search and direct visits may rise when mentions build awareness, but they have other causes, so treat a rise as a clue and not as proof.
  • A lead source question on your forms, such as "how did you hear about us", can catch buyers who say they used an AI tool.

Search Console is part of this too. Google counts traffic from its AI features in the normal Search Console reports and also offers a Generative AI performance report. Use it for Google's tools. For ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity, the prompt test and your referral data are what you have.

Which tools should you test, and are free checkers worth using?

Start with the tools your buyers use. For most businesses that means ChatGPT, Google (AI Overviews and AI Mode) and Perplexity. Add Gemini if your buyers work in Google's tools. Add Claude if your buyers are technical or use it for research. This is a judgment call, so check with your customers, and keep the same set each month.

Several vendors offer free checkers. Ahrefs has a free AI visibility checker that needs no signup. It queries ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and Google AI Overviews and shows total mentions, mentions by platform and the most cited domains and pages. Semrush has a free AI search visibility checker that you can use three times a day without an account. Both vendors sell paid tools, so treat these as a free preview.

A free checker is useful for a quick second opinion on your manual results. It is not a program. It tests a limited set of prompts that the tool chose, not the questions your own buyers ask. That is why the manual test above starts from your own sales and support questions. Prompt choice matters as much as the tool. If you pick 20 prompts that happen to favor your brand, you will look strong, and if you pick 20 that do not, you will look invisible.

What if your brand never appears?

First, check the branded prompts. If a tool cannot describe you even when asked by name, the problem is basic. Work through these in order:

  1. Access. Check that robots.txt, your firewall and your CDN allow the crawlers you want, and that your key pages are indexed in Google.
  2. Basic facts. Make sure your site clearly says who you are, what you sell, where you work and who runs the company, with the same facts on your profiles and listings.
  3. Third-party presence. Check whether you appear on the review sites, directories and lists that the tools cite for your category.
  4. Category pages. Check whether you have a page that answers the main buyer question directly.

Set expectations honestly. An Ahrefs author writes that, in their experience, established brands with strong SEO can see early wins in weeks to months, while new brands with little online authority may need 12 to 18 months. That is one practitioner's view, not a measured rule, but it shows why a new brand should not expect quick results.

Can you report one AI visibility score?

You can, but it hides the cause of any change. A single score blends mentions, links, accuracy and tools that behave differently. If it moves, you will not know why. For your team or your board, report the four numbers by prompt type and by tool, plus a short note on what changed. Add a single combined score only as a summary, and write down how it is calculated.

Branded search volume is a useful clue but it is not a replacement. It can rise when people hear about you in AI answers, and it can rise for many other reasons. Use it next to the prompt test, not instead of it.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Testing once. One run is a sample. The SparkToro study shows how much lists vary.
  • Chasing order. Whether you are first or third in a list changes from run to run. Focus on whether you appear.
  • Testing only branded prompts. You will look better than you are. Include category and comparison questions.
  • Changing the prompts each month. You cannot compare results if the questions differ.
  • Logging in while testing. Memory and history can change the answer.
  • Trusting one tool's score. Keep mentions, citations and accuracy separate.
  • Ignoring wrong answers. Inaccurate answers can cost deals, so track accuracy.
  • Buying mentions. Google says seeking fake mentions is not as helpful as it might seem.

A simple template for your sheet

Create one sheet with these columns and one row per prompt, per tool, per run:

ColumnWhat to enter
Date and toolFor example, 14 Nov, ChatGPT with search
Prompt groupCategory, comparison or branded
PromptThe exact text
NamedYes or no
LinkedYes or no, plus the URL
Competitors namedA short list
AccuracyRight, partly wrong or wrong
Cited pagesEvery URL shown

A second tab can hold the four scores for each month. That tab is the one you show to your team.

A 90-day plan

Days 1 to 30: baseline

Run the 30-minute test. Log everything. Fix wrong facts and access problems that you find. Choose three to five competitors to track.

Days 31 to 60: fix and fill

Update your five key pages with direct answers and sources. Write one or two pages for the gaps. Correct third-party pages where you can. Repeat the test.

Days 61 to 90: earn and compare

Pitch one or two real stories to the sites the tools cite. Run the test a third time. Compare the rates with your baseline and decide what to repeat.

How Reinforce Lab approaches AI brand visibility

Reinforce Lab sells AI search and SEO services, so weigh this section with that in mind. Our free diagnostic works the same way as the test above, with a larger prompt set, repeated runs, competitor tracking and a written 90-day plan. You can read about our SEO and AI search audit, or get your free diagnostic.

Final thoughts

You do not need a paid tool to learn where you stand in AI search visibility. Ten prompts, three tools and a sheet will show whether you are named, linked and described correctly. Treat the first result as a baseline, repeat it each month and read the rate, not a single run. The cited-page list is the most useful output, because it shows where to earn your next mention.

title: AI Brand Visibility Tools for B2B: What They Track and How to Choose
content:
An AI brand visibility tool shows how often AI answers name, describe or link to your brand, and how that compares with your competitors. It runs a fixed set of buyer questions through tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews, then records the answers. A good one shows the full answer, the sources behind it and the trend over time. A weak one gives a single score you cannot check.

This guide is for B2B marketing teams that are deciding whether to buy one. It explains what these tools track, what they cannot do, what the entry plans of two well-known tools cost, and a checklist for choosing. It includes two worked examples and a 14-day test you can run before you sign anything. If you want to try the method by hand first, start with our 30-minute AI brand visibility test.

What is an AI brand visibility tool?

An AI brand visibility tool is software that asks AI search tools a list of questions on a schedule and records whether your brand appears in the answers. The software owner chooses the prompts, the engines and the competitors. The tool then reports results such as mention rate, citations, share of voice and sentiment.

You will see other names for the same thing: AI visibility platform, AI search visibility tool, GEO tool, AEO tool, LLM tracking tool and AI brand monitoring. The names overlap. What matters is what the product records and how you can check it.

Two versions exist. The first is a simple monitor that reports where you appear. The second adds advice, such as which page to change or which site to approach. Decide early which one you need. A monitor is enough to find out if you have a problem. You need more once you know what to fix and who will fix it.

What do these tools track?

Most tools report the same core measures. Ahrefs lists mentions, citations, impressions and AI share of voice in its AI visibility audit guide. Semrush lists an AI visibility score, mentions, citations, platform coverage, top cited pages, topics and a competitor comparison for its free checker. Here are the measures in plain words:

MeasureThe question it answersWatch out for
MentionsIn what share of answers is my brand named?A mention is not a link. Check that the tool counts them separately.
CitationsIn what share of answers does the tool link to a page of mine?Ask to see the exact URL for each one.
Share of voiceOf all brand mentions in my test, what share is mine?Each vendor calculates it differently. Ask for the formula.
Sources citedWhich pages do the tools cite in my market?This list is often the most useful output, because it shows where to earn mentions.
SentimentIs the brand described in a good, neutral or bad way?Read a sample of the answers yourself. Automated scoring can miss tone.
AccuracyAre the facts about us right?Most tools do not check this for you. Plan to check by hand.
HistoryIs the trend going up or down?Ask how long results are kept.

Some tools also report a "position" or "rank" inside an answer. Be careful with it. See the next section.

What can these tools not do?

AI answers are not like search results, so no tool can offer the certainty a rank tracker gives. Four limits matter most.

Answers change from run to run

SparkToro and Gumshoe ran a study in January 2026 with about 600 volunteers and 12 prompts across ChatGPT, Claude and Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode. They found less than a 1 in 100 chance of getting the same list of brands twice for the same prompt, and less than a 1 in 1,000 chance of the same order. Their conclusion was that a "ranking position in AI" figure is not meaningful, while the share of runs in which you appear is a reasonable measure. A good tool therefore repeats each prompt and reports a rate, not a single screenshot.

No tool sees inside Google

Google says that no third-party tool has access to its internal ranking or AI systems, and it warns about tools that claim to use internal Google metrics. For its own AI features, Google points to the Generative AI performance report in Search Console. That report is free, so use it as your first Google signal.

A score is a snapshot

Answers vary by prompt wording, country, model version and date. A score from one day tells you little. Repeated measurements tell you whether a change lasts.

Tools do not fix anything on their own

A dashboard shows a gap. Someone still has to write the page, correct the facts or earn the mention. Decide who owns that work before you buy. The software is the cheap part.

Why do B2B teams track AI visibility at all?

Because buyers use AI tools, and surveys show it, with a catch: each survey asks a different question, so the numbers are not interchangeable. Here are three, with what each one actually measured.

  • Forrester: 94% of business buyers report using AI somewhere in the buying process, up from 89% a year earlier (Buyers' Journey Survey 2025, published January 2026). That counts any use at any stage.
  • Gartner: in a survey of 645 B2B buyers in August and September 2025, 45% said they used generative AI during a recent purchase, mainly to gather information on vendors and products. Buyers used an average of seven information sources. 69% preferred to validate AI-generated insights with a sales rep.
  • 6sense: its 2026 report, based on 4,611 recent B2B buyers, found that 81% use an LLM somewhere in an evaluation, down from 94% the year before. Only 26% use an LLM to discover vendors. Before contacting a seller, 21% said LLMs influenced their view of vendors, against 34% who cited their own existing knowledge and 32% who cited internal discussions.

Read together, they say that most buyers touch AI, a smaller share use it to find new vendors, and it often sorts and checks what buyers already know. 6sense also found that buyers chose the vendor they favored before contacting a seller 82% of the time, and that 92% of eventual winners were on the initial shortlist. That is why being named in AI answers matters before the first sales call: it helps get you onto the shortlist and keeps you on it. Treat the figures as a reason to measure, not as proof that AI answers will win deals for you.

Are AI visibility tools, trackers and monitoring tools the same thing?

Mostly yes. Vendors use different labels for the same job: AI brand visibility tool, AI search visibility tool, AI visibility tracker, AI brand monitoring, LLM tracking tool and GEO tool. Each one runs a set of prompts in AI tools such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. It records whether your brand appears, and it reports mentions, citations, share of voice and sentiment.

The real differences are which AI tools it covers, how often it runs your prompts, how it handles competitor benchmarking and what reporting you get. Several SEO platforms, including Semrush and Ahrefs, list AI visibility features too. Ask whether you need a separate tracker at all.

What are the best AI brand visibility tools?

There is no single best one, and we do not rank vendors here. The best fit depends on the AI tools you need covered, how many prompts you track, whether you need competitor benchmarking, the reports you must send, and the price. Use the checklist and the 14-day test below, on your own prompts, before you pay for a year.

What kinds of tools exist?

TypeWhat it isGood for
Free and built-inGoogle Search Console's Generative AI report. Free checkers from Ahrefs (no signup, queries ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and AI Overviews) and Semrush (three free uses a day, no account).A first look and a second opinion
Add-ons to SEO suitesAhrefs Brand Radar and the Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit.Teams that already use these suites
Dedicated trackersStand-alone products such as Otterly and Peec, which run your prompts daily.Teams that want prompt-level history and competitor views
Enterprise platformsProducts such as Profound and Scrunch, which comparison guides describe as aimed at large or regulated organizations. Check each vendor for its pricing.Large and regulated organizations

We read the Ahrefs and Semrush pages and the Otterly and Peec pricing pages ourselves. We did not test the others. Comparison guides name them, and many of those guides are written by tool vendors, so treat their rankings with care.

How much do AI visibility tools cost?

Prices vary a lot. Here is what two stand-alone trackers listed on their own pricing pages when we read them in November 2026:

Tool and planMonthly pricePromptsPrice per prompt a month
Peec AI, Starter$9550about $1.90
Peec AI, Pro$245150about $1.63
Peec AI, Advanced$495350about $1.41
Otterly, Lite$29See noteSee note
Otterly, Standard$189See noteSee note
Otterly, Premium$489See noteSee note

Both tools also offer a custom enterprise plan. The Peec per-prompt figures are our own arithmetic from its listed prices. For Otterly, the prompt counts shown in the page text differ from the counts in the page's own description, so we do not quote them. Check the current counts on the page before you compare. Also note that entry plans track only some of the engines. Peec's page says to choose three models, and Otterly's lists three of seven engines on each of its first three plans.

The lesson is simple. The monthly price is not the cost. Count prompts, engines, markets and users, and add the staff time to act on the results.

How do you choose one? A 10-point checklist

Comparison guides use similar criteria. These ten are our version. The first five decide whether the data is useful. The last five decide whether you can use it.

  1. Engines. Does it cover the tools your buyers use, on the plan you would buy? A vendor may list an engine that your plan does not include.
  2. Google AI Mode and AI Overviews. Are both covered? Check the plan.
  3. Mentions and citations kept apart. A brand named without a link and a link without a name are different events.
  4. The full answer. Can you read the whole answer and every source, not only a score?
  5. History per prompt. Can you see how one prompt changed over weeks?
  6. Prompt control. Can you add your own buyer questions, or are you stuck with the vendor's list?
  7. Competitors. Can you track three to five named rivals for the same prompts?
  8. Exports and alerts. Can you export the data and get a warning when a prompt that was working drops?
  9. Price per prompt and trial. Is there a trial, and what happens when you pass the prompt limit?
  10. Who acts on it. Does the tool point to the page or source to fix, and do you have a person to do it?

Ask every vendor the same questions and write the answers in one sheet. If a vendor will not show a full answer with its sources, treat that as a warning.

Worked example 1: a B2B software company runs a 14-day test

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company that sells scheduling software to clinics. It wants to know if it needs a paid tool. It writes 25 buyer prompts: 10 for the category, 8 for comparisons and 7 for brand questions. It names three competitors.

On day 1 it runs the 25 prompts by hand in three AI tools and saves the answers. It is named in 4 of 75 answers, which is about 5%. It tries Google Search Console and sees AI feature data for its pages.

On days 2 to 7 it tests two trial accounts with the same 25 prompts. It scores each tool from 0 to 2 on the ten points above. Tool A scores 16 of 20 and shows full answers, sources and history. Tool B scores 11 of 20. It gives a single visibility score, does not show full answers, and counts a mention and a link as one event.

On days 8 to 14 it compares the tools' numbers against its hand checks. Tool A matches within a few answers. Tool B reports a mention rate that is nearly twice what the team saw by hand. The team picks Tool A on the entry plan, because it can read every answer.

The company does not treat the tool as the end of the job. It lists the five pages most often cited for its category, a review site and four blogs, and plans one real story for two of them.

Worked example 2: a small consultancy decides it does not need a paid tool

Again, this is an illustration. Imagine a three-person consultancy that sells compliance training. It has 12 buyer questions and no budget for software.

It tests the 12 questions monthly in three AI tools by hand, which takes about an hour. It also runs the free Ahrefs and Semrush checkers as a second opinion and watches the Search Console AI report. For a paid tool at $95 a month, it would get 50 prompts, so it would use under a quarter of the allowance. After three months the team sees that its results are stable, and that the work it needs is writing and outreach, not more data.

The lesson is that the right tool depends on the size of your prompt list and your team. A spreadsheet can be enough when the list is short, and software saves time when the list is long or covers several markets.

How do you run a 14-day proof-of-value test?

Use this before you sign a contract, especially an annual one.

  1. Days 1 to 2: write the prompts. Write 20 to 30 real buyer questions without your brand name. Add two or three competitors and your country.
  2. Days 2 to 3: run a hand baseline. Ask 5 to 10 of the prompts yourself in each engine and save the answers.
  3. Days 3 to 10: run the trials. Use the same prompts and competitors in every trial.
  4. Days 10 to 12: check the data. Compare each tool with your hand baseline. Open ten answers and confirm that the brand and sources shown are real.
  5. Days 12 to 13: test the follow-up. Can the tool tell you what to fix, or only that there is a gap?
  6. Day 14: decide. Score each tool on the ten points. Count the real cost, including staff time.

Run the test over a period when nothing big changes on your site, so you do not mix tool noise with real change.

How do you monitor brand mentions in ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity?

People search for this in many ways: track brand mentions in ChatGPT, AI brand monitoring, LLM brand monitoring, or tools for monitoring brand visibility in AI interfaces. They all describe one job. You pick a fixed set of questions your buyers ask, run them in each AI tool on a schedule, and record what each answer says about you.

Five things matter when you monitor:

  • Mentions: does your brand name appear in the answer?
  • Citations: does the answer link to your site or to a page that names you?
  • Accuracy: are the facts about your prices, services and locations right?
  • Sentiment: is the wording about you positive, neutral or negative?
  • Competitors: who else is named for the same question?

Check which AI tools a vendor covers. Common ones include ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude, Grok, Microsoft Copilot and Google AI Overviews, and coverage differs by vendor. A paid tool automates the running and the logging. It does not change what the AI tools say. If you want a Perplexity brand mention monitoring tool, a tool that watches ChatGPT and Gemini together, or a tool for AI Mode, check each vendor's list of covered AI tools and how often it runs your prompts. Coverage differs.

How do you track brand mentions in ChatGPT without a paid tool?

You can run a simple test by hand. It is slower than a tool, but it shows you whether paying for one is worth it.

  1. List 15 to 25 buyer prompts. Use the questions your customers ask, such as "best [your category] for [your buyer]."
  2. Run each prompt in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Mode. Use a new chat each time.
  3. Record the result in a sheet: prompt, tool, date, whether your brand appeared, its position, the sources cited, the competitors named and whether the facts were right.
  4. Repeat weekly at the same time with the same prompts.
  5. Read trends, not single answers. Answers change by person, place and time, so treat each run as a sample.

If the sheet shows you rarely appear, fix the pages and facts the answers rely on first. A tool will only measure the same problem faster.

Why should you track AI brand visibility?

Because buyers now ask AI tools to shortlist vendors, and you cannot see those answers in a normal rank report. Tracking tells you whether you are named, whether the facts are right and who is named instead of you. Without it you are guessing. Tracking does not prove the answers cause sales, so treat it as one input next to leads and revenue.

What should you do after the tool finds a gap?

  1. Fix wrong facts first. A wrong price or service description costs more than a missed mention.
  2. Read the cited pages. The pages that AI tools cite for your category show where your competitors are mentioned and you are not.
  3. Add direct answers. Put a clear answer, a named source and a date near the top of your key pages.
  4. Earn mentions where tools already look. Pitch real stories and real data to those sites.
  5. Repeat the test monthly and report a rate with a range, not one number.

Our guides on generative engine optimization, GEO vs SEO and AEO vs SEO cover the page-level work.

What else do B2B teams ask?

How are these tools different from SEO tools?

A rank tracker records the position of your page in a list of results. An AI visibility tool records whether your brand appears inside a written answer, with which sources. The two answer different questions, and you need both. Ahrefs describes GEO as building on SEO, and Google says its AI features rest on the same ranking and quality systems as Search. Strong SEO still helps you get retrieved. The AI tool then shows whether you were named.

Can an SEO suite do the job?

Often, for a first look. Ahrefs and Semrush both offer AI visibility features and free checkers. A stand-alone tracker may offer more prompt control and history. Compare what each one shows against the ten points above rather than assuming that a bigger suite is better.

Should you use more than one tool?

One tool with the right engines is usually enough. Use your hand test as a second opinion. Ahrefs found that the most cited brands differ between Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Perplexity, so check that your one tool covers the engines your buyers use rather than adding a second tool.

How often should you sample?

There is no standard. SparkToro's study found that a brand shows up across many runs of the same prompt even when the list changes each time, so the more runs you have, the better the rate. A tool can run daily. By hand, monthly is a sensible minimum. Report an average and a range, and do not react to one day.

Do these tools show what real people ask?

No. They run the prompts that you or the vendor chose. AI platforms do not share what users ask, so there is no public prompt volume like the search volume in keyword tools. Search Engine Land makes this point in its guide to measuring GEO. Build your prompt list from sales calls, support emails and the questions prospects send you.

Can a tool prove revenue impact?

Not on its own. A tool shows that you appeared in answers. It cannot see the private conversation, so it cannot show who read the answer or what they did next. To estimate impact, combine the tool with referral visits from AI tool domains in your analytics, a "how did you hear about us" field on forms, and your sales team's notes. Treat the link to revenue as a clue and not as proof.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Buying before testing by hand. You cannot judge a tool's data without a baseline.
  • Trusting one score. Keep mentions, citations and accuracy separate.
  • Chasing a rank in AI answers. The order in answers is close to random.
  • Buying the cheapest plan without checking the limits. Prompts, engines and markets decide what you can learn.
  • Tracking only branded questions. You will look better than you are. Include category and comparison questions.
  • Treating the tool as the program. The person who acts on the results matters more than the software.
  • Using a vendor's own "best tool" list as proof. Many such lists are written by vendors.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services. We do not sell an AI visibility tracking tool, and nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. Our free diagnostic works like the test above, with a larger prompt set, repeated runs and a written plan. You can read about our SEO and AI search audit or get your free diagnostic.

Final thoughts

Start with a hand test and the free tools. Buy software when your prompt list or your markets outgrow a spreadsheet. Choose on what you can verify: full answers, sources, history and a price that includes the work after the dashboard. And plan who will act on the results, because that is where visibility changes.

title: How to Rank in AI Overviews: A Practical Checklist for Google
content:
To rank in Google AI Overviews, your page must be indexed and eligible to show in Google Search with a snippet. Beyond that, Google says there are no extra technical requirements and no special tricks. What helps is the same work that helps any page: answer the question clearly, cover the related questions, back your claims with sources, and be talked about by other sites. Ranking well in normal results also helps, but it is no longer enough on its own.

This guide gives you a checklist of ten steps, with the data behind each one and the limits of that data. It also covers how to check whether Google cites you, what does not matter, two worked examples and a 30-day plan. We cite only studies we could read at the source, and we say when a finding is a correlation and not a cause.

What are Google AI Overviews, and when do they appear?

An AI Overview is a short AI-written summary at the top of some Google results, with links to the pages it drew on. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use "query fan-out": the tool splits your question into several related searches and gathers supporting pages for each one. Google also says an AI Overview only shows when its systems decide it adds something to classic Search, so many searches do not trigger one.

Studies agree that they appear far more often on questions and long searches. Two examples, with different samples:

  • Ahrefs analyzed 146 million search results and found that AI Overviews showed on 21% of keywords. They showed on 57.9% of question searches and on 46.4% of searches with seven or more words. "Why" questions had the highest rate, at 59.8%. Of the keywords that triggered one, 99.9% were informational.
  • The Pew Research Center tracked the browsing of 900 US adults in March 2025. About 18% of the Google searches in its sample produced an AI summary. That share was 8% for searches of one or two words and 53% for searches of ten words or more.

The two figures differ because the samples and methods differ. Both point the same way: AI Overviews are mostly about informational and question-style searches. If your pages target buying searches, such as "pricing" or "near me", expect fewer of them to be affected.

Pew also found that people clicked a regular result in 8% of visits to pages with an AI summary and 15% of visits to pages without one, and clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits. Google says clicks from pages with AI Overviews are higher quality. Look at conversions and not only clicks.

What does Google say you need to do?

Google's documentation on AI features is short and plain:

  • To be shown as a supporting link, a page must be indexed and eligible to show in Google Search with a snippet. There are no additional technical requirements.
  • The usual SEO basics still apply: allow crawling, link pages together, give people a good page experience, keep important content in text, and keep structured data matched to the visible text.
  • You do not need new machine-readable files, AI text files, special markup or special schema.org types.
  • Preview controls such as nosnippet, data-nosnippet, max-snippet and noindex apply to AI formats. More restrictive settings limit how your content can be used.
  • Google's guide asks for unique, non-commodity content with a point of view and first-hand experience. It warns that making separate pages for every variation of a question, mainly to influence AI answers, breaks its scaled content abuse policy.

Google also reports AI feature traffic in the normal Search Console performance data and in a Generative AI performance report. Use those for your own measurement.

Do you need to rank on page one first?

It helps, but the link is weaker than it used to be. In July 2025, Ahrefs found that about 76% of pages cited in AI Overviews also ranked in the top 10 for the same query, based on 1.9 million citations. In March 2026 it repeated the study with 863,000 keyword results and about 4 million AI Overview URLs and found about 38%. Ahrefs suggests that query fan-out explains part of the drop, because the tool draws on the results for related sub-questions. That is a guess, since Google does not publish the sub-questions.

The lesson is to rank for the question and for its follow-ups. A page that answers a related sub-question can be cited even when it does not rank first for the main phrase.

How to rank in AI Overviews: a 10-step checklist

1. Check which of your searches trigger an AI Overview

List 20 to 30 searches you want to be cited for. Run each in a logged-out window set to your country. Note which ones show an AI Overview. Work on those first. Skip the rest for now.

2. Make sure the page is eligible

Check that the page is indexed, returns a normal 200 status, is not blocked by robots.txt or your CDN, and is not set to nosnippet or noindex. In Search Console, confirm that the page is indexed. Our guide to robots.txt for SEO covers the access side.

3. Answer the question early

Put a direct answer in the first sentences under each question heading, in plain words. Then add detail. A reader and a tool can both use that answer without the rest of the page.

4. Write headings as real questions

People search with questions, and AI Overviews trigger most often on them. Use the wording your buyers use. Take the questions from sales calls, support emails and the "People also ask" box.

5. Cover the related questions, on the right pages

Ahrefs reports a study it ran with SurferSEO. Pages that ranked for the related fan-out searches were 161% more likely to be cited than pages that ranked only for the main phrase. The correlation between ranking for fan-out searches and being cited was 0.77. Treat that as a pointer, not a law. The practical step is to cover a topic in depth: write the main page, then pages for the real follow-up questions, and link them together. Write each page because a reader needs it. Do not create a page for every wording of a question.

6. Add evidence and what only you know

Name your sources, add dates, and show first-hand experience: your own data, tests and results. Google's guide asks for content that goes beyond common knowledge. A page that restates what everyone already says gives a tool no reason to choose it.

7. Build real mentions across the web

Ahrefs found that branded web mentions had a correlation of 0.664 with AI Overview visibility in its study of 75,000 brands, and that mentions on highly linked pages had a correlation of 0.70 across 76.7 million AI Overviews. These are correlations, so they do not prove cause. Google adds that seeking fake mentions is not as helpful as it might seem. Earn mentions with real stories, real data and real expertise.

8. Use more than text where it fits

Google says its AI features can bring in images and video, and that following its image and video guidance already counts. Ahrefs found that YouTube made up 18.2% of the AI Overview citations that did not rank in the top 100 for the same keyword, and 5.6% of all cited URLs in its 2026 study. If a video answers the question better than text, publish one, and write a clear title and description.

9. Keep pages fresh and markup honest

Update facts and examples on your best pages and show an honest update date. If you use structured data, make sure it matches what the page shows. Google does not require special markup for AI Overviews, so do not expect markup alone to change your result.

10. Measure with repeated checks

Check your list monthly: is an AI Overview shown, are you cited, and who is cited instead? Record the date and market. Use the Search Console reports for the Google side. Because AI answers vary from run to run, look at the trend over several checks and not at one result.

What does not matter?

  • Page length. Ahrefs found a near-zero correlation (about 0.04) between word count and AI citations. Google says there is no ideal page length. Write until the question is answered.
  • llms.txt and "chunking". Google says it does not use llms.txt files and that you do not need to break content into tiny pieces for AI.
  • Special schema. Google says no special schema.org markup is needed. FAQ markup also lost its rich result in Google Search on 7 May 2026.
  • Rewriting only for AI. Google says AI systems understand synonyms and general meaning, so you do not need to write in a special way.

Worked example 1: a software company's "what is" page

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company that sells expense software. Its page "what is expense management" ranks on page one, but an AI Overview shows for that search and does not cite it.

The team reads the cited pages. They are short, answer in the first two sentences, name a source for a statistic and include a one-line definition. The company's page opens with a long story about the company's history. The fix is simple. It moves a two-sentence definition to the top, adds a named source for the one statistic it quotes, and adds a short list of the steps in a typical process. It also writes a page on a fan-out question that the cited pages cover, "how do expense approvals work", and links the two.

The team does not rewrite everything. It sets a monthly check of 25 searches, records whether it is cited, and watches the trend over three months.

Worked example 2: a consultancy that is cited for definitions but not comparisons

Again, an illustration. Imagine a small consultancy that sells compliance training. It is cited in AI Overviews for three "what is" searches but not for any "X vs Y" or "best way to" searches, where buyers compare options.

The team finds that the comparison searches cite review sites and a trade association page, and that the consultancy appears on neither. The plan has two parts. It writes one honest comparison guide with a table, named sources and a note on when each option fits. It also approaches the trade association with a short, original guide based on its own audits. Success is measured by whether the cited pages for those searches change over the next three checks.

The lesson is to look at which sources are cited for each kind of search. Definitions, comparisons and how-to searches often cite different pages.

How do you optimize for AI Overviews?

AI Overviews SEO is mostly ordinary SEO done well. The checklist above gives the steps. In short: make sure the page is indexed and can show a snippet, answer the question clearly under a matching heading, keep facts accurate and current, show who wrote the page and why they know the topic, and check whether Google cites you for your key questions. Content for AI Overviews works best when one page answers one question in plain words.

What does it mean to rank in an AI Overview?

There is no rank number inside an AI Overview the way there is in a list of results. A page is either shown as a supporting link or it is not. Some sites are linked next to a sentence, some in a side panel and some at the bottom. So "ranking in AI Overviews" really means being cited, and sometimes being named in the text. Track whether you are cited, how often, and for which searches, not a position.

How does Google choose its sources?

Google says its AI features rest on its core Search ranking and quality systems. It uses a method it calls retrieval-augmented generation: the system finds relevant, current pages in the Search index, reads the passages and writes an answer that links to the pages that support it. Google does not publish a list of ranking factors for AI Overviews, and no third-party tool can see inside its systems. What the studies add is a set of patterns, such as the share of cited pages that also rank, which we covered above. Use them as hints, and test on your own searches.

Does this work for product pages or only for informational content?

Mostly for informational content. Ahrefs found that 99.9% of the keywords that triggered an AI Overview in its study were informational, and that question searches triggered them far more than other searches. Product and pricing searches show them less often. That does not mean product pages are out of scope. Google asks you to keep Merchant Center and Business Profile information current, and to support text with good images and video. But for most businesses, the larger gains come from guides, comparisons and answers to buyer questions that sit around the product.

How long does it take to see changes?

We found no reliable public figure, so we do not quote one. Pages must be recrawled before a change can show, and the answers themselves vary from run to run. Google also says that indexing and serving are not guaranteed, even when a page meets every requirement. A practical rhythm is to make a change, wait for the page to be recrawled, then check the same searches monthly for at least three months before you decide that it worked.

How do you check whether AI Overviews cite you?

  1. List your searches. Put the ones where you already rank on page one first.
  2. Run each in a logged-out window with your target country. Write down the date.
  3. For each, record whether an AI Overview appears, whether you are cited, which page, and who is cited instead.
  4. Copy every cited URL. The list shows who Google treats as a source in your market.
  5. Repeat monthly and compare. Keep AI Mode results separate from AI Overviews.
  6. Add Search Console's Generative AI performance report for Google's own numbers.

Paid tools can run these checks daily. Our guide to AI brand visibility tools explains what to look for, and our 30-minute AI brand visibility test shows the hand method.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Chasing a trick. Google says there is no special optimization. Fix the basics first.
  • Writing a page for every wording of a question. Google warns that this can break its spam policy.
  • Burying the answer. A long introduction before the point gives a tool no clear passage.
  • Quoting unsourced statistics. A claim with no source is easy to skip and easy to dispute.
  • Ignoring the sources Google already cites. If you are on none of them, your own pages are only part of the answer.
  • Judging by one check. Answers vary. Track a trend.
  • Blocking snippets by accident. A nosnippet or noindex setting limits how your content can be used.

A 30-day plan

Week 1: list and baseline

Pick 20 to 30 searches. Run them logged out and record which trigger an AI Overview and who is cited.

Week 2: fix eligibility and openings

Check indexing, status codes, robots.txt and snippet settings for your target pages. Move a direct answer to the top of each page.

Week 3: fill the gaps

Write one page for the most important follow-up question. Add a source and a date to your key claims. Plan one real story for a site that is already cited.

Week 4: measure and decide

Run the same checks again. Compare with week 1. Decide what to repeat. Then keep checking monthly.

How Reinforce Lab approaches AI Overviews

Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services, so weigh this section with that in mind. We start with a free diagnostic of your Google and AI search visibility, then build a plan. You can read about our AI search optimization service and our SEO and AI search audit, or get your free diagnostic.

Final thoughts

There is no secret way to rank in AI Overviews. Be eligible, answer the question early, cover the follow-ups, show your evidence and earn real mentions. Then check your results on a schedule, because answers change. Do the basics well and the rest is measurement.

title: LLM SEO: What It Is and How to Optimize for LLMs (LLMO)
content:
LLM SEO is the work of making your brand and your pages easy for large language models to find, understand and cite when they answer questions. It is also called LLM optimization or LLMO. It is not a new trick. For Google, it is ordinary SEO plus a few extra jobs: clear facts, quotable pages, a good presence on other sites, and a way to check what the models say about you.

This guide explains what LLM SEO is, how LLMs choose what to cite, and what the evidence shows. It also covers what Google says you can ignore, and gives a nine-step plan, a worked example and an honest answer on how long it takes. We cite only studies and documents we could read at the source, and we say when a finding is a correlation, a vendor view or a single test.

What is LLM SEO?

LLM SEO means improving how often and how accurately large language models mention your brand, recommend your products and cite your pages. The goal is not a rank. The goal is to be part of the answer when someone asks ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity or Google's AI features about your category.

A language model can know about you in two ways. The first is training: the model learned from text in its training data, collected before it was released, so what it says reflects what was on the web then. The second is retrieval: when the model needs fresh facts, it searches the web, reads some pages and writes an answer from them. Google calls the second method retrieval-augmented generation, or grounding, and describes it as relying on its core Search ranking systems to find relevant, up-to-date pages. Most of the work you can control today is about retrieval, because you can change a page this week but not a model that was trained last year.

LLM SEO, LLMO, GEO, AEO and AI SEO: what is the difference?

These names overlap, and different writers use them in different ways. The table shows the common use.

TermCommon meaning
LLM SEO or LLMOGetting a brand and its pages mentioned and cited by large language models and chatbots
GEO (generative engine optimization)The same goal, framed around generative search engines. See our GEO guide.
AEO (answer engine optimization)Writing so that answer boxes and assistants can quote you. See AEO vs SEO.
AI SEOA loose term for any of the above, and sometimes for using AI tools to do SEO

Google takes a plain view. It says optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience, and so it is still SEO. It also advises caution with third-party "AEO" or "GEO" advice. We use the terms as one family of work and write "LLM SEO" for the part that targets language models. Our comparison in GEO vs SEO covers what changes and what stays the same.

How is LLM SEO different from traditional SEO?

Traditional SEO aims to rank pages in search results and win clicks. LLM SEO aims to get your brand named and your pages cited inside an answer. They share a base, and a site that is weak at traditional SEO is rarely strong at LLM SEO.

AreaTraditional SEOLLM SEO
GoalRankings and clicksMentions and citations in answers
Query styleShort keywordsLonger, conversational prompts and follow-ups
Authority signalsBacklinks, content qualityBacklinks and quality, plus brand mentions and consistent facts across other sites
ContentPages that match intentPages with clear headings, answer-first passages and sourced evidence
MeasurementRank, traffic, conversionsMention rate, citation rate and share of voice across a fixed prompt set

How do LLMs choose what to cite?

Nobody outside the AI companies knows the exact rules, and they do not publish them. What the companies do say is limited. Google says its AI features use a technique called query fan-out: the model splits one question into several related searches and gathers pages for each. Its example is a question about fixing a lawn full of weeds, which fans out into searches on herbicides, chemical-free removal and prevention. So a page can be retrieved for a question it never named.

From the documents we read, three things seem to matter. These are our reading and not a published formula:

  • Retrievability. The page must be crawlable, indexed and readable in the HTML. For Google, a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Other tools use their own crawlers or search indexes.
  • Relevance and clarity. The page must answer the question, or one of the fan-out questions, in a passage that makes sense alone.
  • Trust. The page and the brand should look reliable, with named sources, named authors, current facts and agreement from other sites.

What does the evidence say?

There is less hard evidence than the volume of advice suggests. These are the main studies and documents we found, with their limits.

  • Adding evidence can raise visibility, in a test. Researchers from Princeton, IIT Delhi and others built a benchmark called GEO-bench of 10,000 queries and tested nine ways to change content. They reported that adding citations, quotations from relevant sources and statistics boosted source visibility by up to 40% in their tests, and that the methods worked on Perplexity with gains of up to 37%. The effect varied by domain. It is a controlled study from 2024, published at the KDD 2024 conference, not a guarantee for your site.
  • Fresher pages are cited more. Ahrefs analyzed 17 million citations across seven AI search platforms. It found that content cited in AI answers was 25.7% fresher than content in regular results, and that assistants showed a 13.1% preference for more recently updated content. That is a correlation from one vendor's data set.
  • Answers vary. SparkToro had 600 volunteers run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google's AI features 2,961 times. There was less than a 1 in 100 chance of the same list of brands twice and about a 1 in 1,000 chance of the same order. So measure a rate across many prompts, not a rank.
  • Most AI crawlers do not run JavaScript. In December 2024, Vercel reported that none of the major AI crawlers it tested rendered JavaScript, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity. Content that loads only in the browser may be invisible to them. That is a snapshot from one network, so test your own pages.

What does Google say you can ignore?

Google's guide to generative AI features has a section on myths. For Google Search, it says you do not need:

  • llms.txt files or other special files and markup. Google says Search does not use them. It adds that making one is fine for other systems that use it, and will neither help nor harm your visibility in Google Search. See our llms.txt guide.
  • "Chunking" content into tiny pieces. Google says there is no requirement to do this and no ideal page length.
  • Rewriting content only for AI. Google says its systems understand synonyms and meaning, so you do not need every long-tail variation.
  • Inauthentic mentions. Google says seeking them is not as helpful as it might seem.
  • Special structured data. It is not required, though still useful for rich results.

This is Google's view of Google Search. Other tools may behave differently, and Google also says that no third-party tool has access to its internal ranking or AI systems. It is a good check against advice that sounds technical but has no source.

How do you optimize content for LLMs?

Large language model optimization is mostly about writing clearly. Put the answer first, then the detail. Keep one topic per section and use a heading that matches the question. Name your facts, dates and sources. Keep paragraphs short. These habits also help people, which is why they are safe to adopt.

What is an LLM SEO strategy?

An LLM SEO strategy is a short plan: the questions your buyers ask, the pages that should answer them, the sources that back each answer and a routine to test how AI tools describe you. The nine steps below turn that into a plan. An AI search content strategy is the same idea applied to what you publish: fewer, better pages, each built to answer a real question.

How do you write for AI search?

Write the way you would explain the topic to a smart colleague. Say what it is, who it is for, how it works and what it costs. Avoid filler. Add a source or a number only when you can show where it came from.

A nine-step LLM SEO plan

Step 1: Make sure models can reach and read your pages

Check that key pages are indexed, not blocked by robots.txt or your firewall, and show their main text in the raw HTML. OpenAI says sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers. Anthropic says disabling Claude-SearchBot or Claude-User may reduce your visibility in Claude answers. Our robots.txt guide explains the file, and an AI search audit tests each bot.

Step 2: Write a list of buyer prompts

Write 10 to 15 questions in the words your buyers use. Include category questions, comparison questions and a few about your brand. This list is your keyword research for LLMs. It is different from classic keyword research because prompts are longer and more like speech. Semrush offers a Prompt Research feature in its AI toolkit, and you can also use sales calls, support tickets and Search Console queries.

Step 3: Put the answer first

Start each section with one or two sentences that answer the heading's question. Then add detail. A passage that makes sense on its own is easier to quote. Do not break pages into tiny fragments for the sake of it, since Google says that is not needed. Just make each section clear.

Step 4: Add evidence

Back claims with a named statistic, a quote from an expert or a link to a source, each with a date. This is the one tactic that has controlled test evidence behind it. Use only figures you have read at the source and say what the study can and cannot show.

Step 5: Fix your facts and your entity

Keep one set of facts: your name, what you do, who you serve, where you work, prices or price ranges, and who runs the company. Make your site, LinkedIn page and directory listings match. A model that sees three different descriptions of you will repeat one of them, and not always the right one.

Step 6: Keep important pages current

Update pages whose facts change, such as pricing, features, rules and benchmarks. Show a real last-updated date and change something real when you update. Ahrefs' data suggests fresher pages are cited more, though that is a correlation.

Step 7: Build your presence on other sites

Answers often rely on third-party sources: review sites, directories, news, community threads and comparison pages. Run your prompts, list the sites the answers cite, and ask which of them you could be on in an honest way. Do not buy fake reviews or post disguised ads. Google says inauthentic mentions are not as useful as they might seem.

Step 8: Measure what you can

Run your prompt list each month, three runs per prompt, and record mentions, citations, descriptions and competitors. Use Google's Generative AI performance report in Search Console, which reports impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode. Use Bing Webmaster Tools' AI Performance report for citations in Copilot. Our guide to checking if AI tools mention your brand and our list of AI brand visibility tools help with this step.

Step 9: Repeat and keep the record

Repeat the test each quarter and after big site changes. Keep every sheet. The point is to see a trend and to learn which changes helped.

Worked example: a service firm builds an LLM SEO plan

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine an eight-person firm that offers payroll services to restaurants. It writes 12 prompts, such as "payroll service for a small restaurant" and "payroll provider vs doing payroll in house". It runs each three times in three tools, which gives 108 answers, and is named in 9, about 8%.

The source map shows the answers citing two directory sites, a trade association page and a competitor's guide. The firm is on none of them. Its own services page says "we help businesses grow" and gives no price or location.

The plan has four jobs. It rewrites the services page so the first lines say who the firm serves, what it does and a price range. It adds one page with a clear answer to the in-house question, with two sourced statistics. It completes its directory profiles and asks three customers for honest reviews. It tests the same 108 runs after 60 days. The firm records the result whatever it is, because the point is a fair comparison, not a promise.

LLM SEO for service businesses

Service firms have an advantage and a risk. The advantage is that buyers ask specific questions, such as "who does X in my city" or "how much does Y cost". A page with a clear answer can win those. The risk is thin pages. A services page with vague claims gives a model little to quote. Include who you serve, where, what you do, a price range or the factors that set the price, and proof such as named reviews or credentials. Keep your directory and map listings accurate, because answers about local and service firms often rely on them.

Which LLM SEO tools help?

You can start with no paid tool: a spreadsheet, the AI tools, Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. SEO suites such as Ahrefs and Semrush offer AI visibility features, and stand-alone trackers exist. Test any tool against your hand results and treat a precise rank inside AI answers with caution. Our guide to AI brand visibility tools compares what they track and what they cost.

Do you need an LLM SEO agency?

Not to start. The plan above can be run in-house. An agency helps when you lack the time, when the fixes need a developer, or when the source map shows work such as outreach that you cannot do alone. Ask what you will receive: the prompt list, raw answers, the source map, a ranked list of fixes and a date to repeat the test. Be wary of any agency that promises a place in AI answers, because no one can guarantee it. Our LLM optimization service and SEO and AI search audit follow this approach.

How long does LLM SEO take to work?

No study we found gives a reliable time. Fixes to access and facts can show in retrieval-based answers within weeks, since OpenAI says a robots.txt change takes about 24 hours to apply for search. Gains from new content and outside mentions take longer, and training-based knowledge changes only when models are retrained. Treat any firm promise of a timeline as a red flag, and judge progress by your own repeated test.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Chasing a rank. The order of brands in answers changes from run to run.
  • Adding files and markup first. Fix access, facts and content before you add anything special.
  • Writing thin pages for every prompt. Google warns that making pages for each variation to manipulate AI answers breaks its scaled content abuse policy.
  • Using unsourced statistics. An unsourced number is a risk to readers and to models.
  • Ignoring other sites. Answers often come from third-party pages.
  • Testing once. One answer is a clue, not a result.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services, including LLM optimization. Nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. You can get your free diagnostic, which tests your pages and prompts with a written plan.

Final thoughts

LLM SEO is mostly good SEO with clearer facts, better evidence and a plan to check results. Start with access, then facts, then pages that answer questions with sources. Build a real presence on the sites the answers cite, and measure with a fixed prompt list. Ignore advice that has no source, including extra files, until the basics work.
