title: ChatGPT SEO: How to Use It for SEO and How to Show Up in It
content:
"ChatGPT SEO" means two different things. The first is using ChatGPT as a tool to do SEO work faster, such as ideas, outlines, title tags and structured data. The second is doing SEO for ChatGPT: making your brand and pages easy for ChatGPT search to find and cite in its answers. This guide covers both. The short version is that ChatGPT helps with SEO tasks if you check its output, and showing up in ChatGPT depends on crawler access, being found in the search results it uses, clear answers with sources, and what other sites say about you.

We cite only sources we could read at the publisher. We say when a figure is a test, a survey or one vendor's data, and when something is our own recommendation. Nobody outside OpenAI knows exactly how ChatGPT picks sources, and OpenAI does not publish a ranking formula.

Part 1: How does ChatGPT search choose what to show?

OpenAI's Help Center describes the process in plain terms. When ChatGPT decides that a question needs fresh information, it can turn your question into one or more targeted search queries. It says ChatGPT search sometimes partners with other search providers, and it names Microsoft in its privacy notes. It may also use your general location from your IP address, so "restaurants near me" can become "top restaurants" plus the city. After reviewing results, it may send further, more specific queries.

OpenAI says ChatGPT ranks search results using multiple factors meant to help people find relevant, reliable information, and that placement is not guaranteed. It also warns that results and citations can be incomplete, outdated or incorrect. For publishers, it says to allow OAI-SearchBot to crawl the site and to make sure your host or CDN allows traffic from OpenAI's published IP addresses.

Three practical points follow from this:

  • ChatGPT often searches with short rewritten queries, so ranking in regular search for those phrases helps you get read.
  • The search partner's index matters. Being indexed in Bing, as well as Google, is a sensible step.
  • Location can change the answer, so test local prompts with a city in them.

OpenAI also says that when a question looks like shopping, ChatGPT search may show product options drawn from structured data from third-party providers and other third-party content such as reviews. For sellers of products, this means complete, accurate product data and honest reviews on other sites matter as well as your own pages.

Part 2: How do you show up in ChatGPT?

This is our recommended order. Steps 1 to 3 make you findable. Steps 4 to 7 make you worth citing.

Step 1: Let OpenAI's crawlers in

Open yoursite.com/robots.txt and check that OAI-SearchBot is not blocked on the pages you want cited. OpenAI says sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, though they can still appear as navigational links, and that a robots.txt change can take about 24 hours to apply. Then check your CDN, firewall and bot protection, because they can block a bot that robots.txt allows. OpenAI publishes the IP ranges to allow.

Keep the other OpenAI names straight. GPTBot is for model training, and allowing or blocking it is a separate choice. ChatGPT-User visits a page when a user's question needs it, and OpenAI says robots.txt rules may not apply to it. Our robots.txt guide explains the file.

Step 2: Get indexed in Bing and Google

Because ChatGPT search draws on search partners, check that your key pages are indexed in both Bing and Google. Use Bing Webmaster Tools and Google Search Console, submit your sitemap and fix blocked or noindexed pages.

Step 3: Rank for the short searches ChatGPT runs

Take each long question your buyers ask and write the short search ChatGPT is likely to run: the category, a qualifier and a place. Then look at those phrases in Google and Bing. If you do not appear for them, ChatGPT is less likely to read your page, however good it is. This is our reading of how the process works, based on OpenAI's description of query rewriting, and it is not a published rule.

Step 4: Answer the question first, with evidence

Write pages that answer the question in the first sentence or two, then add detail. Give facts a model can quote: prices or ranges, who it is for, how it works, how it compares. Back claims with named sources. A Princeton-led team tested nine content changes on a 10,000-query benchmark and reported that adding citations, quotations and statistics lifted visibility by up to 40%, and by up to 37% on Perplexity. It is a 2024 study and the effect varied by domain, but it is the best controlled evidence we have.

Step 5: Build real mentions on other sites

Answers often rely on third-party pages: review sites, "best of" lists, directories, forums and news. Run your prompts, list the sites ChatGPT cites, and ask how you can appear there honestly. Claim and complete profiles, earn real reviews, and contribute useful answers. Do not buy reviews or hide ads in forums. Google's guidance for its own AI features says seeking inauthentic mentions is not as useful as it might seem, and the same sense applies here.

Step 6: Keep your facts the same everywhere

Use one name, one description, one set of prices and one set of locations across your site, directories and social profiles. A model that sees conflicting facts may repeat the wrong one or skip you.

Step 7: Keep key pages fresh

Ahrefs analyzed 17 million citations across seven AI search platforms and found that content cited in AI answers was 25.7% fresher than content in regular results. That is a correlation from one vendor's data set, but it fits common sense: update pages when prices, features or rules change, and show a real update date.

Step 8: Measure with a fixed prompt list

Write 10 to 15 buyer questions without your brand name. Run each three times in ChatGPT with search on, in a fresh chat, and record whether you are named, whether your page is cited, how you are described and who else appears. Variation is large. SparkToro had 600 volunteers run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google's AI features 2,961 times, and found less than a 1 in 100 chance of getting the same list of brands twice. So look at a rate across many runs, not a rank. Our guides to checking if AI tools mention your brand and AI brand visibility tools go deeper.

Also look at traffic. Ahrefs reported that Google sends about 345 times more traffic to websites than ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity combined, and that ChatGPT accounts for over 80% of AI referral traffic. These are Ahrefs figures from 2025 and they will change, but they show that the main value today is often being named and trusted, with clicks a smaller part.

How do you rank in ChatGPT and get cited?

ChatGPT does not have a ranking list like Google. You are either named or linked in the answer, or you are not. To get cited by ChatGPT, three things have to be true: its crawler can reach your page, the page is indexed where its search partners look, and the page gives a clear, specific, checkable answer to the question. The seven steps above cover each one. Products and brands you want named also need clear facts on your own site and mentions on other trusted sites.

How is ChatGPT search different from Google?

AreaGoogle SearchChatGPT search
OutputA list of links, sometimes with an AI summaryA written answer with citations and a sources panel
QueryWhat the user typedOften rewritten into one or more targeted searches
Crawler controlGooglebot and Google's controlsOAI-SearchBot for search, GPTBot for training, ChatGPT-User for user visits
MeasurementSearch Console shows clicks and impressionsNo OpenAI report for site owners that we found, so you test prompts and read analytics
PlacementRanking positionOpenAI says placement is not guaranteed

The practical result is that you cannot track a position the way you track a rank. You track how often you are named and cited across a fixed list of prompts.

Part 3: How do you use ChatGPT for SEO?

ChatGPT is a fast assistant for drafting and sorting. It is not a source of search data. Treat its output as a first draft that you check. The table shows common uses and the check that each needs.

TaskHow ChatGPT helpsWhat you must check
Keyword ideasExpands a seed topic into related subtopics and questionsIt has no search volume data. Confirm in a keyword tool.
Clustering and intentGroups a long list by topic and labels intentCheck the live results, since intent is shown by what ranks.
Outlines and briefsDrafts headings that cover a topicAdd your own angle, examples and internal links.
Title tags and meta descriptionsGives many options at onceCount the characters yourself, and make sure they match the page.
Structured dataWrites JSON-LD for an article, product or FAQValidate it, and make sure it matches the visible page.
Redirect maps and patternsHelps match old and new URLs, and writes regexTest on a sample before you deploy.
Content refresh ideasCompares your page with a list of subtopics and suggests gapsCheck facts and sources yourself.
FAQ and question listsSuggests questions your readers may askUse real questions from sales calls and Search Console first.

Good prompts give context: the audience, the page goal, the target keyword, the tone and the format of the answer you want. Ask for options, not one answer, and ask it to list what it is unsure about.

Six prompts to start with for SEO tasks

These are examples. Fill in the brackets, and check every output.

  1. Topic map: "Act as an SEO strategist. For a [type of business] that sells to [audience], list 20 subtopics a buyer researches before buying, grouped by buying stage. Mark any you are unsure about."
  2. Intent labels: "Label each keyword in this list as informational, commercial, transactional or navigational, and give a one-line reason."
  3. Brief: "Write an outline for a page that answers [question] for [audience]. Put a direct answer in the first sentence of each section. List the facts I must source."
  4. Title options: "Give 10 title tags under 60 characters for a page about [topic]. Include [keyword] and no hype words."
  5. Structured data: "Write FAQPage JSON-LD for these questions and answers exactly as written. Do not add any content."
  6. Gap check: "Here is my page and a list of questions buyers ask. Which questions does my page not answer?"

Always ask the tool to say what it is unsure about, and never paste private client data into a tool you have not approved.

Is ChatGPT bad for SEO?

Not by itself. Google says appropriate use of AI or automation is not against its guidelines, and that using AI does not give content any special gain. It says content is judged on whether it is helpful, original and trustworthy. The risk is how you use it. Google's spam policy lists using generative AI tools to generate many pages without adding value for users as scaled content abuse. Google also warns that generative models predict likely words rather than retrieve facts, so outputs can be wrong, and it asks you to fact-check and review AI content, including titles, descriptions and structured data, before you publish.

The safe rule is simple. Use ChatGPT to help you think and draft. Add what only you can: first-hand experience, real data, named sources and a point of view. Have a person check every fact.

What about ChatGPT SEO tools?

You will see "ChatGPT SEO tools" in three forms: custom GPTs, browser add-ons and features inside SEO suites. They can save time on drafting. They do not add data that ChatGPT lacks, such as search volume or backlinks, unless they connect to a real data source. Ask what data a tool uses before you pay for it. For tracking how you appear in ChatGPT, see our guide to AI brand visibility tools.

Does the same work help with Perplexity SEO and Gemini?

Largely, yes. Perplexity has its own crawler, PerplexityBot, which it says surfaces and links sites in its results, and a user-triggered fetcher that generally ignores robots.txt. Gemini and Google's AI features rely on Google's index. The base work, which is access, indexing, answer-first pages, evidence and third-party presence, helps all of them. Our guide to ranking in AI Overviews covers Google's side.

Do authority, backlinks and mentions still matter for ChatGPT?

Semrush's guides to ChatGPT visibility say they do, and give a practical method. Ask ChatGPT questions in your niche, note which sites it cites most often, and aim for honest mentions and links from those sites, since links from sources ChatGPT frequently cites may carry more weight than links from unrelated sites. The same guide recommends building brand consensus off your site through third-party lists, reviews, Reddit and YouTube, and it notes a study that found recency bias in several ChatGPT models, so newer pages tended to be favored. These are a vendor's recommendations, and OpenAI does not publish its ranking factors, so treat them as hypotheses to test with your own prompt list. The principle is sound: ChatGPT often reads what other sites say about you, so work on that as well as on your own pages.

Worked example: a small accounting firm tests ChatGPT

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a four-person accounting firm in a mid-sized city. It writes 12 prompts, such as "accountant for a small restaurant in [city]" and "how much does bookkeeping cost for a small business". It runs each three times in ChatGPT with search on, which gives 36 answers, and is named in 3.

The answers cite a local directory, a "best accountants" article from a local news site and a competitor's guide to bookkeeping costs. The firm is on the directory with an old phone number and is not in the article. Its own services page says "full-service accounting" and gives no prices or areas.

Its plan has five parts. It fixes the phone number everywhere. It rewrites its services page to say who it serves, where and a price range. It adds one page with a sourced answer on bookkeeping costs. It asks the news site's editor whether a list update is possible, and asks three clients for honest reviews on the directory. It repeats the same 36 runs after 60 days. The point is a fair comparison, not a promise.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Blocking OAI-SearchBot by accident. A security plugin or CDN setting often does it.
  • Treating ChatGPT as a keyword tool. It does not know search volumes.
  • Publishing unreviewed AI content. Google asks you to fact-check it, and scaled content abuse is a spam policy.
  • Chasing a rank in answers. Lists change from run to run.
  • Testing once. One answer is a clue, not a result.
  • Ignoring Bing. ChatGPT search draws on search partners as well as its own crawler.
  • Only fixing your own site. Answers often rely on third-party pages.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services. Nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. Our AI search optimization service follows the steps above, and you can get your free diagnostic to see how ChatGPT and other tools describe your site.

Final thoughts

Use ChatGPT as a quick assistant and check every output. To show up in it, let its crawler in, be indexed in Bing and Google, answer questions first with sources, build honest mentions on the sites it cites and test with a fixed prompt list. Nobody can promise a place in ChatGPT answers, but each step makes you easier to find, to trust and to quote.

title: Entity SEO: How Search and AI Tools Learn Who You Are
content:
Entity SEO is the work of making it clear what your brand, your people, your products and your topics are, and how they relate, so search engines and AI tools identify you correctly. An entity is a uniquely identifiable thing, such as a company, a person, a place or an idea. It is not a keyword. The practical work is plain: use one name and one description everywhere, state the facts on a clear home page, add accurate structured data, link related pages with clear anchors and earn honest mentions on other sites.

This guide explains what entities are, why they matter for search and AI answers, how to find the entities for your site, and a nine-step plan with a sample of Organization markup. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we say when a finding is a correlation or when a claim is our own view.

What is an entity in SEO?

An entity is a thing or concept that is singular, unique, well defined and distinguishable from other things. Google's Knowledge Graph and Wikidata are two large catalogs of them. Examples are a company such as Reinforce Lab, a person such as an author, a product, a city or a concept such as "robots.txt". An entity has a name, a type, facts about it and links to other entities.

Search Engine Journal's Dixon Jones puts the difference between an entity and a keyword this way: an entity is a record in a database, with an identifier, while a keyword is a word or phrase. Many entities carry a label that looks like a keyword, which is why the two are often mixed up. Google's Knowledge Panel Help says knowledge panels are information boxes that appear for entities in the Knowledge Graph, that they are generated automatically from information across the web, and that they update as information changes.

Entity SEO vs keyword SEO

AreaKeyword SEOEntity SEO
Unit of workA phrase people typeA thing, and its facts and links to other things
QuestionDoes the page contain the phrase?Is it clear which thing the page is about?
Main riskMissing a phraseBeing confused with another thing, or described wrongly
Typical tasksTitles, headings, copyFacts, structured data, internal links, profiles, mentions
MeasureRankings and trafficCorrect descriptions, knowledge panels, AI answers, branded search

Both matter. Entity work does not replace keyword research. It adds a check on whether the systems reading your site can tell who you are.

Why do entities matter for SEO and AI search?

Search engines and language models both work with meaning, not only matching words. If your name matches another company, or your pages describe you in several ways, a system may attach the wrong facts to you or skip you. Three pieces of evidence help set expectations.

  • Brand mentions correlate with AI visibility. Ahrefs studied 75,000 brands and found that branded web mentions had the strongest correlation with brand visibility in Google AI Overviews, at 0.664, against 0.218 for backlinks. The next two were branded anchors (0.527) and branded search volume (0.392). Ahrefs also found that 26% of brands had zero AI Overview mentions. This is a correlation, not proof of cause, and Ahrefs says so. The sample was domains with a Domain Rating above 40 and a top keyword of at least 800 searches a month, and the study covers Google AI Overviews only.
  • Google uses organization data to tell organizations apart. Its Organization structured data documentation says adding the markup to your home page can help Google understand your organization's details and disambiguate it in search results. It also says some properties influence the logo shown in Search results and in your knowledge panel.
  • Google says AI features need no special markup. Google lists no extra technical requirements beyond being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. So entity markup is not a trick for AI answers. It is a way to state facts clearly.

There is a fair counter view. In a 2024 article titled "Stop overcomplicating things. Entity SEO is just SEO," Ahrefs argues that you do not need to treat entity work as a separate discipline. We agree with part of that. Most of the plan below is ordinary good practice. We still find the entity lens useful, because it points to a short list of checks that many sites fail, such as an old company description on a directory or no clear About page.

How do you find the entities for your site?

Start with what you already know, then use tools to find what you missed. This answers a common question: how to find entities for SEO optimization.

  1. List your own entities. Your company, its legal and short names, your products and services, your leaders and authors, your locations and your main topics.
  2. Check what search shows. Search your brand and your topics. Note any knowledge panel, the "People also ask" questions and the related searches. These show the things Google links to your topic.
  3. Look at public catalogs. See whether Wikipedia or Wikidata has an entry for your topics. Note the standard names they use for each concept. Use the same names where they fit.
  4. Read what competitors cover. Open the top pages for your topic and list the people, tools, terms and concepts they mention. Our semantics check does this for every post we write.
  5. Use an entity tool. Google's Cloud Natural Language API can list the entities it finds in a text. Run your own page through it and see whether the main entity is the one you meant.
  6. Ask AI tools. Ask "What is [brand]?" and "Who is [person]?" in ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. Compare each answer with your facts.

To find related entities, look at the terms and concepts that appear around your topic on several top pages, and at the questions people ask. Include the ones a reader would expect to see, and skip the rest. Do not stuff a page with names.

A nine-step entity SEO plan

Step 1: Write your fact sheet

Write one page of facts: your legal name, trading name, a one-sentence description, what you sell, who you serve, locations, founding date, leaders and official profile links. Every later step uses this sheet.

Step 2: Build a clear entity home

SEO practitioners describe an "entity home": a main page that acts as the source of truth for an entity, which Helen Pollitt says search engines often look for. This is practitioner advice, not a Google rule. For a company, that is usually the About page or the home page. Put the facts from your sheet there in plain text. For each person who writes for you, build an author page with a short bio, credentials and profile links.

Step 3: Add Organization structured data

Google's documentation says there are no required properties, and it recommends adding as many relevant ones as you can. Useful ones include name, alternateName, url, logo, description, address, contactPoint, legalName, foundingDate and sameAs. Google says to use the same name and alternate name that you use for your site name, and that sameAs can list pages about your organization on other sites, such as social or review profiles. Here is a short sample with a made-up company:

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Organization",
  "name": "Example Co",
  "legalName": "Example Company Limited",
  "url": "https://www.example.com/",
  "logo": "https://www.example.com/logo.png",
  "description": "Example Co builds scheduling software for clinics.",
  "foundingDate": "2018",
  "sameAs": [
    "https://www.linkedin.com/company/example-co",
    "https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/example-co"
  ]
}

The markup must match what the page shows. Validate it before you publish.

Step 4: Mark up people and connect them

Use Person markup for authors and leaders, with sameAs links to their real profiles, and connect each person to the organization with a property such as worksFor. Describe real relationships only.

Step 5: Make your profiles match

Compare your website, Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, directories and review sites against your fact sheet. Fix old names, addresses, phone numbers and descriptions. AI answers often repeat an old directory line, so a wrong listing can cost more than a weak page.

Step 6: Handle Wikipedia and Wikidata with care

These catalogs feed knowledge systems, but you cannot simply add yourself. Wikipedia has notability rules, and self-promotional edits break its policies. If your company or a person meets the rules, an independent editor can write the entry from reliable sources. Otherwise, build the independent coverage first. Never create fake pages or sources.

Step 7: Write pages that make the entity clear

Define each core term in the first sentence of its page. Use the standard name for each concept, and use it the same way throughout. Place related entities in context, for example "Reinforce Lab" with its founder, "Jamil Ahmed". Link related pages with descriptive anchor text, and keep one main topic for each page. Our guide to generative engine optimization shows how this carries into AI answers.

Step 8: Earn real mentions

Given the Ahrefs correlation, honest mentions on other sites matter. Good sources are press, industry sites, partner pages, reviews, podcasts and communities where you help people. Do not buy mentions or post fakes. Google's guidance for AI features says seeking inauthentic mentions is not as helpful as it might seem.

Step 9: Test and repeat

Every quarter, ask AI tools what they say about your brand, your key people and your products, and compare with your fact sheet. Check your branded search results and any knowledge panel. Our guide on checking if AI tools mention your brand gives a 30-minute test, and our list of AI brand visibility tools covers tracking at scale.

How does entity SEO relate to topical authority?

Search Engine Journal's Helen Pollitt notes that the structure of a site can reinforce the relationships between entities. Classifying products or posts by their relationship to each other, and linking subtopics back to a main category, signals that the site has deep, structured expertise on a subject, in place of keyword targeting. This is the link between entity work and topical authority: a clear brand entity, a clear set of topic entities and pages that connect them with descriptive links. In practice, give each main topic one strong page, link the supporting pages to it, name the same concept the same way throughout, and use images with descriptive file names and alt text that name what they show. These are practitioner recommendations. Google does not publish a topical authority score, so judge the work by whether the pages answer questions and the facts are consistent.

Worked example: a company with a shared name

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a nine-person analytics firm called "Apex Data". Another company, a data-center operator, uses a similar name. When the firm asks AI tools "What is Apex Data?", two of three answers describe the data-center operator.

The firm writes its fact sheet and puts a clear description on its About page, starting with "Apex Data is a nine-person analytics firm that builds dashboards for restaurants." It adds Organization markup with its LinkedIn and Crunchbase profiles in sameAs. It fixes its directory listings, which gave an older name. It adds author pages for its two writers. It earns a feature in a restaurant trade publication and two customer reviews on a software review site. After 60 days it repeats its test. It keeps the results either way, because the goal is a fair comparison, not a promise.

How does entity SEO work for local and service firms?

For a local or service firm, the main entities are the business, its locations and its people. Use the same business name, address format and phone number on your site, your Google Business Profile and every directory. Give each lawyer, doctor, consultant or engineer a page with credentials, and link each person to the services they provide. Add LocalBusiness or a more specific type in your markup if it fits, and keep the address in the markup the same as the address on the page. Check that your name does not collide with another business nearby, and if it does, add a clear descriptor, such as the type of work, in your profiles and your About text.

How does entity SEO work for online stores?

For a store, products are the key entities. Search Engine Journal's Helen Pollitt notes that identifying codes such as SKUs, ISBNs and GTINs help search engines see that products are different from each other, and that using them consistently across the site helps. Keep product names, brand names and categories the same across your pages, your feed and marketplaces. Link each product to its brand and category, and keep prices and availability current. Our technical SEO service includes this kind of data check.

How do you measure entity SEO?

There is no single score. Use a short list of checks and record them with dates:

  • Accuracy test. Ask ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity "What is [brand]?", "Who runs [brand]?" and "What does [brand] sell?" three times each. Count answers with a material error.
  • Consistency audit. Compare your fact sheet with your site, profiles and directories. Count mismatches and fix them.
  • Branded search. Watch branded impressions and clicks in Search Console, and see which pages show for your brand name.
  • Knowledge panel and rich results. Search your brand and note whether a panel appears, and whether its facts are right. Use Google's Rich Results Test to check markup.
  • Mentions. Track new, honest mentions on other sites, and check which sites AI answers cite for your category.
  • AI impressions. In Search Console's Generative AI performance report, check impressions for pages that state your core facts.

Treat changes as signs, not proof. Answers vary from run to run, so repeat each test and compare rates over time.

Does entity SEO help with AI search?

It can help models describe you correctly, because models learn about brands from text that mentions them. The Ahrefs data fits that idea, though it is a correlation. Remember the limits: Google says no special markup is required for its AI features, and no one outside the AI companies knows exactly how they choose sources. So use entity work to remove confusion, not to chase a trick.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Treating entities as keywords. Repeating a name many times does not clarify it.
  • Using different names. A short name on the site and a legal name on a directory, with no link between them, makes a system unsure.
  • Over-marking pages. Markup that does not match the page can be ignored or cause problems.
  • Chasing a knowledge panel. Panels are generated automatically. Focus on clear facts and independent coverage.
  • Faking Wikipedia or Wikidata entries. It breaks their rules and risks your reputation.
  • Ignoring old listings. Wrong facts on third-party sites often feed wrong answers.
  • Stopping after the markup. Mentions, profiles and clear pages do most of the work.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services. Nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. Our technical SEO service covers structured data, and you can get your free diagnostic.

Final thoughts

Entity SEO is mostly clarity. Know your entities, state the facts once and use them everywhere, mark them up accurately, link related pages clearly and earn honest mentions. Then test what search and AI tools say about you, fix what is wrong and repeat each quarter.

Google lists no extra markup requirement for its AI features, so use entity work to state facts clearly, not as a trick.
Knowledge panels are generated automatically. Focus on clear facts and independent coverage, not on chasing a panel.
Never fake Wikipedia or Wikidata entries. Build independent coverage first.
Test what ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity say about you each quarter and fix the sources that are wrong.

title: What Is llms.txt and Should You Add One?
content:
llms.txt is a proposed plain-text file, written in Markdown and placed at the root of a website, that gives language models a short guide to the site and links to its most useful pages. It is not a web standard, and the evidence so far shows that few AI tools read it. Google says Google Search does not use it, a 2026 Ahrefs study found that 97% of llms.txt files received no requests in a month, and an SE Ranking study found no link between having the file and being cited. Adding one is cheap and harmless, but it should come after the basics that do move results.

This guide explains what llms.txt is, who reads it, what the data shows, whether you should add one, and how to write one if you decide to. It includes a sample file, a way to test it and a worked example. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we state the limits of each study.

What is llms.txt?

The llms.txt file was proposed by Jeremy Howard in September 2024. The proposal calls for a Markdown file at /llms.txt on a website, or at a subpath such as /docs/llms.txt, that offers brief background, guidance and links to detailed pages. The idea is to give an AI model or agent a clean, short map of the site, so it does not have to wade through navigation, scripts and ads in ordinary HTML pages.

The proposal also suggests that pages with information agents might need provide a clean Markdown version at the same address with .md added, and that sites use standard link relations to point to those files. The proposal was updated in 2026, so check the current text at llmstxt.org if you build one.

What does an llms.txt file contain?

The proposed format is simple. It has these parts, in order:

  • A heading of level one with the name of the site or project. This is the only required part.
  • A quote block with a short summary of the site, containing the key facts needed to understand the rest of the file.
  • Optional paragraphs or lists with more detail on how to read the files.
  • Optional sections, each with a level-two heading, that hold lists of links. Each list item has a Markdown link and, if you like, a colon and a short note.
  • An optional section named "Optional" for secondary links that an agent can skip when it needs less context.

Here is a short sample for a made-up company:

# Example Co

> Example Co makes scheduling software for medical clinics in the United States. Plans start at a fixed monthly price per location.

Key facts: founded in 2018, based in Austin, Texas. Support is available on weekdays.

## Product

- [Features](https://www.example.com/features/): What the software does and who it is for
- [Pricing](https://www.example.com/pricing/): Plans, prices and what each includes
- [Integrations](https://www.example.com/integrations/): Systems it connects to

## Help

- [Setup guide](https://www.example.com/help/setup/): Step-by-step setup for a new clinic
- [Security](https://www.example.com/security/): How patient data is protected

## Optional

- [Blog](https://www.example.com/blog/): Articles and updates

Who reads llms.txt?

This is the key question, and the answer today is "very few tools." We found three sources.

  • Google says Google Search does not use it. In its guide to generative AI features, Google lists llms.txt files among things you do not need, because Google Search itself does not use them. It adds that creating one is fine for other services that use it, and will neither harm nor help your visibility in Google Search.
  • Almost no one requests it. Ahrefs studied 137,210 domains in its Web Analytics product that received traffic in May 2026. It found that 28% published an llms.txt file, and that 97% of those files received no requests at all that month. Of the requests that did arrive, 96% came from bots. Among named AI tools, GPTBot made the most requests, and Claude Code was second. Ahrefs also found that AI bots never asked for llms.txt files that did not exist, so publishing one does not put you on an AI radar. Limits: Ahrefs customers skew technical, so the 28% adoption is an upper bound, a fetch does not prove a read, and the study did not check whether files followed the specification.
  • No measurable link to citations. SE Ranking analyzed nearly 300,000 domains. It found llms.txt on 10.13% of them, with adoption about the same across low, mid and high traffic sites. It reported no correlation between having the file and how often a domain was cited by AI tools, and its model got slightly more accurate when it removed the llms.txt factor. Limits: it is an observational study of one dataset, it has no crawler logs, and the authors call the results context-dependent. It bounds the size of any effect and does not prove that no effect exists for any site.

The two studies used different methods and data, and they point the same way. Neither one shows that major AI search tools use the file to decide what to cite.

Does llms.txt help you get cited by AI tools?

We found no evidence that it does. OpenAI's documentation tells site owners to allow OAI-SearchBot and to allow requests from its published IP addresses. It does not mention llms.txt as a factor. ChatGPT search, Google's AI features and Perplexity retrieve pages through their own search systems, and a separate file that lists your best pages does not change which pages those systems retrieve. That is our reading, and the studies fit it, but no one outside the AI companies can say for certain.

There is one group where the file may have more use: tools that read documentation. Ahrefs found that Claude Code was the second most frequent named AI fetcher of llms.txt files, ahead of the AI search bots. That suggests developer tools and coding agents may look for the file when working with documentation. This is an inference from request counts, so treat it as a lead to test on a documentation site, not as proof.

Why do audit tools and guides mention llms.txt?

Because the idea spread faster than the evidence. Ahrefs reports that Google's Chrome Lighthouse audit for llms.txt accounted for roughly 1 in 1,000 of the fetches it measured, and that about 12% of fetches came from the industry studying itself, such as GEO and AEO tools, llms.txt checkers and researchers. In other words, a good share of the traffic to these files comes from people and tools that check for them. That does not show that AI platforms use the file to answer questions. If a tool tells you that a missing llms.txt is a failing grade for AI visibility, ask for the source. Google lists no such requirement, and the two studies we read found no link to citations. A fair audit marks it as optional.

How is llms.txt different from robots.txt and a sitemap?

The three files do different jobs, and only two of them are well established.

FileJobWho reads it
robots.txtTells crawlers which parts of a site they may fetchSearch and AI crawlers that honor it, such as Googlebot, OAI-SearchBot and ClaudeBot
XML sitemapLists the URLs you want search engines to findSearch engines such as Google and Bing
llms.txtOffers a short guide and curated links for language modelsNo major AI platform has committed to it. A few bots and tools fetch it.

If a page is blocked in robots.txt, listing it in llms.txt does not open it. If a page is missing from your sitemap, listing it in llms.txt does not make a search engine index it. So the file cannot fix access or indexing problems. Those need their own checks.

What do the studies prove, and what do they not?

It helps to read the two studies with care, since each answers a different question.

  • Ahrefs measured requests. It asked who fetches llms.txt files. The answer was almost no one in the month it studied. It could not say whether a fetch changed an answer, and it noted that its figures are ceilings on real use.
  • SE Ranking measured an outcome. It asked whether domains with the file were cited more. It found no link. It could not look at crawler logs, so it could not say whether retrieval bots ever requested the files. A fair reading is that any effect is too small to see in that data.
  • Neither covers the future. AI platforms may change what they read. The proposal itself was updated in 2026. If a major platform announces support, the advice here should change, and we would update this guide.

The honest summary is that the file has no proven benefit today and a small, easy cost.

What about Markdown versions of your pages?

The proposal goes further than a single file. It suggests that pages with information agents might need offer a clean Markdown copy, at the same address with .md added, and that sites point to those copies with standard link relations or HTTP headers. This helps most when a page is hard to read, for example when it is full of scripts, tabs or widgets. For ordinary articles that already render clean HTML, the benefit is smaller. If you try it, serve the same content as the page, since showing a model different facts from what people see risks trust problems. Test on a small set of pages first, and check logs to see whether anything fetches them.

Should you add an llms.txt file?

Type of siteOur viewWhy
Developer documentation or API siteWorth tryingCoding tools and agents may read it, and docs are already structured
Software company marketing siteOptionalLow cost, no proven effect. Do access, answers and facts first.
Local or service businessLow priorityAI answers rely more on listings, reviews and clear pages
Online storeLow priorityProduct data, feeds and reviews matter more
Publisher or blogOptionalNo evidence of a citation effect

If you add one, the risks are small: a few hours of work, and the file can go out of date. A stale file that points to removed pages or old prices adds wrong facts to a place that tools may read. So add it only if someone will keep it current.

How do you create an llms.txt file?

  1. Pick your most useful pages. Choose 10 to 30 pages that explain who you are, what you offer, prices, help and key policies.
  2. Write the summary. One or two plain sentences with the key facts. Use the same name and description you use everywhere else.
  3. List the links. Group them under clear headings, with a short note for each that says what the page contains.
  4. Keep it short and true. Do not add claims you would not put on your site. Do not stuff it with keywords.
  5. Publish it at the root. Make it available at yoursite.com/llms.txt with a normal 200 response. Open it in a browser to check that it shows as plain text.
  6. Keep it current. Review it whenever you change prices, services or key pages.

Many "llms.txt generator" tools can draft a file from your sitemap. Because the file is short, writing it by hand takes little time, and it lets you choose which pages matter. If you use a generator, read the output and remove pages you do not want promoted, such as thin or outdated ones.

The file does not control access. It is not a replacement for robots.txt. To allow or block AI crawlers, use robots.txt and your firewall settings. Our robots.txt guide explains the file.

How do you test whether llms.txt does anything on your site?

Treat it as an experiment with a clear test.

  1. Check your logs. After you publish, look at your server or CDN logs for requests to /llms.txt. Note the user agents. If nothing asks for it in a month, you have your answer for now.
  2. Run a prompt baseline first. Before you publish, run 10 to 15 buyer questions three times in ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity, and record whether you are named and cited. Repeat after 60 days. SparkToro found less than a 1 in 100 chance that the same prompt returns the same list of brands twice, so a change must be large and repeated to mean anything.
  3. Change one thing at a time. If you also rewrite pages in the same month, you cannot tell which change did what.

Our guide to checking if AI tools mention your brand gives a 30-minute version of this test.

What should you do before llms.txt?

These steps have better support:

  1. Let search crawlers in. OpenAI says sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers.
  2. Make pages readable in HTML. In December 2024, Vercel found that none of the major AI crawlers it tested rendered JavaScript.
  3. Answer questions first, with sources. A Princeton-led test of nine content changes found that adding citations, quotations and statistics lifted visibility by up to 40%.
  4. Keep your facts consistent across your site and your profiles.
  5. Earn honest mentions on the sites that AI answers cite.

Our guides to generative engine optimization and ranking in AI Overviews cover these steps in detail.

Worked example: a software company with a docs site

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a company with a marketing site and a separate documentation site for its API. Its docs site has 300 pages, and developers often ask coding assistants how to use it.

The team first checks that crawlers can reach the docs, and that pages render as HTML. It then writes an llms.txt file for /docs/ with a two-sentence summary and 25 links in four groups: quick start, authentication, API reference and troubleshooting. It adds Markdown versions of the 25 pages. For the marketing site, it decides not to add a file yet, because it has no evidence that the file would help there.

After 30 days the team reads its logs for requests to the docs file and notes which user agents asked. It also asks three coding assistants the same 10 setup questions before and after, and records whether the answers use the right steps. It keeps the sheet whatever the result. The file stays only if the logs and tests show that something uses it.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Expecting a ranking or citation boost. No study we found shows one.
  • Treating it as robots.txt. It does not allow or block crawlers.
  • Listing everything. A long file defeats the purpose of a short guide.
  • Letting it go stale. Old prices and removed pages add wrong facts.
  • Publishing a generator's output without a check. Remove thin, old or private pages.
  • Doing it before the basics. Access, readable pages and clear answers come first.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services. We keep an llms.txt file on our own test site as a low-cost experiment, and we do not expect it to move results. Nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. Our AI search optimization service focuses on the steps with better support, and you can get your free diagnostic.

Final thoughts

llms.txt is a small, optional idea with little proof behind it so far. Google says it does not use the file, and two large studies found it either unread or unrelated to citations. If you run a documentation site, try it and test it. For most other sites, fix access, readable pages, clear answers and honest mentions first, and revisit llms.txt if the evidence changes.

title: What Is AEO? Meaning, Definition and How It Works in Marketing
content:
AEO stands for answer engine optimization. In marketing, AEO is the practice of making your content and brand easy for answer engines, such as Google's AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity, to understand, trust and use in their answers. The goal moves from "get the click" to "be named and cited when a buyer asks a question." It builds on SEO. It does not replace it.

This guide gives a plain definition, shows how AEO differs from SEO and GEO, and explains why it matters for marketers. It also covers how to use content marketing for AEO, a seven-step plan, how to measure it and a worked example. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we say when a figure is a survey, a forecast or one vendor's data.

What is AEO in marketing? What does it stand for?

AEO means answer engine optimization. An answer engine is a tool that gives a direct answer to a question, instead of only a list of links. Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, ChatGPT search, Gemini, Perplexity and Microsoft Copilot are examples. Voice assistants and featured snippets work in a similar way. So when people ask "what is AEO in digital marketing", the answer is this: it is the work of earning a place in those answers.

You may also see "what is AEO and GEO in marketing". GEO stands for generative engine optimization. The two terms overlap a great deal. AEO is often used for being the direct answer, including in snippets and voice. GEO is often used for being cited by generative AI tools. Many teams do one body of work and use both names. Our guide to AEO vs SEO and our guide to GEO vs SEO cover the details.

What is the meaning of AEO? A short definition

AEO means answer engine optimization. It is the practice of shaping your content so that search engines and AI tools can take it as the direct answer to a question. In digital marketing, that means a clear answer first, then proof, then structure that a machine can read.

The same letters mean something else in trade. In customs, AEO stands for Authorized Economic Operator, a status for trusted traders. If you searched for "AEO certification," that is a different subject. This guide covers the marketing meaning.

What is AEO and GEO in marketing?

GEO means generative engine optimization. AEO aims to make your page the answer. GEO aims to get your brand cited or named in answers that AI tools write. Marketers often do both with the same pages. Read our guides to AEO vs SEO and GEO vs SEO for the differences.

What is AEO in digital marketing?

In digital marketing, AEO is short for answer engine optimization. The full form is "answer engine optimization." It is the work of making your content easy for search answer boxes and AI tools to find, understand and quote. Some writers say "AEO and GEO" together. GEO, or generative engine optimization, is a close cousin that focuses on being mentioned in AI-written answers. The two share most of their tasks.

One note on the letters. In trade and customs, AEO means Authorized Economic Operator. That is a different subject. This guide is about the marketing meaning.

How is AEO different from SEO?

Forrester describes AEO as significantly, but not fundamentally, different from SEO. Both shape what people see on and off your site, both span content and technical work, and both are hard to measure. That is a fair summary. The table shows the main differences in daily work.

AreaSEOAEO
GoalRankings and clicksBeing named, cited and described correctly in answers
Question styleShort keywordsFull questions, comparisons and follow-ups
Content shapeA page that matches intentA page with a direct answer, then proof and detail
Off-site workLinksLinks, mentions, reviews and consistent profiles
MeasurementRank, traffic, conversionsMention rate, citations, branded search, AI impressions

Google takes a plain view. In its guide to generative AI features, it says that optimizing for generative AI search is optimizing for the search experience, and so it is still SEO. It advises care with third-party "AEO" or "GEO" advice.

Why does AEO matter for marketers?

Three kinds of evidence point the same way. They differ in quality, so we state the limits.

  • Buyers use AI to research. G2 surveyed 1,169 B2B decision-makers in April 2025. It found that 79% said AI search had changed how they research, and 29% said they start with AI search more often than Google. Generative AI chatbots were the top source influencing vendor shortlists, at 17.1%. The sample is software buyers who answered G2's survey, and G2 sells software review services.
  • Clicks fall when an AI summary appears. The Pew Research Center tracked 900 US adults in March 2025. People clicked a regular result in 8% of visits to pages with an AI summary and 15% of visits to pages without one, and clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits. Google disputes the study's method.
  • A forecast says search volume will fall. In February 2024, Gartner predicted that traditional search engine volume would drop 25% by 2026, with search marketing losing share to AI chatbots and other virtual agents. It is a forecast, not a measurement. We did not find a source that confirms the figure, so treat it as a view that was current when it was made.

The practical lesson is that being named in the answer matters, even when no click follows. That is why AEO measures mentions and citations as well as traffic.

How do answer engines choose what to cite?

The companies do not publish exact rules. What they say is limited. OpenAI says ChatGPT ranks search results using multiple factors meant to help people find relevant, reliable information, and that placement is not guaranteed. Google says its AI features use query fan-out, where one question is split into related searches, and that a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to be a supporting link. From the documents we read, three things seem to matter. This is our reading and not a formula:

  • Access: the page can be crawled, indexed and read in the HTML.
  • Fit: the page answers the question, or a related one, in a passage that stands alone.
  • Trust: the facts are clear and sourced, the author is named, and other sites agree with what you say.

Content marketing for AEO

Content marketing is where most teams do their AEO work. The shift is small in method and large in discipline. Start from questions, not topics, write the answer first, prove it, and keep it current. Here is how to adapt a normal content program.

Start with a question map

List 20 to 30 questions your buyers ask, from sales calls, support tickets, review sites, Search Console queries and "People also ask". Group them by stage: awareness ("what is X"), consideration ("X vs Y", "best X for Z") and decision ("how much does X cost", "how do I switch"). Mark which ones your site already answers well, and which it does not.

Choose the content types that answer questions

Content typeAnswersAEO tip
Definition page or glossary entry"What is [term]?"A one or two sentence definition first, then detail
How-to guide"How do I [task]?"Numbered steps and a short summary at the top
Comparison page"[A] vs [B]", "best [category]"A dated table and a verdict, with honest limits
Pricing and cost page"How much does it cost?"State prices, or the factors that set them
FAQ sectionCommon follow-upsUse real questions in the buyer's words
Original data or researchQuestions with no good source yetState the method, sample and limits
Case study"Does it work for someone like me?"Dates, a baseline and what else changed

Write for people first

Put the answer in the first sentence under each question heading, then add context, examples and sources. Keep paragraphs short and give each section one idea. Google warns that making separate pages for every small variation of a question, mainly to manipulate rankings or AI answers, breaks its scaled content abuse policy. So build fewer, better pages, and answer related questions inside them.

Add evidence

A Princeton-led team tested nine content changes on a 10,000-query benchmark. It reported that adding citations, quotations from relevant sources and statistics lifted visibility by up to 40%. That is a 2024 benchmark, and results varied by domain. It still supports a good habit: name the source, the date and the method for every number.

Refresh and repeat

Ahrefs analyzed 17 million citations across seven AI search platforms and found that content cited in AI answers was 25.7% fresher than content in regular results. That is a correlation from one vendor's data. Still, review key pages each quarter, fix facts that changed and show a real update date.

What is an answer engine optimization strategy?

An answer engine optimization strategy is a short plan for which questions you want to answer, which pages will answer them and how you will check the results. It has three parts: a list of the questions your buyers ask, a clear answer for each on the right page, and a routine to test whether AI tools and answer boxes use you. The seven steps below turn that into a working plan.

A seven-step AEO plan

  1. Check access. Make sure the search crawlers you want, such as Googlebot, Bingbot and OAI-SearchBot, are not blocked by robots.txt or your firewall. Our robots.txt guide explains the file.
  2. Run a baseline. Test your question list in several AI tools, three runs each, and record whether you are named, cited and described correctly.
  3. Fix your facts. Make your name, description, prices and locations match on your site and in directories.
  4. Write or rewrite the key pages with answer-first openings, clear headings and sourced evidence.
  5. Build real presence on other sites. Run your prompts, list the sites the answers cite, and ask how you can appear on them honestly, with profiles, reviews and useful contributions.
  6. Measure. Repeat the test monthly, and use free reports from Google and Bing.
  7. Refresh. Update pages when facts change, and review the plan each quarter.

How do you measure AEO?

No single number captures it. Use a small set of signs:

  • Mention and citation rate across a fixed prompt list. SparkToro had 600 volunteers run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google's AI features 2,961 times, and found less than a 1 in 100 chance of getting the same list of brands twice. So run each prompt several times and report a rate, not a rank.
  • Google's Generative AI performance report in Search Console, which shows impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode.
  • Bing Webmaster Tools' AI Performance report, which shows citations in Copilot and Bing's AI summaries. Bing says its grounding queries are a sample.
  • Branded search in Search Console, which may rise when you are named without a link.
  • Leads and sales from pages you updated, tracked in analytics.

Our guide to checking if AI tools mention your brand gives a 30-minute test.

What does AEO not require?

Much AEO advice online has no source. Google says that for Google Search you do not need llms.txt files or other special files, "chunking" content into tiny pieces, rewriting content just for AI, or special structured data. It also says no third-party tool has access to its internal ranking or AI systems. This is Google's view of Google Search, and other tools may behave differently. Do the basics first, and test any extra step before you spend on it.

Worked example: a three-person B2B marketing team

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a team that sells HR software to mid-sized companies. It builds a map of 24 questions from sales calls. Its site answers six well, answers nine poorly and does not answer nine.

The team tests the 24 questions three times in three tools, 216 answers in all, and is named in 14. The answers cite two review sites and a competitor's comparison page. The team picks six questions, including "how much does HR software cost" and "[competitor] alternative", and writes or rewrites six pages with answer-first openings, dated tables and two sourced statistics each. It also completes its profiles on both review sites. After 60 days it repeats the same 216 runs and compares the rate of mentions, then looks at the demo requests from the six pages. The result may be small or large. The plan makes it readable.

What does AEO look like for different businesses?

BusinessTypical questionsFocus
B2B software and services"Best [category] for [role]", "[A] vs [B]", "how much does it cost"Comparison, pricing and use-case pages, review-site profiles, clear integration facts
Online stores"Best [product] for [need]", "is [brand] worth it"Complete product data, honest reviews, buying guides, consistent names and codes
Local and service firms"Who does [job] near me", "how much does [service] cost"Accurate listings, service pages with prices or ranges, named experts
Publishers and educators"What is [term]", "how does [thing] work"Clear definitions, named authors, sources and dates, original data

In every case, start with the questions your own buyers ask. The test is whether a stranger who asks an AI tool that question would be told about you, and told the truth.

Which AEO tools help?

You can begin with a spreadsheet and free tools: the AI tools themselves, Search Console's Generative AI performance report, Bing Webmaster Tools and your analytics. SEO suites such as Ahrefs and Semrush offer AI visibility features, including prompt research, and stand-alone trackers run prompts on a schedule. Run a hand test first, so you can judge whether a tool's numbers are right, and be careful with any tool that reports a precise rank inside AI answers. Our guide to AI brand visibility tools compares what they track and what they cost.

How long does AEO take, and what does it cost?

We found no independent data on typical timelines or fees. Access and fact fixes can change retrieval-based answers within weeks, while new content, reviews and outside mentions take longer. The cost depends on how many questions you cover, how much content you write, and whether you need technical fixes and outreach. If you hire help, compare proposals on deliverables, not on the monthly figure, and be wary of promises of placement. Nobody controls AI answers.

Does structured data matter for AEO?

Vendor guides often list FAQ, how-to and article markup as AEO tactics. Google's position is narrower. It says structured data is not required for its generative AI features and that no special schema.org markup is needed, though it still helps with rich result eligibility and clear facts. So use markup that matches your visible content, validate it, and do not expect it to earn a citation by itself. Put the effort first into the answer, the evidence and the facts. Then keep important pages fresh: Ahrefs found that content cited in AI answers was 25.7% fresher than content in regular results, a correlation from one vendor's data, and the practical step is to review key pages on a schedule and show a real update date.

What can you do this week?

You do not need a big program to begin. In one week, you can do five things. On day one, write down 15 questions your buyers ask. On day two, run each three times in ChatGPT and Google, and save the answers in a sheet. On day three, check your robots.txt and firewall for blocks on search crawlers. On day four, compare your name, description and prices across your site and your top three profiles, and fix the mismatches. On day five, pick the one question where you lose most clearly, and rewrite the page that should answer it, with the answer in the first sentence and two sourced facts. Then repeat the same test in a month. That small loop teaches more than any report.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Treating AEO as a separate trick. Most of it is good SEO with clearer answers and evidence.
  • Making a page for every phrasing. Google calls mass pages made to manipulate results scaled content abuse.
  • Using unsourced numbers. A figure with no source is a risk to readers and to models.
  • Chasing a rank in AI answers. Lists change from run to run.
  • Ignoring other sites. Answers often rely on reviews, lists and directories.
  • Testing once. One answer is a clue, not a result.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services. Nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. Our SEO content systems service and AI search optimization service follow the plan above, and you can get your free diagnostic.

Final thoughts

AEO in marketing is the discipline of being the clear, trusted answer. Start with your buyers' questions, write the answer first, prove it with sources, keep facts consistent and current, and earn honest mentions on the sites that answers cite. Test with a fixed prompt list and expect to adjust.

title: GEO for Law Firms: How to Get Found and Recommended by AI Tools
content:
GEO for law firms means making your firm and your lawyers easy for AI tools to find, understand and name accurately when people ask legal questions. GEO stands for generative engine optimization. In practice it is good SEO plus clear firm facts, answer-first practice pages, strong lawyer bios, honest profiles on the sites AI answers cite, and a monthly check of what the tools say. It must also follow your advertising rules, because a false or misleading claim is a risk whether a person or an AI tool repeats it.

This guide explains how GEO works for a firm, what the data shows, and a plan you can run. It includes a worked example and a short section on choosing an agency. This is general marketing information, not legal advice. Advertising rules differ by state and country, so check your own bar or regulator before you publish. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we say when a figure is a survey or a test.

What is GEO for law firms?

Generative engine optimization is work that helps AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews cite and recommend your content. For a law firm it covers two kinds of questions. The first is informational: "how long do I have to file a claim", "do I need a lawyer for a slip and fall", "what does probate cost". The second is a shopping question: "best family lawyer near me" or "what should I ask a divorce lawyer".

Our guide to generative engine optimization explains the general method. This article applies it to legal services, where trust, accuracy and ethics rules matter more than in most fields.

Why does it matter for law firms?

Clients are already using AI. Clio's 2025 Legal Trends Report surveyed 1,000 US adults, a sample that matches the US population by age, gender, region, income and race. It found that 24% had already used AI to answer a legal question, and another 40% would consider it. 46% said they would consult AI before contacting a lawyer. Of those who had used AI for a legal question, 28% were directed by the AI to contact a lawyer, and in 12% of cases the AI convinced them their problem was not worth pursuing. Clio also found that more consumers say they would look for their next lawyer online. This is a survey of self-reported behavior by a software company, so read it as a direction, not an exact count.

The same report notes that many consumers asked AI how to find "the best" lawyer. If AI tools are shaping how people shop, your firm needs to be named correctly in those answers.

What do the advertising rules say?

In the US, ABA Model Rule 7.1 says a lawyer shall not make a false or misleading communication about the lawyer or the lawyer's services. It adds that a communication is false or misleading if it contains a material misrepresentation of fact or law, or leaves out a fact needed to keep the statement from being misleading as a whole. States adopt their own versions, and many add rules on testimonials, specialist claims and past results. Check yours.

For GEO, the practical meaning is simple. Everything on your site and your profiles can be quoted by an AI tool, so every claim must be accurate, current and supportable. That includes:

  • No promise or implied guarantee of a result.
  • No "best" or "top" claim you cannot support.
  • Past results stated with the context your bar requires.
  • No specialist or certified label that your jurisdiction does not allow.
  • A lawyer reviews every page, including pages drafted with AI help.

Never write GEO content that is designed to mislead a model. Even if it worked, it would put your license and your reputation at risk.

What does the evidence say about getting cited?

  • Evidence in the page helps, in a test. A Princeton-led team tested nine content changes on a 10,000-query benchmark. They reported that adding citations, quotations from relevant sources and statistics boosted visibility by up to 40%, with gains up to 37% on Perplexity. The effect varied by domain, and the study dates from 2024. For lawyers, the natural version is to cite the statute, the court rule or the agency page.
  • Answers change from run to run. SparkToro had 600 volunteers run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google's AI features 2,961 times. There was less than a 1 in 100 chance of the same list of brands twice. So measure how often you appear across many prompts, and do not chase a rank.
  • Crawl access can decide it. OpenAI says sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot are not shown in ChatGPT search answers. Security plugins and CDN settings sometimes block bots without anyone noticing.
  • Google adds no special requirements. To be a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, a page must be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet, and Google lists no additional technical requirements.

An eight-step GEO plan for a law firm

Step 1: Let the right crawlers in

Open your robots.txt and your security settings. Make sure Googlebot, Bingbot and OAI-SearchBot are not blocked on the pages you want cited. Whether you allow training bots is a separate choice. Our robots.txt guide explains the file.

Step 2: Fix your firm facts

Write one set of facts: the legal name, address format, main phone number, offices, practice areas, and the names and roles of your lawyers. Make your website, Google Business Profile, bar and directory listings, and social profiles match. An AI tool that sees three versions of your address may repeat the wrong one, or skip you.

Step 3: Build practice pages that answer the question first

For each practice area, answer what a client actually asks: who you represent, what the process looks like in your state, how long it usually takes, how fees work and what to do now. Put a direct answer in the first sentence under each heading, then add detail and exceptions. Name the state or country the answer covers, and the date it was checked. Law changes, and old advice can mislead.

Step 4: Show who stands behind the content

Give each lawyer a real bio page with bar admissions, courts, practice areas, education and published work. Link each practice page to the lawyers who handle that work, and add a named author or reviewer to legal articles. Google's guidance for generative AI features says unique, expert-led content with a clear point of view matters more over time than tricks. Use LegalService markup for the firm and Person markup for each lawyer if you like. Google says special markup is not required for its AI features, but accurate markup can make the facts clearer.

Step 5: Cite your sources

Link to the statute, rule, court decision or government page that supports each factual claim, and quote the key text where it helps. This matches the tactic with the best test evidence, and it makes your page more useful to a reader who wants to check it.

Step 6: Keep your profiles and reviews honest and current

AI answers often draw on third-party sources, not only your site. Common ones for lawyers include your state bar's public directory, legal directories, Google reviews and local press. Run your prompts, list the sites the answers cite, and claim and complete the profiles that matter. Ask real clients for honest reviews, and follow your bar's rules on how you ask. Never post fake reviews.

Step 7: Build local pages only where they are real

Create a city or county page only where you have an office or regularly handle matters, and make it useful: local courts, procedures, how to meet you. Google warns that making many pages to manipulate rankings or AI answers breaks its scaled content abuse policy, and pages that only swap a city name add risk and no value.

Step 8: Measure monthly

Write 15 to 25 prompts your clients would use, split by practice area and city. Run each three times in ChatGPT, Google and Perplexity, and record whether your firm is named, whether your site is linked, which sources the answers cite and which competitors appear. Use Search Console's Generative AI performance report for Google impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode. Our guides on checking if AI tools mention your brand and AI brand visibility tools explain how to do this.

What should a practice page contain?

A practice page works for people and for AI tools when each part answers one clear question. Use this outline and adapt it to your practice area and your state.

SectionWhat it answersTip
Opening answerWhat this area of law covers and whom you helpOne or two plain sentences, then detail
How the process worksThe usual steps and who is involvedName the state, court or agency and the date you checked
Time limits and key rulesDeadlines and rules that matterCite the statute or rule, and say when it changed if it did
Fees and costsHow you charge and what affects the priceA range or the factors, if your rules allow it
What to do nowSafe first steps for a clientKeep it general and add a notice that it is not legal advice
Your lawyersWho handles this workLink to bios with admissions and experience
FAQsThe questions clients ask on callsUse the client's words, and answer in the first sentence

The fee question matters. Marketers who work with small firms say one of the first questions a prospective client asks an AI tool is what a lawyer will cost, and a page that answers it has a better chance of being cited. That is a practitioner view, not a measured result. Answer it only as far as your rules and your practice allow.

What do clients ask AI about lawyers?

Clients ask two kinds of questions, and each needs a different page.

  • Information questions: "how long does probate take", "what happens at a first DUI hearing", "can my landlord keep my deposit". These are answered by practice pages and plain guides. Be careful to give general information and to say it is not legal advice.
  • Shopping questions: "best personal injury lawyer in my city", "what to ask a divorce lawyer before hiring". These are answered by third-party sources, reviews and lists, and by your own pages on how to choose a lawyer. Write that page honestly, with questions a client should ask any firm, and include what you do.

Clio found that many consumers asked AI how to find "the best" lawyer. If an AI tool typically lists key questions to ask, prepare strong, honest answers to each on your site.

How is GEO different from local SEO for law firms?

Local SEO aims to put your firm in the map pack and local results. It rests on your Google Business Profile, reviews, consistent name, address and phone number, and local pages. GEO builds on those same facts, and adds work on how AI tools describe you: answer-first pages, lawyer credentials, sourced claims and the third-party sites that AI answers cite. If your local SEO is weak, fix it first, because many AI answers about local services rely on the same listings. Our local SEO service covers that base.

Does GEO work for every practice area?

The method is the same, but the risks and the questions differ. Personal injury, family, immigration, criminal defense and estate planning all attract AI questions, and each has its own rules on advertising, results and confidentiality. Practice areas with strict rules on solicitation or testimonials need more care. Competition also differs by city and by area, so test your own prompts to see which firms and sources the tools name before you plan content.

What about Bing, ChatGPT and attorney markup?

OpenAI says ChatGPT search sometimes partners with other search providers, and its notes name Microsoft, so check that your key pages are indexed in Bing as well as Google. Bing Webmaster Tools lets you submit a sitemap and see AI citations in its AI Performance report. For markup, one law-firm guide recommends LegalService for the firm and Person for each lawyer, with sameAs links to the lawyer's state bar profile and legal directories, kept consistent with what the page shows. Google says no special markup is required for its AI features, so treat markup as a way to state facts clearly and not as a trick. A short audit for a firm is to check four things: crawler access, Bing and Google indexing, matching facts across the site and profiles, and a bio page for every lawyer with admissions and focus areas.

Worked example: a six-lawyer family law firm

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a firm with offices in two cities. Its site has one page called "Family Law" with 300 words, no author, and an address that differs on its site and its directory listings.

The team runs 18 prompts three times in three tools, 162 answers in all. The firm is named in 11, about 7%. The answers cite two directories and a local news site where the firm is not listed, and one competitor's guide to custody rules.

The plan has five parts. The firm fixes its address everywhere. It splits the family page into five pages, such as divorce process and custody, each with an answer-first opening, the state statute cited and a reviewer byline. It adds bios for all six lawyers. It completes its two directory profiles, and asks former clients for honest reviews in line with its bar's rules. After 60 days it repeats the same 162 runs. Whatever the result, the firm keeps the sheet. The aim is a fair comparison, not a promise of leads.

How do you choose a GEO agency for a law firm?

Choose an agency that knows legal advertising rules and says so in writing. Ask who will review claims for compliance, how past results and testimonials are handled, and whether a lawyer at your firm approves each page. Ask for the prompt list, the raw answers, a source map and a ranked fix list. Be wary of any promise of a place in AI answers, because the AI companies do not publish how they choose. Our generative engine optimization service follows this method, and our professional services work covers firms like yours.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Thin practice pages. One short page for each practice area gives a model little to quote.
  • Unreviewed AI content. A lawyer must check every page for accuracy and for advertising compliance.
  • Inconsistent firm facts. Different addresses and names across sites cause confusion.
  • City pages with swapped names. They add risk and no value.
  • Chasing a rank in AI answers. The order changes from run to run.
  • Ignoring third-party sources. The answer may rely on a directory you have not claimed.
  • Skipping the rules. Superlatives, guarantees and unclear results can breach your bar's rules.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells SEO and AI search services, including to professional services firms. We are a marketing firm, not a law firm, and nothing here is legal advice. Nothing is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. You can get your free diagnostic, which tests your site and a prompt list with a written plan.

Final thoughts

For a law firm, GEO starts with trust. Get crawlers in, fix your facts, write practice pages that answer first and cite the law, show the lawyers behind them, and earn honest profiles on the sites AI answers cite. Keep every claim inside your advertising rules, test monthly, and judge the work by what clients ask and who calls.

How do I choose a GEO agency for a law firm? | Choose one that understands legal advertising rules and has a lawyer at your firm approve each page. Ask for the prompt list, raw answers, a source map and a ranked fix list, and avoid promises of placement.
