title: SEO for Professional Services: How Firms Win the Who Should I Hire Search
content:
SEO for professional services is the work of helping law firms, accountants, consultants, engineers, advisers and similar firms be found, and be trusted, when a buyer searches for expert help. The buyer is choosing people as much as a firm, so the pages that matter most are practice and service pages, partner profiles, proof of past work and clear ways to get in touch. Measure the work by qualified inquiries, not by traffic.

This guide covers how clients choose a professional firm, what the data shows about AI search, the keywords and pages that win, the rules you must respect, a 90-day plan and a worked example. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we say when a figure is a vendor survey. This is marketing information, not legal or accounting advice. Check the advertising rules of your own professional body before you publish.

What is SEO for professional services?

It is search engine optimization for firms that sell expertise and judgment: law, accounting and tax, management and technology consulting, engineering, architecture, financial advice and similar fields. There is no product to demonstrate. Buyers look for evidence that specific people have handled a specific problem before. So the work combines normal SEO with proof of expertise, accurate profiles and a clear path to an inquiry.

How do clients choose a professional services firm?

Most engagements start with a trigger: a dispute, a deal, an audit, a new rule or a problem the buyer cannot solve alone. The buyer then builds a short list, often from a referral, and checks each name. A practitioner view from a UK agency is that, for specialist business advice, search often confirms a referral as much as it replaces one. That is an agency's observation, not a measured result, but it matches how most firms win work: people check you out before they call.

That checking is changing. Two 2026 surveys show where buyers now start.

  • VML's Future Buyer study. VML, a marketing agency, reports that in its professional services report, 58% of buyers begin supplier research on generative AI tools, ahead of traditional search engines (48%) and direct outreach (41%). It also reports that 34% form a firm supplier preference before ever speaking to one, and that 62% have shortlisted an unfamiliar supplier because of high-quality thought leadership. The series is based on first-party research with 750 buyers across eight international markets. It is an agency's study and we could not see the full method, so treat the figures as a direction.
  • Semrush's B2B buyer survey. Semrush surveyed 643 US B2B professionals in March and April 2026. Of the 519 who use AI at work, 66% regularly use it to research vendors and solutions, and 92% said AI had shaped their vendor shortlist. Agencies and service providers topped the list of things researched with AI, at 51%. About 14% of the respondents were in professional services. Semrush sells SEO software, and the sample is people who use AI at work.

For legal services, Clio's 2025 Legal Trends Report surveyed 1,000 US adults. It found that 24% had already used AI to answer a legal question, and 46% would consult AI before contacting a lawyer. Clio is a software company, and this is self-reported behavior.

The common message is that buyers now ask AI tools early, and that clear expertise helps you appear. It does not remove the need for classic SEO. It adds a second place to be found.

What do professional services buyers search for?

Group searches by what the buyer knows.

Search typeExamplePage that serves it
Problem"What happens if we miss a tax filing deadline"A guide or insight article
Service"Transfer pricing advice for a mid-sized manufacturer"A practice or service page
Service and place"Employment lawyer in Chicago"A practice page with a real local office
Provider check"[Firm name] reviews", "[Partner name]"Your profile, partner pages, listings
Comparison"How to choose an audit firm"A buyer's guide, with honest criteria
Fees"How much does a business valuation cost"A page on how you charge and what affects the price

For private clients, such as conveyancing or personal tax, searches look more like consumer local SEO: high volume, location-led and price-aware. For business clients, searches are rarer, more specific and read in depth.

The pages that win clients

Practice and service pages

Give each practice, service and client type its own page. A single "Services" page with a paragraph for each topic rarely ranks for specific searches. Use the same outline for each page so partners can review it quickly.

SectionWhat it answers
Who it is forThe industry, size or situation, in the first screen
The problemWhat the client faces, in their words
The processSteps, timeline and who they will work with
ProofCredentials, representative work (anonymized if required), publications
FeesHow you charge and what changes the price
Next stepOne clear action: a call, a consultation or a proposal request

Partner and team profiles

Buyers evaluate people. A profile should show roles, credentials, areas of focus, the kind of matters handled, published work, talks and a direct way to get in touch. Thin profiles with only a title and a school lose referred clients at the last step.

Industry pages

If you serve sectors such as healthcare, manufacturing or software, give each its own page with real examples and the rules that matter in that sector.

Insight articles and guides

Write from your own work. Short partner interviews are a good source of content that carries your firm's view. Answer the questions clients ask on calls, put the answer first, cite sources and date the page. Google warns against making many pages mainly to manipulate results, so build fewer, better pages.

Case studies

Proof matters, and confidentiality limits it. Use anonymized examples, or get written consent to name a client. State the situation, what you did, the result and the dates. Never overstate a result, and follow your professional body's rules on results and testimonials.

Location pages

Build a location page only for an office or a market where you actually work, and make it useful, with local details, who is based there and how to visit. Pages that only swap a city name add risk and no value.

What proof do buyers trust?

Buyers of expert services cannot test the work first, so they look for signs that it will be done well. The strongest signs are those that a stranger can check.

  • Credentials they can verify. A license number, a registry entry or a professional body listing, linked from the bio.
  • Named people with a track record. Experience in the buyer's sector, with dates and the type of work.
  • Published thinking. Articles, talks, research and rule-change explainers that show how you reason. VML's survey suggests this thought leadership can put a firm on a short list. Treat that as a survey result from an agency, and still make the content real and useful.
  • Reviews from real clients. On Google and the sites your field uses, collected within your body's rules.
  • Clear fees and process. Buyers worry about cost and effort. A page that explains both builds trust.
  • Consistent facts. The same names, offices and services across your site, directories and social profiles.

How do business buyers differ from private clients?

Private clients, such as a family with a will or a person with a tax return, search by service and place, compare prices and decide quickly. Local SEO, reviews and clear fees matter most. Business buyers, such as a general counsel or a finance director, search rarely, read deeply and ask colleagues. Partner profiles, sector pages and published views matter most, and a referral often starts the process. Many firms serve both, so build the pages for each group separately, with their own questions, tone and calls to action.

What rules do you need to respect?

Professional bodies set advertising and conduct rules, and they differ by field and place. For lawyers in the US, ABA Model Rule 7.1 says a lawyer shall not make a false or misleading communication about the lawyer or the lawyer's services, and states adopt their own versions. Accountants, engineers, financial advisers and others have their own bodies and rules. Common themes are the same:

  • No guarantee or implied promise of a result.
  • No unsupported claims such as "the best" or "leading".
  • Client confidentiality, and consent before you name a client or use a logo.
  • Accurate use of titles, credentials and specialist labels.
  • Rules on testimonials, reviews and how you ask for them.
  • A named person who approves each page.

Write the rules for each credential and place down, and decide who signs off each page. Our guide to generative engine optimization notes that anything on your site can be quoted by an AI tool, so every claim must be accurate and current.

Local SEO for offices

For firms with offices, local search combines the office and the service. Each office needs its own Google Business Profile with the right primary category and honest secondary categories, the same name, address and phone number on your site and every directory, and reviews that you earn from real clients and answer politely. Reviews that name the service help more than "great team". Follow your professional body's rules on how you ask for reviews. Our local SEO service covers this base.

How do you show up in AI search?

The steps are the same ones that serve SEO, with a few additions. Make sure search crawlers can reach your pages. Keep the facts about your firm, partners and services the same across your site and profiles. Put a direct answer at the top of each practice page, with named sources. Earn honest mentions on the sites that AI answers cite, such as directories, professional bodies, press and review sites. Then test with a fixed list of buyer questions, run three times in several AI tools. Our guides to checking if AI tools mention your brand and ranking in AI Overviews explain how.

One caution. Google lists no extra technical requirements for AI Overviews beyond being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. So do not buy special markup or files in the hope of a shortcut.

How do you measure it?

Measure by practice, not as one "leads" number. Track consultation requests and proposal requests from organic landing pages, the share that become real clients, impressions and clicks for each practice page, Google Business Profile calls and direction requests, and branded search. Add a question to your intake form: "How did you hear about us?", with an option for AI tools. Use Google's Generative AI performance report in Search Console for AI impressions, and a prompt sheet for mentions. If a practice page ranks and no one inquires, the offer or the form is the problem. If nothing ranks, the page depth and keyword map are the problem.

How do you report SEO results to partners?

Partners care about clients and fees, not rankings, so report in their terms. A one-page monthly report works well: inquiries by practice, how many became consultations and clients, the pages that produced them, Google Business Profile calls and direction requests, and a short list of what you changed and plan next. Add the AI search check, with the share of test questions on which the firm was named and the sources the answers cited. State the limits, such as small numbers and long sales cycles, since a single large client can swing a month. Many engagements also begin with a referral, so ask every new client how they heard about you, and record when search or an AI tool was part of the path.

A 90-day plan

PeriodWorkResult to check
Weeks 1 to 2Baseline: pages, rankings, inquiries, AI prompt test. Write the rules and sign-off list.A baseline sheet
Weeks 3 to 6Fix profiles and listings. Rewrite the two or three practice pages closest to revenue. Upgrade partner profiles.Matching facts everywhere, new pages live
Weeks 7 to 10Publish two partner-led insight pieces and one case study. Start honest outreach to the sources AI answers cite.Pages indexed, outreach list with status
Weeks 11 to 13Repeat the baseline test. Compare inquiries by practice.A short report with limits and next steps

Worked example: a 30-person accounting firm

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a firm with two offices that offers audit, tax and advisory services. Its site has one "Services" page and short partner bios. Its two office listings use different phone numbers.

The team lists the matters it wants more of: tax planning for owner-managed businesses, and audit for nonprofits. It builds two practice pages with the outline above, with a fees section and a named reviewer. It rewrites four partner profiles with credentials, sectors and published work. It fixes the phone numbers, and asks clients for honest reviews in line with its professional body's rules. It publishes a partner-led guide on year-end tax steps, with dated sources. It also tests 15 buyer questions three times in three AI tools and records the result.

After 90 days it compares inquiries for the two practices with the baseline and repeats its prompt test. The result may be small or large. What matters is that the plan was built around real matters and measured by inquiries.

Should you hire an SEO agency for a professional services firm?

Hire help when you lack time, need technical fixes or want a plan before you spend on content. Choose one that understands your professional body's rules and says so in writing. Ask for a keyword and page map by practice, a list of technical fixes, a sample report tied to inquiries and a statement of who approves each page. We did not find independent data on typical fees, so ask for written quotes and compare deliverables, and be wary of promises of rankings. Google says no one can guarantee a number one ranking. Our professional services work follows this approach.

What are the common mistakes?

  • One page for every service. Specific searches need specific pages.
  • Thin partner profiles. Buyers judge the people.
  • Generic content. Articles written without partner input read like everyone else's.
  • Ignoring the rules. A claim that breaches your body's rules is a risk, however well it ranks.
  • Naming clients without consent. Confidentiality comes first.
  • Measuring only traffic. Track inquiries by practice.
  • Forgetting AI search. Buyers now ask AI tools early.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells SEO and AI search services, including to professional services firms. We are a marketing firm, and nothing here is legal, accounting or other professional advice. Nothing is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. You can get your free diagnostic for a view of your search and AI visibility with a written plan.

Final thoughts

Professional buyers choose people they trust. Build a page for each practice, make your experts visible and verifiable, keep your facts consistent and your claims inside the rules, and earn honest mentions. Test what search and AI tools show, and judge the work by qualified inquiries.

title: SEO AI Agent: What AI Agents for SEO Can and Cannot Do
content:
An SEO AI agent is software that uses a language model plus tools, such as your SEO data, a site crawler or Search Console, to carry out a search task with several steps, like finding keyword gaps, auditing a template or drafting a refresh list. It works best on bounded, repeatable jobs with real data and a person approving the result. It does not guarantee rankings, and without real data it can invent numbers and issues.

This guide explains what SEO AI agents are, what they do well, where they fail, what Google says about AI content, and how to start safely. It includes a checklist, sample prompts and a worked example. We cite only pages we could read at the publisher, and we separate vendor how-to guides, which describe what is possible, from evidence that something works.

What is an SEO AI agent?

An agent is more than a chatbot. A chatbot answers a question. An agent is given a goal, plans steps, uses tools to get data or take actions, and checks its own work along the way. Ahrefs describes an SEO agent that is plugged into live search data and works through a whole task, pulling what it needs and deciding what to do next. Semrush makes a related point: you usually have to connect external tools to an AI platform, by an API or a Model Context Protocol (MCP) connection, so that the agent can use data providers such as Semrush.

The word is used loosely. Gartner warned in 2025 about "agent washing," where vendors rebrand existing products, such as assistants, robotic process automation and chatbots, as agents. It estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of agentic AI vendors were real. So before you buy a tool called an "SEO AI agent," ask what it can see and what it can do.

What can SEO AI agents do?

The table lists the tasks that vendors and practitioners describe, with the data each needs and where a person must check. These are descriptions of what is possible, not proof of results.

TaskWhat the agent doesData it needsHuman check
Keyword research and clusteringExpands a seed topic, groups terms, scores them by your thresholds, drafts a briefLive keyword data (volume, difficulty)Strategist chooses targets and checks intent
Content briefsReads top results, notes common topics and gaps, drafts an outline and questionsSearch results and competitor pagesWriter confirms the angle
Content refresh listsFinds pages with falling traffic and compares them with current top pagesSearch Console and rankingsEditor decides what to update
Technical auditsReviews a crawl, compares with the last run, ranks issues by severityA crawl export or audit toolDeveloper verifies each finding
Internal linkingMaps related pages and suggests links with anchor textA crawl and a topic mapEditor adds only links that help a reader
Monitoring and change detectionChecks sitemap, status codes, schema and sample prompts on a scheduleSite access and scheduled dataOwner acts on alerts
ReportingPulls data into a template and drafts the narrativeSearch Console, analytics, rank dataAnalyst verifies numbers and claims

Practitioners say agents are most reliable on bounded, reversible work with clear acceptance tests, and least reliable where strategy, brand judgment or uncertain evidence decides the right action. Ahrefs and Semrush both advise starting with one workflow that has clear inputs, clear outputs and easy-to-check success measures.

Can AI help with SEO reporting and keyword research?

Yes, with limits. An AI agent can pull numbers into a weekly SEO report, summarize what changed and flag odd drops. It can group a keyword list into topics and suggest questions to cover. It cannot know search volume or difficulty by itself. Those numbers come from your SEO tools, so give the agent the data and check its work. Automating SEO with AI works best on repeatable chores, with a person reviewing the output.

Where do SEO AI agents fail?

  • Made-up data. Without a real data source, an agent can produce plausible search volumes, rankings or competitor facts. Google's guidance on generative AI content explains why: generative models do not retrieve facts, but predict a likely sequence of words based on their training data, so outputs may contain inaccuracies. Google says to fact-check and review AI content, including titles, meta descriptions, structured data and alt text, before you publish.
  • Thin pages at scale. Google's spam policy on scaled content abuse lists, as an example, using generative AI tools to generate many pages without adding value for users. Agents that promise to publish dozens of pages a week raise this risk.
  • Weak strategy and brand judgment. An agent can mistake a correlation for a ranking rule, overwrite brand nuance, duplicate an existing page's intent or expand a page until it competes with a stronger one.
  • Stale facts. An agent may repeat old product or pricing details.
  • Unsafe write access. An agent that can edit your site can change hundreds of pages before anyone notices.
  • Tricks hidden in pages. Agents that read competitor pages or search results can be steered by instructions planted in that content, a risk known as prompt injection.

What does the evidence say about agents in general?

We found no independent test of how well SEO agents cluster keywords or run link building, and the guides that describe them are mostly written by tool vendors. The broader evidence on business agents is cautious. Gartner's June 2025 prediction is that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, because of rising costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. In a January 2025 Gartner poll of 3,412 webinar attendees, 19% said their organization had made significant investments in agentic AI, 42% had made conservative investments, 8% had none and 31% were waiting or unsure. Gartner's 2025 marketing technology survey found that 29% of marketing technology leaders had AI agents in production and 52% were piloting, and that 45% of those with pilots or agents in production said vendor-offered agents were not meeting expectations for business performance. These are forecasts and surveys, mostly of large organizations, so treat them as a caution to start small and measure.

Can AI agents write SEO content?

They can draft it, and many do. Google says that using AI or automation is not against its guidelines when it is not used to manipulate rankings, and that AI does not give content any special gain: if it is useful, helpful, original and trustworthy, it might do well, and if it is not, it might not. The practical approach is to use an agent for the parts that save time, such as a brief, a source pack and a first draft inside a fixed brief, and then add what only your team can: first-hand experience, real data, named sources and a point of view. A person checks every fact. Our ChatGPT SEO guide covers safe uses of AI for SEO tasks, and our post on generative engine optimization explains the AI search side.

How do you start using an SEO AI agent safely?

  1. Pick one narrow job. For example, a weekly Search Console check, internal link suggestions for new posts, or an audit of one page template.
  2. Connect real data. Use an API or an MCP connection to your crawl, Search Console and rank data, so the agent does not guess.
  3. Start read-only. Let it analyze and recommend before it has permission to change anything.
  4. Require evidence. Ask it to quote the page, query or row behind every finding, and to say what it could not check.
  5. Separate planning from writing to production. Use a branch, a preview or a staging site for any edit.
  6. Add approval gates. A person approves the brief, the draft and the publish step, and any redirect, deletion or index change.
  7. Protect secrets and personal data. Do not give an agent credentials or client data it does not need.
  8. Log and measure. Keep a record of prompts, actions and changes, and compare results with a baseline period before the change.

Sample prompts for a first agent task

These examples show the style: specific, evidence-based and bounded. Replace the brackets.

  • Technical review: "Review this crawl export and the listed URLs. For each possible issue, quote the row that supports it, say whether it is confirmed or a hypothesis, and tell me how to reproduce it. Do not infer site-wide problems from one URL."
  • Refresh list: "Using this Search Console export, list pages whose clicks fell over the last 90 days against the previous 90. For each, show the numbers and suggest one check. Do not suggest content changes without data."
  • Internal links: "Here is a topic map and the text of a new post. Suggest up to five internal links, with the sentence for each and the reason. Do not link to redirecting URLs."
  • Brief: "Compare these five competing pages with our draft. List reader questions the sources answer and our draft does not. For each gap, say whether it belongs on this page or elsewhere, and flag claims that need a source."

Worked example: a weekly refresh review

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a site with 200 articles and one person who handles SEO part time. The team builds a small agent job that runs each Monday.

The agent pulls Search Console data through an approved connection, finds pages whose clicks fell by a set amount against the previous period, and lists the 10 largest drops with the numbers. For each page it fetches the current top results for the main query, notes headings the leaders cover that the page does not, and drafts a one-paragraph note. It does not edit anything.

The SEO lead reads the list, checks two or three suspect causes by hand, such as a lost snippet or a seasonal drop, and picks three pages to update. Writers update them with new sources and dates. The team records each change, and after 8 weeks compares clicks for updated pages with a similar set of pages it left alone. If updated pages do not do better, it changes the method. The agent saved the time spent on collecting data. The judgment stayed with people.

Should you build a custom agent or use a product?

You can do either, and the choice depends on your team. Semrush and Ahrefs both publish guides that show how to connect an AI assistant to their data, through an API or an MCP connection, and to build a simple agent for a task such as keyword clustering and a content brief. Ahrefs describes a multi-step prompt that does this inside one of its tools. A custom build gives you control over data, steps and approvals, and it needs someone who can test and maintain it. A product is faster to start and shows its limits only when you test it. We found no independent data on cost or accuracy for either route, so run the same small job on both for two weeks and compare the findings that a person confirms.

A 30-day plan for your first agent job

  1. Week 1: choose the job, write the steps and the acceptance test, and record a baseline.
  2. Week 2: connect the data read-only and run the job in shadow mode next to a person doing it today.
  3. Week 3: compare outputs, count confirmed and wrong findings and fix the prompt or the data.
  4. Week 4: decide whether to keep it, widen it or stop, and write down why.

How do you choose an SEO AI agent or tool?

Ask five questions of any product.

  • What can it see? Does it read your pages, crawl, Search Console and analytics, or only text you paste in?
  • What can it do? Does it only advise and draft, or can it change your live site?
  • Does it show evidence? Can it cite the page, query or row behind each finding?
  • What controls exist? Is there approval before publishing, changing metadata or editing canonical links, and a log of actions?
  • How will you measure it? Compare results with real search data, not with the tool's confidence.

Ahrefs and Semrush both publish guides to building agents on their data. We do not recommend a product. Test with one workflow and your own data, and avoid long contracts before you see results.

How do you measure whether an agent helped?

Measure the work and the outcome separately.

  • Work measures: hours saved on the task, number of findings that were confirmed, number that were wrong or invented, and time from finding to fix. Count wrong findings. A tool that is fast and often wrong costs time at the review step.
  • Outcome measures: impressions, clicks, indexed pages, conversions and, for AI search, mentions and citations across a fixed prompt list. Compare updated pages with similar pages you left alone, over the same period.
  • Baseline first. Record the numbers for 4 to 8 weeks before the agent runs. Search results move for many reasons, such as seasons, updates and competitors, so a change is a sign to investigate, not proof of cause.
  • One change at a time. If you start two agent jobs together, you cannot tell which one mattered.

What should an agent log?

A log protects you when something goes wrong, and it lets you improve the job. Keep the prompt and the data version the agent used, the tools it called, the findings with the evidence for each, any change it proposed, who approved or rejected it, and the final result. Store the log where the whole team can read it. If an agent ever edits your site, add the exact change, a before and after copy and a way to roll it back.

Are SEO AI agents useful for small businesses?

They can be, for a small set of jobs. A small business rarely has time for weekly audits, refresh checks or reporting. A narrow agent job that pulls Search Console data once a week and lists the five biggest changes can give an owner a short, useful brief. The risks are the same as for large firms: invented data, unchecked edits and wasted spend. Start with a read-only job, check the first few outputs by hand, and avoid tools that ask for broad access to your site or accounts. If you do not have the time to review the output, an agent will not save you effort, because the review is where the value lies.

Do SEO AI agents replace SEO specialists?

Not on the evidence we found. Agents take over data collection and first drafts. People still set strategy, judge brand fit, check facts, earn mentions and decide what to publish. Vendors who write guides on agents say the same: build human approval into the process. For a small team, an agent may free several hours a week for that work.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Asking an agent to "improve our SEO." The goal has no bounds. Give it a narrow outcome.
  • No real data. The agent will guess.
  • Giving write access too early. Start read-only.
  • Publishing at volume. Scaled content abuse is a spam policy.
  • Trusting the numbers it states. Check every figure against the source.
  • Automating everything at once. Build one workflow, then the next.
  • No baseline. You cannot tell if it helped.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells search services and builds AI-assisted workflows with people reviewing what matters. Nothing here is paid placement, and we do not endorse any product named. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. You can read about our AI workflow automation or get your free diagnostic.

One more point is about expectations. An agent will not make a weak site strong. It speeds up work that a good process already defines. If your goals, data and approvals are unclear, an agent will produce unclear work faster, so fix the process first, and use the agent to remove the repeat effort.

Final thoughts

SEO AI agents are useful for bounded work on real data: research, audits, link suggestions, monitoring and reporting. They are risky when they guess, publish at scale or act without approval. Start with one narrow task, keep a person at the gates, require evidence and measure against a baseline.

title: AI Visibility Score: What It Measures and How to Calculate One
content:
An AI visibility score is a single number, usually from 0 to 100, that a tool builds from how often AI answers name your brand, link to your site and place you ahead of competitors. There is no standard formula. Each tool picks its own inputs and weights, so a score of 40 from one tool is not the same as a 40 from another. The useful way to read a score is as a trend from one tool, with the parts shown separately and an honest margin for noise.

This guide explains what the score measures, shows the formulas that several tools publish, and applies two of them to the same sample data so you can see how the numbers differ. It also covers how to calculate your own, what a "good" score means, and how to report it. We cite only pages we could read at the publisher, and we state when a source is a vendor's own documentation.

What is an AI visibility score?

An AI visibility score is a composite metric. It condenses several counts from a fixed set of AI answers into one figure. The counts come from running a list of buyer questions through tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews, then recording what each answer says. The goal is to show, in one number, whether AI tools include your brand when buyers ask about your category.

You may also see the phrases "AI brand visibility score" and "AI visibility". They mean the same idea. Our guide to checking if AI tools mention your brand shows how to run the underlying test by hand.

What goes into an AI visibility score?

Most tools use some mix of the following parts. The names differ, but the ideas are alike.

PartWhat it measuresSimple formula
Mention rateHow often an answer names your brandAnswers that name you divided by all answers
Citation rateHow often an answer links to your site as a sourceAnswers that cite your domain divided by all answers
Prompt coverageHow many different questions name you at least oncePrompts where you appear divided by prompts asked
PositionHow early you are named in an answer that lists brandsOften 1 for first, 1/2 for second, 1/3 for third
Share of voiceYour mentions compared with all brand mentions in your setYour mentions divided by mentions of you and your competitors
SentimentHow the answer describes youA positive, neutral or negative label

A mention and a citation are different. An answer can name you without a link, or link to your page without naming you. Keep them in separate columns. They need different fixes.

How do different tools calculate it?

Several vendors publish their formulas. Reading them shows that "AI visibility score" is a label, not a shared standard. The table uses each vendor's own documentation.

ToolFormula, as publishedNotes
RankRaft100 × (0.45 × mention rate + 0.35 × citation rate + 0.20 × prompt coverage)Leaves position out on purpose. Shows a 95% margin.
AnswerixAI100 × (0.6 × mention rate + 0.25 × citation rate + 0.15 × position factor)Scales the position factor down when few answers name you.
cloro100 × (0.6 × mention rate + 0.25 × citation rate + 0.15 × position factor)Same weights as AnswerixAI. Position is the mean of 1 divided by position.
BugViso0.35 × visibility + 0.20 × share of voice + 0.20 × position + 0.15 × citations + 0.10 × sentimentCounts unbranded prompts only, and averages engines equally.
MentionOwlNot publishedIts guide says you cannot recompute the headline number.

Am I Cited's guide describes a "typical" weighting of about 25% for mention frequency, 25% for citation rate, 20% for position, 15% for query coverage and 15% for share of voice, and says there is no industry-standard formula. Verticality makes the same point: a score means something only once you know its questions, engines, time window and denominator.

Worked example: one set of answers, different scores

This example uses the sample data in RankRaft's documentation. It shows 10 prompts run across 3 engines in a week, which gives 210 answers. You are named in 63 answers, cited in 21 answers, and named at least once for 6 of the 10 prompts. The arithmetic below is ours.

  • Mention rate: 63 divided by 210 is 30%.
  • Citation rate: 21 divided by 210 is 10%.
  • Prompt coverage: 6 divided by 10 is 60%.

Now apply two published formulas.

  • RankRaft: 100 × (0.45 × 0.30 + 0.35 × 0.10 + 0.20 × 0.60) = 100 × (0.135 + 0.035 + 0.12) = 29.
  • AnswerixAI: this formula needs a position factor, which the sample does not give. We assume that on average you are named at position 2, so the raw factor is 0.5. AnswerixAI scales it by mentions divided by mentions plus 20, which is 63 divided by 83, or 0.76, so the factor becomes about 0.38. The score is 100 × (0.6 × 0.30 + 0.25 × 0.10 + 0.15 × 0.38) = 100 × (0.18 + 0.025 + 0.057), which is about 26.

The same 210 answers give a mention rate of 30%, a score of 29 from one tool and about 26 from another. Neither is wrong. They weight the parts differently, and the second uses a position input we assumed. This is why you should never compare a score from one tool with a score from another.

How noisy is the score?

Answers vary from run to run. SparkToro had 600 volunteers run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google's AI features 2,961 times, and found less than a 1 in 100 chance of getting the same list of brands twice for the same prompt. So a score from one run is a snapshot.

RankRaft shows the effect in its own formula. It gives a 95% margin of 100 × 1.96 × the square root of p(1 − p) divided by n, where p is the mention rate and n is the number of answers. With a 30% mention rate and 210 answers, that is about plus or minus 6 points, by our arithmetic. The formula treats every answer as independent, so the true uncertainty may be larger, since answers to the same prompt are related. The lesson is that small changes in a score may be noise. Use more prompts, repeat runs and read trends over weeks.

Why do two honest tools show different scores?

  • Different weights. One tool may weight mentions at 60% and another at 45%.
  • Different prompts. A prompt set built from your sales calls gives a different result from a generic set.
  • Branded prompts. A question that names you is answered with your name almost every time. BugViso reports that all 120 branded answers in its data named the brand, and so it counts unbranded prompts only.
  • Different engines. A tool that tracks two engines gives a different number from one that tracks five.
  • Different counting rules. Some tools leave out failed or empty answers. RankRaft leaves out runs where Google shows no AI Overview, instead of counting them as misses.
  • Different timing. Weekly, daily and one-off checks smooth noise in different ways.

Does the score include Google AI Overviews?

Check the tool's documentation, because tools differ. Google shows an AI Overview for only some searches, so a score that counts every run as a miss when no overview appears will look lower than one that leaves those runs out. RankRaft, for example, says it counts only answers that were actually shown, and leaves out a run where Google shows no AI Overview, instead of scoring it as "not mentioned". Some tools do not track Google's AI features at all, and some also blend ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Claude with equal or unequal weights. When you compare periods, make sure the engine list, the prompt list and these counting rules did not change. For Google's own data, use the Generative AI performance report in Search Console, which shows impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode for your site.

How do you calculate your own AI visibility score?

  1. Write 10 to 15 buyer questions in your customers' words, mostly without your brand name.
  2. Pick your engines and run each prompt three times in each, in a fresh session. Save the full answers.
  3. Record, for each answer, whether you are named, whether your site is cited, who else is named and in what order.
  4. Count the parts. Mention rate, citation rate and prompt coverage are easy to compute in a spreadsheet. Add share of voice against three to five named competitors.
  5. Report the parts first. Show each number with its denominator, for example "named in 63 of 210 answers".
  6. Only then combine them, if you must have one number. Publish the weights, keep them fixed and note the date and the prompt set.

A simple sheet is enough. Our guide to AI brand visibility tools compares software that does this at scale.

What is a good AI visibility score?

We found no reliable public benchmark. A score depends on the prompts, engines and formula, so a "good" number for one tool says nothing about another. Share of voice also depends on how many brands the tools name in your market. If the tools name three brands per answer, a share near 33% is average. If they name 15, a share near 7% is average.

So judge yourself in three ways. Compare with the competitors in your own test, with the same tool and prompts. Compare with your own baseline over time. And look at the parts, because a rising mention rate with a flat citation rate tells a different story from the reverse. Be wary of any vendor that offers a grade such as "good" or "excellent" without showing its method.

What is AI brand monitoring?

AI brand monitoring is the ongoing version of this test. Software runs your prompts on a schedule, stores each answer and shows the trend, often with alerts when something changes, such as a new competitor or a wrong fact. It is useful when your prompt list or your markets outgrow a spreadsheet. A tool still needs a person to act on what it finds. Test any tool against a hand baseline before you rely on it.

How do you improve a low score?

Read the parts and fix the weakest one.

If this is lowIt may meanStart with
Mention rateAI tools do not know you, or rarely pick youClear facts, answer-first pages and honest mentions on other sites
Citation rateYour pages are not used as sourcesCrawler access, readable HTML, sourced answers. See how to rank in AI Overviews.
Prompt coverageYou appear for few questionsPages for the questions you miss, built from sales calls
Share of voiceCompetitors are named far more oftenStudy the sources the answers cite, and earn a place on them
SentimentThe description is old or negativeFix the pages and profiles the answers use

Our guide to generative engine optimization explains the method in more detail.

One more rule helps. Decide in advance what counts as a mention, and write it down. A brand name inside a longer word should not count, a repeated mention inside one answer should count once, and a cited link that is not named in the text is a citation, not a mention. Tools that publish their counting rules, such as AnswerixAI and cloro, say that matching is by whole word and that links are removed before the text count. A clear rule keeps the numbers the same from one month to the next, even when different people run the test.

How should you report it to leadership?

Keep the report short and honest. Show the three or four parts with their denominators, the trend over at least three periods, the margin or the number of runs, and the list of actions taken. Say which tool and prompt set you used. Avoid a single headline number without the parts behind it, and never compare it with a score from another tool. Add the link to business results, such as demo requests from pages you updated, when you can measure them.

What does a simple scoring sheet look like?

You do not need software to start. This layout gives you every part of the score. The three rows are made up to show the format.

Prompt IDEngineRunNamedCitedOrder namedCompetitors named
P-03ChatGPT1YesNo3 of 5A, B, C, D
P-03ChatGPT2NoNononeA, B, E
P-03Perplexity1YesYes1 of 4A, C, F

From this sheet you can count mention rate, citation rate, prompt coverage and share of voice with simple formulas. Add a date and the exact prompt text in another tab. Keep the sheet after every test. In six months, the history is more useful than any single score.

How does the score differ for different businesses?

  • B2B software: Comparison and "best for" questions drive shortlists, so include them. Citations from review sites and your own comparison pages matter.
  • Local and service firms: Include questions with a city name. Answers often depend on listings and reviews, so check those sources.
  • Online stores: Include product and "is it worth it" questions. Product data and reviews on other sites matter.
  • Publishers and educators: Citation rate may matter more than mention rate, since the aim is to be the source.

In every case, build the prompt set from real buyer questions. A score based on questions your buyers never ask tells you nothing.

What questions will leaders ask about the score?

Be ready for these three. "Is it going up?" Show the trend, the number of runs and the margin. "Why is a competitor higher?" Show the source map: which sites the answers cite for them and not for you. "What did we do about it?" Show the list of fixes, with dates and the pages changed. If you cannot answer the third question, the score is a dashboard and not a program.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Trusting one number. Keep mentions, citations and share of voice separate.
  • Comparing tools. Scores from different formulas are not the same measure.
  • Counting branded prompts. They inflate the result.
  • Running each prompt once. The same prompt gives different answers.
  • Ignoring the margin. A move of a few points can be noise.
  • Changing prompts between periods. You can no longer compare.
  • Chasing the score. The goal is accurate, useful presence, not a number.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab sells search and AI search services. We do not sell an AI visibility score or a tracking tool, and nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. Our free diagnostic reports the parts with their denominators. You can get your free diagnostic or read about our SEO and AI search audit.

Final thoughts

An AI visibility score is a summary, not a measurement of the truth. Read the parts, know the formula, repeat the runs and watch the trend. Use the score to decide what to fix next, and judge the work by accurate answers and by the leads that follow.

title: Generative Engine Optimization Agency: How to Choose One
content:
A generative engine optimization agency helps your brand get found, understood and cited by AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews. To choose a good one, look for a method you can inspect: a prompt list you approve, a baseline measured before work starts, named changes, honest limits and clear ownership of your data. Walk away from any firm that guarantees citations or rankings, because no one controls AI answers.

This guide explains what these agencies do, whether you need one, twelve questions to ask with good and poor answers, red flags, how to compare proposals and what the cost depends on. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher. Reinforce Lab is one of the agencies you may compare, so we say at the end how to test us the same way.

What does a generative engine optimization agency do?

Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is work that improves how often and how accurately AI tools name your brand and cite your pages. Our guide to generative engine optimization explains the method. An agency usually sells some mix of these services:

  • A baseline audit. A fixed list of buyer questions run through several AI tools, with mentions, citations, descriptions and competitors recorded. Our AI search audit guide covers the method.
  • Technical fixes. Crawler access, indexing, rendering, structured data and site facts.
  • Content work. Answer-first pages, comparison pages, updates and sourced evidence.
  • Off-site work. Profiles, reviews, digital PR and presence on the sites the AI answers cite.
  • Measurement. Repeated prompt tests, Search Console and Bing reports, and AI referral traffic in analytics.

The names vary. Some firms say GEO, others AEO, LLM SEO or AI SEO. Google says that from its point of view, optimizing for generative AI search is still SEO, and it advises care with third-party "AEO" or "GEO" advice. So judge the work, not the label.

Do you need an agency at all?

Not always. The options are in-house, an agency or a tool. The table shows when each tends to fit.

OptionFits whenWatch for
In-houseYou have an SEO lead, a writer and developer timeNobody owns off-site work or measurement
AgencyYou lack time or skills, need a plan, or need outreach and technical fixesOverlap with your SEO provider, vague scope
Tool onlyYou want monitoring and have people to act on itA dashboard that nobody acts on. See our guide to AI brand visibility tools.

Google's own advice on hiring an SEO applies here too. It says some sites do not need a hire, and it warns that no one can guarantee a number one ranking on Google, and to beware of firms that claim a special relationship with Google or a "priority submit".

What does the evidence say about GEO agencies?

Independent evidence is thin, and we found none on average fees. Four sources help you set expectations.

  • Agency case studies are often weak. OpenServed analyzed 142 GEO case studies published by 68 agencies. It found that 27% reported no AI metric, only 13% tied AI search to leads or revenue, and only 5 of 142 mentioned the prompts they tracked. None of the 142 stated a budget. The median result was measured over six months, and only 15% within three months. This is one directory's review of agency-published material, classified by its own method, so treat the figures as a rough picture.
  • No one can promise a result. Google says no one can guarantee a number one ranking, and Google says that no third-party tool has access to its internal ranking or AI systems.
  • Answers change. SparkToro had 600 volunteers run 12 prompts through ChatGPT, Claude and Google's AI features 2,961 times. There was less than a 1 in 100 chance of the same list of brands twice. A good agency reports a rate across many runs, not a rank.
  • Some measurement is free. Google's Search Console has a Generative AI performance report for AI Overviews and AI Mode impressions, and Bing Webmaster Tools has an AI Performance report for citations in Copilot. A good agency uses both in its baseline.

Twelve questions to ask a GEO agency

Ask every candidate the same questions and compare the answers in writing. The table shows what a good answer and a poor answer sound like.

QuestionA good answerA poor answer
1. How do you choose the prompts?From your sales calls, tickets and search data, agreed with you, then frozen"We use our standard set", or most prompts contain your brand name
2. What is our baseline today, by engine?A citation map built before the proposal, per question and per engineOne visibility score with no questions behind it
3. How do you measure, and how often?Repeated runs, mentions and citations reported separately, with the numerator and denominatorOne screenshot, or "we monitor continuously" with no method
4. What will you change on our site?A written list by item, with an approval path"We will optimize your content for AI"
5. How do you handle AI crawlers?Names each bot and separates search from training"Block or allow all AI bots"
6. Which sources outside our site will you work on?A named list of sites the answers already cite for your questions"We will publish more blog posts"
7. Who writes and who checks?Named people, human review, your approval before publishingVolume promises, unnamed writers, AI-only drafts
8. How do you connect citations to leads?Tagged AI referrals, analytics and CRM records"Citations are the KPI"
9. What can you not promise?Placement in any AI answerGuaranteed citations or "position 1 in ChatGPT"
10. Show one case: what changed and when?Dated changes, a before and after per question, caveats about other changesA percentage with no baseline or dates
11. What do we own if we stop?The prompt list, reports, content and tracking data, in usable formatsEverything lives in their tool
12. When would you tell us not to buy?A real list, such as no buyer use of AI for your category or basic site problemsThey can never say no

What are the red flags?

  • A guarantee of citations, rankings or traffic.
  • No baseline before the proposal.
  • Prompts that the agency chose and will not show, or that contain your brand name.
  • One AI tool only, or one screenshot as proof.
  • Reports that stop at mentions or a single score.
  • A price with no deliverables.
  • A claim of a special relationship with Google or any AI company.
  • Work only on your own site, with nothing on the sources the answers use.
  • A contract that locks your data and content in their platform.
  • Unreviewed AI-written content, especially in health, finance and legal fields.

Google adds a point worth remembering: you are responsible for what companies you hire do on your site. A deceptive tactic is your problem as well as theirs.

How much does a generative engine optimization agency cost?

We found no independent data on typical fees. Published ranges come from agencies' own pages and guides, and they disagree. OpenServed notes that price ranges in other guides are unsourced and conflict, and that none of the 142 case studies it reviewed states a budget. Instead of comparing monthly numbers, compare what you receive.

These things move a price:

  • How many AI tools and markets are tracked.
  • How many prompts are tested, and how often.
  • How much content is written, and by whom.
  • How much technical work your site needs.
  • Whether outreach and digital PR are included.
  • Whether tracking tool fees and CRM reporting are in scope.
  • How much of your team's time the work needs, for approvals and input.

GEO is usually sold in three ways: a one-time audit, a project such as a rebuild of key pages, or a monthly retainer. A fixed audit first is often the safest start. It gives you a baseline and a plan at a known cost, and you can use it to judge a longer program.

What should the first 90 days look like?

A sensible first quarter has a clear order. This is our recommendation, not a standard. Ask any agency to show its own version in writing.

PeriodWorkWhat you should receive
Weeks 1 to 2Agree the prompt list, competitors and success numbers. Run the baseline. Check crawler access and rendering.The prompt list, raw answers, a source map and a technical check
Weeks 3 to 6Fix access, facts and the few pages closest to buying questions. Claim and correct key profiles.A change log with dates and reasons
Weeks 7 to 10Publish or refresh answer-first pages with sourced evidence. Start outreach to the sources the answers cite.The pages, a list of sites approached and the status of each
Weeks 11 to 13Repeat the same prompt test and compare with the baseline. Review Search Console and Bing reports.A report that separates mentions from citations and says what else changed

If an agency cannot describe its first 90 days in this much detail, it probably does not have a repeatable method.

Should one firm run both your SEO and your GEO?

It often helps, because the two share a base. Access, indexing, content quality and links serve both, and a plan that treats them separately can send two teams to edit the same pages. If another agency runs your SEO, ask each firm to state who owns which pages and who approves changes. Be careful with any firm that sells GEO as a separate product and ignores SEO, or that asks you to drop a provider that is doing sound work. Google's own view is that its AI features rely on its core Search systems, so weak SEO tends to limit GEO.

How do you compare proposals?

Send every candidate the same request: a sample report, a case study with dates, a first-month plan, a list of owners and a proposed scope. Then score each on the same table.

CriterionAsk forWhat to check
MethodSample prompts, raw answers, citationsCan you inspect the scoring?
FitYour priority questions and competitorsDo the prompts reflect real buying decisions?
DeliveryOwners, approvals, access, change logCan changes ship and be checked?
ProofA dated case with a baselineAre limits and other changes stated?
TermsScope, exclusions, notice period, handoverDoes the fee match the work, and do you own the output?

Add the hours your own team will spend. A cheaper retainer that needs several hours a week from your marketing lead can cost more than a dearer one that runs on a short weekly review.

Worked example: a software company compares three proposals

This is an illustration, not a client case. Imagine a 40-person software company that sells to logistics teams. It asks three agencies for the same packet. Agency A sends a visibility score and a promise of top citations in 90 days. Agency B sends a baseline of 15 prompts it chose, several containing the company's name. Agency C asks for the company's sales call notes, builds 14 prompts from them with the company, and sends a baseline of 126 answers across three tools, with a map of the sites the answers cite and a list of eight site changes.

The company drops Agency A for guaranteeing a result and sending no method. It drops B because the prompts flatter the brand. It starts a fixed-price audit with C, owns the prompt list and the data, and decides on a retainer after reading the results. The choice did not depend on price. It depended on what could be inspected.

Generative engine optimization agencies for SaaS and B2B

If you sell software or B2B services, ask for experience with long buying cycles and comparison pages, since AI tools often answer "X vs Y" and "best tools for Z" questions. Ask which review sites and community threads the answers cite in your category, and how the agency will help you appear on them honestly. Our SaaS SEO guide covers the search side of this work, and our page on B2B SaaS explains how we work with software firms.

GEO consultant or agency?

A consultant is a good fit when you need a plan and an expert's review, and you have people to do the work. An agency fits when you also need the work done. In either case, ask the same twelve questions, and check who does the hands-on work.

How long does it take to see results?

Access and fact fixes can change retrieval-based answers within weeks. OpenAI says a robots.txt change can take about 24 hours to apply for ChatGPT search. Content and off-site work take longer. OpenServed found a median measurement period of six months in published case studies, but those are agency-chosen examples. Ask what the agency will count at day 30, day 90 and month six, and treat any promise of a date for citations as a red flag.

What should you own when the work ends?

Get these in writing: the prompt list, the baseline, access to or exports from the tracking tool, AI referral traffic tagged in your own analytics, and the pages and content created for you. Ask about the notice period and what happens to your data if you leave.

Which free checks can you run to test an agency's claims?

You can check much of what an agency tells you without paying for a tool. Open your Search Console and read the Generative AI performance report, which shows impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode. Open Bing Webmaster Tools and read its AI Performance report for citations in Copilot. Run the agency's sample prompts yourself, three times in each tool, and compare your results with its screenshots. Check your robots.txt and your firewall for the bots it says it will manage. Ask for the prompt list behind any case study, and run those prompts today. If the agency says a page now ranks or is cited, check that it still does. An agency with a sound method will welcome these checks.

How do you test Reinforce Lab the same way?

Reinforce Lab is an agency, so you should apply this guide to us. Our generative engine optimization service starts with a baseline, and our SEO and AI search audit works like the audit above. We will show you a sample report, the method and the limits. We do not guarantee citations. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. You can get your free diagnostic and judge it by the questions above.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Choosing on price alone. A low fee for vague work can cost more than a clear scope.
  • Letting the agency choose the prompts alone. You know your buyers.
  • Accepting a score as proof. Ask for the answers behind it.
  • Paying a large retainer before a baseline exists.
  • Ignoring overlap with your SEO provider. Agree who does what.
  • Forgetting approvals. The fee runs on while drafts wait.

Final thoughts

The best generative engine optimization agency for you is the one whose method you can inspect. Ask for a baseline, a prompt list you approve, named changes, honest limits and clear ownership. Start with a fixed audit, compare proposals on deliverables and decide on a longer program after you have read the results.

title: How to Build an AI Marketing Agent System: Architecture and Human Review
content:
To build an AI marketing agent system, start with one narrow task and a written list of its steps. Connect only the data and tools that task needs, add checks between the steps, and put a named person at every gate where a mistake would reach a customer or cost money. Build it as a fixed workflow first, and use a more autonomous agent only where the path cannot be known in advance. Measure the results and the quality of your controls, then widen the scope.

This guide explains the parts of such a system, a six-layer architecture, how workflows and agents differ, how to design human review, and a nine-step build plan. It also covers readiness data, permissions, measurement and a worked example. We cite only sources we could read at the publisher, and we label practitioners' frameworks as such, since there is no industry standard for this architecture.

What is an AI marketing agent system?

An AI marketing system is a set of connected parts that do marketing work with the help of language models: research, briefs, drafts, lead scoring, routing, campaign checks and reports. The parts share data, follow written rules and report to people. It differs from a single AI tool because it joins steps across your CRM, content system, email platform, analytics and ad accounts. Some call this approach AI growth marketing: search, content and automation working as one engine, with people reviewing what matters. At Reinforce Lab we use the term AI Growth Systems for the same idea, and our guide to what an AI growth system is explains it.

What is agentic marketing, and what can AI agents do in marketing?

Agentic marketing means marketing work that AI agents carry out in part: they pursue a goal, choose steps and use tools, inside limits that people set. The term has no official definition, so vendors use it in different ways. We use it for the system this guide describes.

An AI marketing agent is software that uses a language model to work toward a marketing goal. For example, it can read a report, draft an email or update a field in your CRM. It is different from a chat assistant, because it takes actions in your tools and not only answers questions.

Which jobs suit an AI agent for marketing?

  • Preparing weekly reports and flagging odd changes in the numbers.
  • Researching a topic or a competitor and writing a summary with sources.
  • Scoring and routing new leads by rules you write down.
  • Drafting briefs, outlines and first drafts for a person to edit.
  • Checking campaign setup, tags and links before launch.
  • Drafting personalized outreach for a person to review, using fields from your CRM.
  • Summarizing campaign performance and suggesting what to test next.

Start with bounded, repeatable, measurable tasks. Keep customer-facing content, budgets and claims behind a person's approval. The nine-step plan below shows how.

How do you use an AI agent for marketing?

Pick one task. Write the steps as you do them today. Give the agent only the tools and data that task needs. Run it in read-only mode first, check every output, and widen its permissions only after it has been right for weeks.

Workflows or agents: what should you build?

Anthropic, which publishes guidance on building agents, draws a clear line. Workflows are systems where language models and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. Agents are systems where the model dynamically directs its own process and tool use. Its advice is to find the simplest solution possible and to increase complexity only when needed, which may mean not building an agentic system at all. Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance. Workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks, and agents suit open-ended problems where you cannot predict the number of steps. Anthropic also warns that agents' autonomy means higher costs and the potential for errors to build up from step to step, and recommends extensive testing in sandboxes with guardrails.

For marketing, that means most tasks should be workflows: a fixed chain of steps, with checks and a gate. Use an agent where a task is open-ended, such as researching a market across many sources, and keep it inside tight limits.

Five patterns and where they fit marketing

Anthropic describes patterns that you can combine. The table maps them to marketing jobs. The marketing examples are ours, except where Anthropic names them.

PatternWhat it doesMarketing example
Prompt chainingSplits a task into fixed steps, each using the last output, with checks between themOutline, check the outline against rules, then write the draft. Anthropic also names writing marketing copy and then translating it.
RoutingClassifies an input and sends it to a specialized next stepSort inbound inquiries into sales, support and partnership paths
Orchestrator and workersA central model breaks down a task, delegates and combines the resultsResearch a topic across several sources and merge the findings
Evaluator and optimizerOne model generates and another critiques, in a loopDraft a brief, score it against a rubric, revise
Autonomous agentThe model plans and uses tools in a loop, pausing for human inputAn open-ended research task with stop conditions and approval points

A six-layer architecture

Practitioners describe the layers in different ways. The version below combines the common parts. Skip a layer and the system becomes useless or risky.

LayerJobTypical parts
1. Data and identityHolds the facts the system may read, and who each person or account is across channelsCRM, warehouse, analytics, consent records
2. KnowledgeHolds approved brand rules, offers, product facts and claims for retrievalA knowledge base, approved-claims library, style guide
3. ToolsLets the system read and act: create a draft, update a record, pause a campaignAPIs, connectors, MCP servers for CMS, CRM, email, ads, analytics
4. OrchestrationRuns the steps in order, handles retries and handoffs between steps and peopleWorkflow code, automation platforms, step limits
5. Controls and human approvalEnforces permissions, spend caps, privacy rules, checks and approvalsReview queues, code checks, scoped access
6. Observability and measurementRecords what happened and whether it workedRun logs, alerts, evaluation sets, dashboards

One principle holds across the sources we read: your CRM and warehouse stay the systems of record. If identity is messy, every agent repeats the mess faster. Keep decisions and actions separate. An agent or rule proposes a change with a reason, and the tool that owns the setting carries it out after an approval that matches the risk, with a log of who approved it.

What technical stack do you need to build an AI marketing agent?

You do not need a big stack to start. An autonomous AI marketing agent usually has the same few parts, whether you build it or buy it:

PartWhat it doesKeep it simple by
ModelReads the task and writes or decides.Starting with one model and one task.
OrchestrationRuns the steps in order, calls tools and handles retries.Using a workflow tool before writing your own code.
Tools and connectionsLets the agent read your CRM, ad account, analytics and CMS.Giving read access first and write access later.
Knowledge storeHolds brand rules, approved facts and past results.Starting with a short, approved document set.
Review queueSends drafts and actions to a person for approval.Requiring approval for anything that goes public or spends money.
Logs and measuresRecords what the agent did and what happened next.Logging every action from day one.

This matches the six layers above. The stack is the set of tools you choose for each layer. Pick the smallest set that does one job well, then add parts when a real need appears.

How should human review work?

Design review before you build the agent. Set each gate by what a mistake would cost, not by how confident the model sounds, because models are often wrong in fluent prose. One practitioner framework sorts actions into three levels, which we find useful:

LevelMarketing actions
Always approvePublished content, paid campaign launches, budget changes, email sends, price or results claims, anything that uses customer data
Spot-check a sampleInternal drafts, keyword clusters, competitor summaries
Usually safe to automateFormatting, tagging, scheduling approved drafts, routine report generation

A related model uses four autonomy bands: human-only, AI-assisted drafting, approval-gated automation and bounded autonomous execution. Every workflow sits in exactly one band, and the band sets its permissions, approvals and monitoring. Keep most work at the draft-only band longer than feels necessary.

Make the reviewer real. A reviewer needs to understand the output, to actually read it, and to have the authority to change or stop it. A person clicking "approve" on a queue of forty items they cannot judge is a logged rubber stamp, not oversight. Limit the queue size, show the evidence next to each item and track how often reviewers change or reject output. A rate near zero may mean the review is not working.

What goes in the knowledge layer?

The knowledge layer is what stops the system from improvising. It holds the approved information that drafts must draw on, kept in one place and owned by a named person. A useful starting set has six parts:

  • Product and service facts: what you sell, who it is for, prices or price ranges, limits and what is not included.
  • An approved-claims library: statements you may make, each with its source and date, and a list of claims you may not make.
  • Brand voice rules: tone, words to use and avoid, and two or three examples of writing you like.
  • Required disclosures: legal notices, affiliate or sponsorship statements, and regulated wording.
  • Customer and market facts: your ideal customer profile, segments and objections, without personal data.
  • Past results: a few strong examples and the reasons they worked, so the system learns from your own record.

Review this layer on a set schedule, and whenever a price, offer or rule changes. If the knowledge is old, every draft will be old as well. Keep it separate from the prompts, so a person can update a fact without editing code, and so the system can show which source each statement came from.

A nine-step build plan

  1. Pick one narrow task. Content briefs, lead scoring or report drafts work. "Run marketing" does not. Check first whether the task should be automated at all.
  2. List the steps in plain words. A fixed list is a chain. Branches mean routing.
  3. Connect only the tools the task needs. Read access comes first. Publishing, sending and budget changes come last.
  4. Load the grounding material. Brand rules, product facts, an approved-claims library, required disclosures and a few past examples.
  5. Put checks between steps. Length limits, banned claims, disclosures, broken links and suppression lists belong in code, where a check is cheap and certain. A prompt cannot guarantee them.
  6. Add an evaluator pass if you can write the rubric. If you cannot, skip it.
  7. Gate anything public or paid behind a person.
  8. Log every run. Inputs, sources with dates, tool calls, outputs, reviewer decisions, cost and time.
  9. Measure, then widen the scope. Test in a sandbox or a small pilot first, with normal and odd inputs, and add autonomy one level at a time.

How do you set permissions and protect data?

Give each agent only the applications, fields and actions its task needs. Prefer read-only, draft-only or sandbox access, and remove tool functions the agent does not need, instead of trusting it to skip them. Run the agent under its own identity rather than someone's personal login, so each action can be scoped, audited and revoked. Treat reading analytics, publishing, reading CRM records, updating a lead, sending email and moving budget as separate permissions.

Agents that read web pages or files can be steered by instructions hidden in that content, a risk called prompt injection. Security practitioners recommend minimizing the tools an agent can call, granting the least permissions each tool needs, requiring human approval for high-impact actions and enforcing authorization in downstream systems instead of trusting the model. Keep personal data out of tools without a data-handling agreement, and check consent and local law before you use customer data in a new way.

How do agents handle context, memory and failure?

A system that runs for many steps needs rules for what it knows, when it must stop and what happens when something breaks. Anthropic's guidance gives a useful base. It says an agent should gain "ground truth" from its environment at each step, such as tool results, to judge its progress, and that agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when they hit blockers. It also recommends stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations, to maintain control, and says the design and documentation of an agent's tools deserve as much care as its prompts. For marketing, translate that into five rules. Give each run only the context it needs, and keep long-term facts in the knowledge layer, not in a chat history. Check each tool result before the next step. Set a step limit and a spend limit. Stop and escalate when data is missing or sources conflict, and never guess. Log the failure with the inputs, so that a person can fix the cause and not only the symptom.

What does the readiness data say?

Surveys of large organizations suggest caution. They are not forecasts for a small team.

  • Gartner predicted in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, because of rising costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. It also found "agent washing," with only about 130 real agentic vendors among thousands.
  • Gartner's 2026 CMO Spend Survey of 401 marketing leaders found that 70% say their internal marketing processes are not mature enough to implement and scale AI, and only 30% report mature or fully developed AI readiness. Most were at companies with over $1 billion in revenue.
  • Gartner's 2025 marketing technology survey found average stack utilization of 49%, 29% of leaders with agents in production, and 45% of those with pilots or production agents reporting that vendor agents were not meeting expectations.

The message is to define value first, start small and keep the controls simple.

How do you measure the system?

Track two sets of measures. One shows whether the system creates value. The other shows whether the value is real and safe.

Value measuresControl measures
Time saved per task, cycle time from request to liveShare of outputs changed or rejected by reviewers
Qualified leads, conversions, revenue per messageFactual-error rate found at review
Cost per asset or per qualified leadPolicy violations and incidents
Response time to new leadsExceptions and escalations

Record a baseline for 4 to 8 weeks before you start, and compare after the pilot. Results move for many reasons, so treat a change as a sign to investigate.

Worked example: a content-to-lead system for a B2B firm

This is an illustration, not a client result. Imagine a 15-person B2B services firm that wants more qualified leads from its guides and fewer delays in follow-up. It plans one system with three connected workflows, built in this order.

First, a lead intake workflow. A form creates a CRM record, tags the source and routes the inquiry. A model reads the free-text message to label topic and urgency, and drafts a first reply from approved facts. A salesperson reviews and sends each draft. Second, a content workflow. A strategist approves a brief. The system attaches a dated source pack. A writer drafts from the brief and sources. An editor checks each claim. The system then runs checks for links, tags and consent, and creates tasks for email and sales. Third, a weekly report workflow. The system pulls Search Console, analytics and CRM numbers into a fixed template and drafts a short narrative. An analyst verifies the figures.

The team starts each workflow in shadow mode, where the AI step runs next to a person doing the task today, and compares the outputs. It tracks response time, qualified leads from the guides, reviewer changes and factual errors. After 90 days it keeps the steps with low error rates and removes the rest. Only then does it consider letting the system act without approval, and only for formatting and scheduling.

Should you build or buy?

We found no independent data on typical costs. The choice depends on your team and your data. Buying a platform suits standard jobs, such as email flows or lead routing, where the vendor has proven features. Building with an automation tool or code suits jobs that depend on your own data, rules and approvals. Many teams do both: buy the platforms and build the glue and the controls. Before you buy, audit what you own, since utilization of existing tools is often low, and ask each vendor what its agent can see, what it can change and what logs and approval controls it provides. Our AI workflow automation, marketing automation and lead generation systems pages describe how we approach these builds.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Starting with an agent. Most tasks need a workflow.
  • Skipping the data layer. Messy identity and unchecked facts spread faster with automation.
  • Giving write access too early. Start read-only and draft-only.
  • Rubber-stamp review. Make reviewers real, and track their changes.
  • Putting rules in prompts. Banned claims, disclosures and suppression lists belong in code.
  • No logs. Without records you cannot learn or investigate.
  • Many pilots, no system. One connected workflow beats five separate experiments.
  • No owner. Each workflow needs one named person who is accountable.

Our interest in this topic

Reinforce Lab builds AI Growth Systems and sells the services named above. We have an interest in this method, and nothing here is paid placement. Jamil Ahmed, who wrote this guide, is a Semrush Ambassador, and Reinforce Lab uses affiliate links for some tools. Read our FTC and affiliate disclosure. You can read about our AI Growth Systems or get your free diagnostic.

Final thoughts

A good AI marketing system is more plumbing than magic: clean data, approved knowledge, narrow tools, fixed steps, checks in code, real human review and honest measurement. Build one workflow, prove it, and widen the scope only when the record shows it works.
